### What platform is your computer?

Darwin 25.6.0 arm64 arm

### What issue are you seeing?

### Summary

Codex Desktop on macOS repeatedly fails with `server_overloaded` when executing tool-based tasks, while simple text-only prompts succeed.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Open Codex Desktop on macOS.
2. Start a new conversation.
3. Send: `Reply OK without using any tools.`
4. Codex successfully replies `OK`.
5. Send: `Run pwd using the terminal tool and report the output.`
6. Codex indicates that the command was run, but the task then fails with a model capacity error.
7. The same error also occurs when attempting to use ChatCut Desktop MCP tools.

### Actual behavior

The application displays:

`Selected model is at capacity. Please try a different model.`

Local Codex session logs repeatedly contain:

`"codex_error_info":"server_overloaded"`

This issue has occurred multiple times on November 4, 2026.

### Expected behavior

Codex should complete tool calls and return their results without repeatedly failing with a model capacity error.

### Additional findings

- Simple text-only prompts can succeed.
- The failure occurs with multiple models, including GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT-6.1 Sol.
- The failure is not specific to ChatCut MCP. The built-in terminal tool also triggers the same error.
- ChatCut Desktop MCP previously completed `get_active_project` and `list_projects` successfully.
- `list_projects` successfully returned three local projects.
- A previous session showed a network transport error, but the repeated current failures are explicitly recorded as `server_overloaded`.
- Repeated retries and switching models have not consistently resolved the problem.

### Request

Please investigate whether this is caused by backend model capacity, request routing, or tool-call continuation handling in Codex Desktop.

I can provide additional redacted logs and session identifiers through a private support channel if needed.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

### Steps to reproduce

1. Launch Codex Desktop on macOS and start a new conversation.
2. Select GPT-5.6 Sol (Medium reasoning).
3. Send: `Please reply OK without using any tools.`
4. Codex successfully responds with `OK`.
5. In the same conversation, send: `Please run pwd using the terminal tool and report the output. Do not use any MCP tools or modify files.`
6. Codex displays that `pwd` was executed, but then fails to complete the response.
7. The following error appears:

   `Selected model is at capacity. Please try a different model.`

8. Repeat with a ChatCut Desktop MCP tool such as `mcp__chatcut_desktop__get_active_project`. The same error can occur.
9. Similar failures also occurred with GPT-6.1 Sol.

### Log evidence

Local Codex session logs repeatedly show:

`"codex_error_info":"server_overloaded"`

The issue was reproduced multiple times on November 4, 2026.

### Reproducibility

Intermittent but frequent. Simple text-only prompts succeed, while tool-based tasks frequently fail.

Token usage and context-window usage were not captured. The problem can occur in a new conversation with minimal context.

### What is the expected behavior?

Codex Desktop should execute tool calls and successfully return their results without failing with a model capacity error.

For example, when asked to execute `pwd`, Codex should display the current working directory and complete the response normally.

Similarly, when invoking a registered MCP tool such as `mcp__chatcut_desktop__get_active_project`, Codex should return the tool result and continue the conversation.

Tool-based requests should work reliably under the same conditions in which text-only requests succeed. If temporary service capacity is unavailable, the application should provide appropriate retry handling and a clear error message.

### Additional information

### Environment and troubleshooting

- Platform: macOS on Apple Silicon.
- Application: Codex Desktop.
- Subscription: ChatGPT Plus.
- Affected models: GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT-6.1 Sol.
- Network: Local HTTP/HTTPS proxy, with successful HTTPS tunnel establishment.
- ChatCut Desktop MCP is registered and has previously worked successfully.

### Findings

1. ChatCut MCP successfully executed `get_active_project`.
2. ChatCut MCP successfully executed `list_projects`, returning three local projects.
3. The issue also occurs with the built-in terminal tool (`pwd`), without invoking ChatCut MCP.
4. Text-only requests such as `OK` can succeed.
5. Multiple Codex session logs contain `server_overloaded`.
6. An earlier session also recorded a network transport error, but the repeated failures currently show `server_overloaded`.
7. Restarting Codex and switching models have not consistently resolved the issue.

This suggests that the failure may be related to tool-call continuation, model capacity handling, or backend request routing rather than the ChatCut MCP integration itself.

Please investigate the repeated `server_overloaded` errors affecting tool-based tasks on Codex Desktop.

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: windows-os
labels.description: Issues related to Codex on Windows systems

labels.description: Issues involving session (thread) management, resuming, forking, naming, archiving

issues.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

Codex Desktop `26.715.4045.0`, bundled command runner `0.145.0-alpha.18`.

### What subscription do you have?

Education

### What platform is your computer?

Windows 11 x64

### What issue are you seeing?

An existing general-chat/projectless task changed from working `approval_policy=on-request` behavior to an explicit granular policy between turns, while the UI continued to show **Ask for approval** and no permission-mode change was made:

```text
GranularApprovalConfig {
    sandbox_approval: false,
    rules: false,
    skill_approval: false,
    request_permissions: true,
    mcp_elicitations: true
}
```

After the transition, commands using `sandbox_permissions="require_escalated"` were rejected before an approval prompt could be created.

This has the same lower-level policy failure as #32563, but a different lifecycle. That report deterministically reproduces the policy in a newly created projectless task. Here, the same existing task first used `OnRequest` successfully and then Desktop changed its outgoing permission request between two later turns.

The Desktop log records the transition:

```text
11:09:48.561Z requestApprovalPolicy=null
             resolvedApprovalPolicy=on-request
             useAppServerPermissionDefault=true

11:32:30.296Z requestApprovalPolicy={granular:{sandbox_approval:false,...}}
             requestPermissionProfile=:workspace
             useAppServerPermissionDefault=false
```

The session rollout independently records `thread_settings_applied` with `on-request` at `11:09:48.765Z` and the granular policy at `11:32:30.721Z`, for the same task and working directory.

The renderer therefore supplied the granular override explicitly; the command runner did not spontaneously convert `OnRequest`.

Two suspected triggers occurred later and can be excluded:

* The rollout's `compacted` event occurred at `11:33:54Z`, approximately 84 seconds after the granular profile was active.
* Denial of an unrelated in-app browser request also occurred after the transition.

The task could be toggled between the two behaviors. **Approve for me** restored `on-request` with `approvals_reviewer=auto_review`; switching back to **Ask for approval** immediately restored `sandbox_approval:false` and the pre-prompt rejection.

After two Desktop restarts, the same task again used ordinary `on-request` approval and an elevated command successfully reached a user prompt. Its persisted Desktop record was then healthy: `approvalPolicy="on-request"`, `approvalsReviewer="user"`, and no active granular profile.

The failure later recurred in this same existing task. A normal GitHub CLI network command was blocked by the sandbox, and its `require_escalated` retry was again rejected before prompting with the granular profile above. This demonstrates that restart can temporarily restore the task while a later turn can reintroduce the bad policy.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

The exact event that changes the existing task's renderer state is not yet isolated, but the observed sequence is:

1. Open an existing general-chat/projectless task with **Ask for approval** selected.
2. Confirm that its effective policy is `on-request` and that an escalated command can produce an approval prompt.
3. Continue the same task across later turns without changing the permission mode.
4. Observe that Desktop eventually starts a turn with an explicit granular `requestApprovalPolicy` and `useAppServerPermissionDefault=false`.
5. Retry an otherwise identical command with `sandbox_permissions="require_escalated"`.
6. Observe that it is rejected before prompting because `sandbox_approval=false`.
7. Restart Desktop and observe that the same task may return to `on-request`, then later regress again.

### What is the expected behavior?

An existing task should not silently change its effective permission model between turns or app restarts.

**Ask for approval** should either preserve the established `on-request` command-approval flow or expose a complete and consistent granular-permission contract. In particular, Desktop should not leave an existing task and its agent with an escalation interface that is guaranteed to be rejected before the user can be asked.

### Additional information

Related reports:

* #32563 covers the same policy failure for newly created projectless tasks.
* #33322 covers a separate task-profile persistence symptom in which a task becomes `read-only`; its permission-mode toggle repairs the sandbox instead of deterministically reselecting `sandbox_approval:false`.
* #23359 covers the lower-level granular policy and tool-schema mismatch.

The relevant redacted Desktop log and rollout excerpts can be provided if needed.

### Summary

- Codex CLI: 0.124.0-alpha.2

- Architecture: arm64

From the bundled frontend code, UI message loading appears to be gated behind a remote feature flag named `enable_i18n`. This would also explain why the issue only reproduces on some machines/accounts.

### Expected behavior

When the user selects Simplified Chinese in Settings, Codex Desktop should render the UI in Chinese after restart or reload.

The UI remains in English even though the saved setting and Electron language are both `zh-CN`.

Workaround: After backing up and fully closing Codex, restored local-projects, project-order, and thread-project-assignments in .codex-global-state.json from the existing SQLite records, and removed 32 conflicting projectless markers. After restart, verification confirmed all 9 project IDs and 159 conversation associations were preserved. No database edits or migration-flag resets were needed.



### What steps can reproduce the bug?

Launching the ChatGPT app after the `newest` update. 

### What is the expected behavior?

All projects intact.

### Additional information

_No response_

issues.title: Dots: hallucinated completion claims, cloud/local confusion, missing updates, and an unexplained “Paused” state

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: model-behavior
labels.description: Issues related to behaviors exhibited by the model

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

labels.name: dots
labels.description: Issues involving setting up ChatGPT dots or managing their ongoing work.

issues.body:
## Summary

I am reporting several problems I experienced in one ongoing dot conversation, mainly on November 6, 2026. I asked my dot to improve an existing job-research workflow on its own cloud computer, using Superpowers as part of a full implementation plan.

My main concern is hallucination: confident, inaccurate or unsupported claims about the dot's own task completion and prior understanding, followed by corrections only after I challenged them. The examples below concern what it said it had completed or understood; they do not establish a specific model defect or root cause.

The dot gave overly broad completion reports and then acknowledged unfinished implementation, left me repeatedly asking for the next update, and used “local” in a way that made it unclear whether it meant its cloud computer or my PC. When I challenged that, it initially agreed with the premise that it had misunderstood the computer destination, then later said it had found no actual instruction or proposal to use my PC.

Separately, the desktop app displayed the whole dot as “Paused” after I had reported rebooting it. I had deliberately paused the scheduled job search, but I had not intentionally paused the whole dot. A screenshot shows the whole-dot indicator. I cannot establish why it appeared.

These problems made it difficult to trust what was completed, where work happened, and whether work was continuing. I am reporting the symptoms together for context, not claiming they share one cause.

## Environment

- Product: ChatGPT desktop app, using a dot.
- Local platform: Windows desktop, visible in the screenshots. Exact Windows version/build is not verified.
- Work setup: the dot's cloud computer, with a separate local-PC connection visible in the app. The requested implementation was intended for the dot's computer.
- Exact desktop app version/build: not captured in the available evidence.
- Exact active model for the affected responses: not verified. A later tool/model comparison does not establish which model generated the earlier responses.
- Time zone: Philippine Time, PHT (UTC+8). All times below use PHT.
- I reported seeing two desktop updates that day. I do not have evidence identifying their versions or showing that either caused these problems.

## What happened

### 1. Hallucinated or confidently inaccurate completion claims

At 11:13 AM on November 6, the dot presented an eight-phase implementation plan. I approved implementation at 11:18 AM and asked it to pause scheduled searches at 11:45 AM while it finished the improvements.

At 12:00:42 PM, it said:

> “The offline improvements are done and tested, bro, but the full workflow isn’t proven yet because the searches are paused.”

It described the next step as a real search. After I asked whether all phases were done, it corrected itself at 12:15:03 PM:

> “No, bro. I was too broad when I said the offline improvements were done.”

At 12:16:05 PM, its phase breakdown said source-rotation and employer-watchlist improvements were “not implemented yet,” and Superpowers was not verified as installed. These were unfinished implementation items, not merely a live test being deferred because I had paused searches.

There is an important limitation to this complaint: the original 11:13 AM plan itself explicitly said it had found Superpowers reference material, “but not a verified complete installed skill,” and that the plan had not yet been implemented. I am not claiming that original message explicitly said the full plugin was installed. My concern is that the requested full-tool use remained unresolved while later progress and completion messages were too broad and confusing.

### 2. Missing updates and unclear continuation

At 1:13 PM, I asked which phase the dot was on. It replied that it would check. At 1:20 PM, I had to ask again and supplied a screenshot showing that exchange without the promised phase answer.

At 1:21:13 PM, it said:

> “You got my ‘I’ll check’ message but not the phase-by-phase answer. I sent that answer to the wrong reply destination.”

That is the dot's explanation. I do not have independent delivery logs proving whether the cause was reply routing, UI display, or another problem.

There was another gap after a 1:39:27 PM timing-fix update. At 1:53:56 PM, I asked why there were no further updates. At 1:54:02 PM, it replied:

> “I stopped after reporting the timing fix instead of continuing the implementation and keeping you updated.”

The problem was not simply the number of minutes between messages. I could not tell whether the requested work was continuing, complete, or blocked, and had to keep prompting it to clarify.

### 3. Cloud-computer/local-PC confusion and premature agreement

My original request at 11:01 AM said to use Superpowers “on your pc,” meaning the dot's computer. Later updates repeatedly used terms such as “local tests” without clearly identifying the machine.

At 2:09 PM, the dot focused on plugin administrator settings. At 2:10 PM, I clarified that I meant using the GitHub repository and terminal on its own computer. It immediately said it had misunderstood, and repeated that admission before establishing whether it had actually proposed using my PC.

At 2:15 PM, it clarified that “local testing” meant the cloud computer. At 2:16 PM, it reported checking its work records and said the relevant tests ran on the Linux cloud computer. At 2:17:07 PM, it corrected its earlier agreement: it had found no actual instruction or proposal in the checked messages to run this work on my PC. It said the concrete error was focusing on plugin/admin settings instead of the requested GitHub/terminal setup, then making the explanation more confusing.

This report does not allege proven unauthorized execution on my PC. It documents ambiguous wording and an explanation that changed after the dot checked the evidence.

At 2:15:12 PM, it also said the repository had been downloaded but was not installed or activated. At 2:19 PM, it acknowledged that a plan based on saved reference guidance did not establish that the full requested tool had been installed and run. Plugin availability, repository download, installation, activation and actual use need to be reported distinctly.

### 4. Unexplained whole-dot “Paused” indicator after a reported reboot

At 1:23:03 PM, I told the dot I had rebooted it. At 1:25 PM, it reported that the improvement files and saved test evidence remained available, and that the scheduled job search was still intentionally paused. That was its reported check, not proof of complete recovery or a fresh execution test.

A screenshot with the Windows clock showing **1:29 PM, November 6, 2026** shows:

- The dot's right-hand status panel displaying **“Paused.”**
- A separate **“Paused”** indicator at the bottom of the conversation.

I sent it at 1:30:29 PM with the message:

> “LOOK RIGHT NOW YOU JUST GOT PAUSED what happend??? i ddint touch you or anything”

The dot responded afterward. It acknowledged that the whole-dot pause indicator was distinct from the deliberately paused job-search schedule and said it could not identify the cause or an actor.

The screenshot proves the indicator was displayed. It does not establish when the state changed, who or what changed it, whether it was a stale UI state, or how long background work was affected. The reboot happened earlier in the reported sequence, but I do not know that it caused the pause.

## Earlier continuity concerns

On November 4 at 1:57 AM, I had already reported that the dot seemed reset after an earlier pause of almost two hours. On November 5 at 7:44 PM, I described noticing a pause after returning to the app with Alt+Tab. Those are my observations and concerns, not proof that pausing or Alt+Tab caused data loss.

The dot had separately reported missing working-project/history files and degraded searches. Its later review said that file-availability problem appeared before the earlier automation pause. I cannot verify a common cause between those older problems and the November 6 whole-dot indicator.

I was worried about context loss and asked whether a desktop update or model change could explain the behavior. Neither explanation is established. The November 6 conversation alone does not prove that stored context was deleted.

## Observed sequence, not a deterministic reproduction

1. Continue an existing, multi-stage workflow conversation with a dot that has its own cloud computer.
2. Ask it to use an external development tool on that computer, produce a full plan, and then implement the approved plan.
3. Pause only the recurring search while implementation continues.
4. Ask for completion and phase status. Compare the broad “done” reports with later admissions that planned implementation remains unfinished.
5. Ask where “local” work happened. In this case, the dot initially accepted the PC-related concern, then revised that explanation after checking.
6. Separately, after reporting a dot reboot, observe the desktop status. In this case, the whole-dot “Paused” indicator appeared without an intentional whole-dot pause by me.

I do not have a minimal prompt that reliably reproduces all of this or evidence that these steps will reproduce the pause on another account.

## Expected behavior

- Completion reports should match the approved scope and distinguish implemented, tested offline, tested live, blocked and not started.
- Reading reference guidance or downloading a repository should not be presented as equivalent to installing, activating or using the full tool.
- The dot should identify the cloud computer versus the user's PC explicitly and check evidence before agreeing that it used or planned to use the wrong machine.
- Promised updates should appear in the relevant conversation/reply, with a clear explanation when work stops or needs input.
- The UI should clearly distinguish a paused scheduled task from a paused whole dot. Unexpected pause states need a useful explanation or diagnosable event trail.
- Recovery after a reboot should clearly state what was checked and what remains unknown.

## Evidence and request

Two original screenshots were reviewed privately: the 1:20 PM missing-update view and the 1:29 PM whole-dot pause view. They contain unrelated conversation/sidebar details. No screenshots are attached to this report.

Please investigate task-state reporting, continuation/update delivery, machine identification, and whole-dot pause-state transitions around these timestamps. Please also advise which version information or diagnostic export is needed to investigate further. If these are separate issues, please help split or route them rather than assuming one root cause.

Personal details, account identifiers, private document links, job-application information and unrelated sidebar content have been omitted.

issues.title: Locked Use fails with two macOS accounts logged in: shared authorization socket ownership conflict

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

issues.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

26.1103.41825 (25679). Computer Use helper and installed authorization plug-in: 26.1102.1001824 (1001824).

### What subscription do you have?

Pro 200

### What platform is your computer?

macOS 15.8.1 (24H32), Apple Silicon. Two macOS user accounts using Fast User Switching; a Codex/Computer Use helper runs in each account.

### What issue are you seeing?

Locked Use works with only one macOS account logged in, but fails reproducibly when a second account is logged in and running its own Computer Use helper. The second helper reports `SocketError Code=7` (`socketDirectoryWrongOwner`) against a shared machine-wide authorization socket directory.

This is a focused follow-up to #58452, which I closed with the repair/workaround findings. It may explain a subset of reports like #57709; I am not claiming all automatic-unlock failures have this cause.

The visible error is: “Mac is locked and automatic unlock could not unlock it.” Keeping the first account logged in but switching to the second also produced a case where a Finder accessibility tree and screenshot were readable, while actual window control failed with `Computer Use server error -10005: cgWindowNotFound`.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

Use two macOS accounts, A and B, with Locked Use enabled.

1. Start with only account A logged in and the desktop app running. Lock the Mac and request a native Computer Use task from a connected device, such as opening a Finder window.
2. Confirm the task succeeds and the authorization plug-in logs `ALLOW`.
3. Log into account B through Fast User Switching, leaving A logged in, and start the desktop app/Computer Use helper in B.
4. Lock B and request Computer Use from a connected device targeting B. On my machine, B's helper has already logged the socket ownership error, automatic unlock fails, and the authorization plug-in logs `DENY`.
5. Log B out, return to A, and lock it. Repeat the Finder task targeting A. Automatic unlock and opening a new Finder window succeed again without restarting.

The helper startup failure was also observed with the account roles reversed: whichever account did not own the shared directory reported Code 7.

### What is the expected behavior?

Having a second macOS account logged in should not silently break Locked Use in another account or make functionality depend on which account owns a shared temporary directory.

Ideally, Computer Use/Locked Use should isolate and route authorization correctly for each macOS user session. If concurrent macOS sessions are unsupported, please document that limitation and surface an actionable error instead of the generic automatic-unlock failure.

### Additional information

#### Evidence from local diagnostics

Both helpers use:

```text
/tmp/com.openai.sky.CUAService/LockScreenLoginAuthorization.sock
```

The parent directory was mode 0755 and owned by one account. The other account's helper emitted:

```text
log[2f5fac05e5d0ba21df22]
Error Domain=ComputerUse.(unknown context ...).SocketError Code=7
```

Read-only inspection of the installed helper's symbols/disassembly showed that `LockScreenLoginAuthorizationSocketServer.start` checks whether the existing directory's owner matches `geteuid()`; the owner-mismatch branch produces error discriminator 7, corresponding to `socketDirectoryWrongOwner`.

**Observed:** the non-owning helper fails the directory ownership check; automatic unlock fails in the two-account setup; reversing startup/account order reverses which account hits the error.

**Hypothesis requiring maintainer confirmation:** the shared endpoint prevents independent per-user authorization handling, potentially routing a request to a helper without the matching pending unlock attempt. The exact causal path from this startup error to each `DENY` is not proven.

#### Controlled tests on November 8, 2026 (EST)

| State | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Only A logged in after restart; directory owned by A | Automatic unlock succeeded; plug-in logged `ALLOW` at 22:23:00 |
| B logged in afterward; both helpers running; directory still owned by A | B's helper logged Code 7; unlock attempts logged `DENY` |
| A in the background while B was active and locked | Finder tree/screenshot retrieval succeeded, but an attempt to open a window failed with `-10005: cgWindowNotFound` |
| B logged out again; only A logged in and locked | Plug-in logged `ALLOW` at 22:27:51; a new Finder window opened successfully, without another restart |

The background-session window-control failure is an additional observation, not proof that it has exactly the same cause as the socket ownership failure.

#### Stale plug-in was repaired before these tests

Initially, the installed authorization plug-in was build 1001631 while the bundled plug-in/helper were build 1001824. Turning Locked Use off/on and approving the administrator prompt updated the installed plug-in to 1001824. The installed executable then matched the bundled copy, signatures verified, and the screensaver authorization rule referenced the expected remote authorization mechanism. The two-account failure persisted afterward, so matching plug-in versions alone did not resolve it.

#### Workaround and regression history

Logging the other macOS account out restored native Computer Use on this machine. Merely switching accounts did not. An initial reboot with only the target account logged in helped isolate the issue; the later successful logout-only test showed that another reboot was not necessary.

I previously used this while the other macOS account was active. It began failing consistently a few updates ago, but I do not have an exact last-known-good version.

No socket permissions, ownership, or authorization rules were manually changed during this investigation. The newer “Show user name and photo” Lock Screen setting was absent on this macOS version and was not part of the workaround.

issues.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

26.1007.21434 (build 13901, prod)

### What subscription do you have?

ChatGPT Plus

### What platform is your computer?

Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.26200.0 x64

### What issue are you seeing?

### Bug description

Codex Desktop on Windows disables network access inside the workspace-write sandbox even though Allow network access is enabled in Settings and network_access = true is configured in config.toml.

Codex Desktop version: 26.1007.21434 (build 13901, prod)

Application settings:
- Approval policy: On request
- Sandbox settings: Workspace write
- Allow network access: Enabled
- Web search: Live

Actual sandbox environment:
CODEX_PERMISSION_PROFILE=:workspace
CODEX_SANDBOX_NETWORK_DISABLED=1
Effective sandbox mode: workspace-write
Effective network policy: restricted

Prompt used: Check Internet access inside the current Codex Desktop Windows sandbox. Do not request elevated permissions, run outside the sandbox, or modify any files. Run whoami, inspect sandbox environment and resolve www.nuget.org.

Observed failures:
Resolve-DnsName www.nuget.org: Access is denied
Node HTTPS api.nuget.org: getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND api.nuget.org
npm.cmd ping: No PONG received

The problem persists after restarting Codex Desktop and opening a new conversation.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

### Steps to reproduce

1. Open Codex Desktop on Windows 11.
2. Go to Settings > Configuration > Codex.
3. Set Approval policy to "On request".
4. Set Sandbox settings to "Workspace write".
5. Enable "Allow network access".
6. Open the user `config.toml` and verify:

```toml
sandbox_mode = "workspace-write"

[windows]
sandbox = "elevated"

[sandbox_workspace_write]
network_access = true
```

7. Close and restart Codex Desktop.
8. Open a new conversation in a local workspace.
9. Ask Codex to execute the following commands inside the sandbox only:

```powershell
whoami
$env:CODEX_SANDBOX_NETWORK_DISABLED
$env:CODEX_PERMISSION_PROFILE
Resolve-DnsName www.nuget.org
```

10. Observe that the sandbox has `CODEX_SANDBOX_NETWORK_DISABLED=1`, and DNS resolution fails with `Access is denied`.

The issue reproduces in newly created conversations, not only previously restored ones. No elevation or system modifications are required to reproduce it.

### What is the expected behavior?

When "Allow network access" is enabled and `[sandbox_workspace_write].network_access = true`, Codex Desktop should permit outbound network requests within the workspace-write sandbox.

Expected results:
- Effective network policy allows network access.
- `CODEX_SANDBOX_NETWORK_DISABLED` is not set to `1`.
- DNS resolution and HTTPS requests work without requiring execution outside the sandbox.
- The selected network permission remains effective after restarting the application and opening or restoring conversations.

The sandbox should retain its normal workspace-write filesystem restrictions and On-request approval policy. Full Access should not be necessary.

### Additional information

### Diagnostic findings

Codex Desktop: 26.1007.21434, build 13901, prod.

A restored-session event on October 12, 2026, at 12:11:48 (UTC+7) contained:

sandboxPolicySource=default
hasLatestThreadSettings=false
hasLatestTurnParams=false
shouldSendPermissions=false
derivedSandboxPolicy: workspaceWrite, networkAccess=false
responseSandboxPolicy: workspaceWrite, networkAccess=false
responseActivePermissionProfile=:workspace
responseApprovalPolicy=on-request

At 12:11:59: useAppServerPermissionDefault=true

Additional observations:
- UI and config.toml both enable network access.
- No duplicate sandbox/network settings or relevant profile overrides found.
- Two permissionProfile/list calls appear without response payloads.
- Logs do not reveal the merged configuration or why the default has networkAccess=false.
- Codex CLI --no-daemon successfully accesses HTTPS under CodexSandboxOnline.
- One Desktop session temporarily accessed HTTPS, but became restricted again after restart.

Please investigate default profile generation and policy merging, including permissionProfile/list, config/read, configRequirements/read, and restored-session permission derivation. The root cause remains unconfirmed.

issues.body:
### Summary

The in-session TUI `/resume` picker always starts with the `Cwd` filter selected. This happens even when Codex was launched through `codex resume --all`, so the behavior changes after entering a session: the startup picker can show all sessions, but the slash-command picker narrows back to the current working directory.

### Environment

- Codex CLI: `0.146.0`
- Surface: TUI

### Steps to reproduce

1. Create or keep interactive Codex sessions from at least two different working directories.
2. Start Codex with:

   ```bash
   codex resume --all
   ```

3. Select or start a session.
4. From inside the running TUI, enter:

   ```text
   /resume
   ```

### Expected behavior

The in-session `/resume` picker should make it straightforward to see the same all-session view available from `codex resume --all`. Reasonable fixes would include one of the following:

- Default the in-session `/resume` picker to `All`.
- Preserve the launch-time `--all` preference for later `/resume` usage in that TUI session.
- Add a persisted/default picker-filter setting, similar to the existing persisted session picker view setting.
- Add an explicit slash-command option such as `/resume --all`.

### Actual behavior

The in-session picker opens in `Cwd` mode and only lists sessions whose stored session cwd matches the current session cwd. When the current cwd has only one matching session, the picker appears to show only the current session even though other sessions exist and can be listed through the all-session path.

### Current workaround

After opening `/resume`, use the picker toolbar to switch the filter from `Cwd` to `All`. The filter control is focused initially, so the left/right arrow key toggles it in the current picker implementation.

### Implementation notes

In `rust-v0.146.0`, the in-session slash-command path calls the resume picker with `show_all` hardcoded to `false`:

```rust
crate::resume_picker::run_resume_picker_from_existing_session_with_app_server(
    tui,
    &self.config,
    /*show_all*/ false,
    /*include_non_interactive*/ false,
    picker_app_server,
)
```

The picker initializes its filter mode from that value:

```rust
filter_mode: SessionFilterMode::from_show_all(show_all, filter_cwd.as_deref()),
```

The current config schema exposes `tui.resume_cwd` and `tui.session_picker_view`, but does not appear to expose a default `Cwd`/`All` filter preference for the picker.

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: TUI
labels.description: Issues related to the terminal user interface: text input, menus and dialogs, and terminal display

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

issues.body:
### Summary

Vim mode in the Codex CLI does not support `Ctrl+C` as a way to leave Insert mode and return to Normal mode. Instead, pressing `Ctrl+C` clears the entire prompt. When an agent turn is running, it can also cancel the turn.

The missing mode transition affects ordinary prompt editing even when the agent is idle, not just editing during an active turn.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Enable Vim mode in the interactive Codex CLI.
2. Enter Insert mode in the composer and type a prompt without submitting it.
3. Press `Ctrl+C`, expecting to return to Normal mode.
4. Observe that the full prompt is cleared instead of switching to Normal mode.

To reproduce the turn-cancellation behavior, enter Insert mode while the agent is working and press `Ctrl+C`.

### Actual behavior

- `Ctrl+C` clears the entire draft prompt rather than moving from Insert mode to Normal mode.
- When a turn is running, `Ctrl+C` can also cancel the turn instead of first leaving Insert mode.

### Expected behavior

While in Vim Insert mode, `Ctrl+C` should switch to Normal mode and preserve the full draft, whether the agent is idle or running. This mode transition should not cancel an active turn. Once in Normal mode, `Ctrl+C` can retain its existing behavior.

### Why this matters

Using `Ctrl+C` to leave Insert mode is established Vim muscle memory. In Codex, that habit can erase a prompt being edited and interrupt the agent when composing a follow-up message.

### Environment

- Currently installed CLI version: `codex-cli 0.153.4`
- Platform: macOS

### Related issues

- #12582 requests requiring Escape twice to interrupt, addressing a related accidental-interruption problem.
- #29883 requests a configurable `jj` sequence for leaving Vim Insert mode.

This report specifically requests support for `Ctrl+C` to leave Vim Insert mode, with that transition taking priority over clearing the prompt or cancelling the turn.

issues.body:
# Bug: Missing rollout leaves an unarchivable “ghost” thread in the Windows sidebar

## Summary

On the Codex/ChatGPT Windows desktop app, a local thread remained visible in the sidebar and repeatedly failed to archive because its rollout file was missing while the state database still retained the thread row and stale rollout path. The item survived full app restarts and was also treated as a pinned thread by the renderer even after the backend could no longer load it.

The UI eventually reported archive success only after the stale local state was cleaned up and an explicit unpin operation was sent. The app should self-heal this state without requiring manual SQLite/session cleanup.

## Environment

- Platform: Windows 10 Home China 22H2, build 19045.6466, x64
- Desktop app release reported in logs: `26.814.41957`
- App server version: `0.148.0-alpha.15`
- Selected Codex runtime bundle: `26.819.11345`
- Date observed: 2026-08-20
- Thread title: `11`
- Thread ID: `01a01437-8518-78d2-8485-d0512fcbc1c5`
- Deep link: `codex://threads/01a01437-8518-78d2-8485-d0512fcbc1c5`

## Preconditions inferred from logs and local state

1. `state_5.sqlite` retained a row for the thread.
2. Its `rollout_path` pointed to a JSONL file that no longer existed.
3. The renderer/sidebar still retained the thread in its pinned/recent state.

The stale path was equivalent to:

```text
%USERPROFILE%\.codex\sessions\2026\08\18\rollout-...-01a01437-8518-78d2-8485-d0512fcbc1c5.jsonl
```

## Steps to reproduce

The original cause of the missing rollout is unknown, but the broken state can be described as follows:

1. Have a local thread row in `state_5.sqlite` whose `rollout_path` no longer exists.
2. Keep that thread visible or pinned in the sidebar.
3. Restart the desktop app.
4. Try **Archive** from the thread overflow menu, sidebar context menu, or Recent tasks menu.

## Actual behavior

- The app repeatedly shows archive failure.
- Restarting does not remove the sidebar item.
- The stale thread can remain visible even though `thread/read` and `turn/start` report that the thread is missing/not loaded.
- Archive may fail through two related paths:
  - internal OS error because the rollout file is missing;
  - `no rollout found`, followed by failure to persist the inactive-thread archive.
- The renderer can continue trying to hydrate the item as a pinned thread.

## Expected behavior

If a thread's rollout is missing but a state-database/sidebar record remains, Archive should still remove the item from active and pinned sidebar state. The app should transactionally reconcile or quarantine the stale database row, clear its pinned state, invalidate the renderer cache, and optionally surface a recoverability warning. It should not require the missing rollout file merely to hide/archive the sidebar entry.

## Sanitized log evidence

```text
Archive requested ... method=thread/archive
errorCode=-32603
failed to archive session: thread-store internal error: failed to archive thread:
The system cannot find the file specified. (os error 2)

Archive skipped because thread has no active rollout
errorMessage="no rollout found for thread id 01a01437-8518-78d2-8485-d0512fcbc1c5"

Failed to persist inactive thread archive
errorMessage="Inactive thread archive did not persist"

state db list_threads returned stale rollout path for thread
01a01437-8518-78d2-8485-d0512fcbc1c5
state db discrepancy during list_threads_db: stale_db_path_retained

thread/read ... errorCode=-32600
message="thread not loaded: 01a01437-8518-78d2-8485-d0512fcbc1c5"

Failed to read pinned thread
threadId=01a01437-8518-78d2-8485-d0512fcbc1c5
```

## Recovery that ultimately worked

The user observed successful archiving only after all of the following stale state had been reconciled:

1. removed the stale thread row and exact-ID references from local structured state;
2. confirmed the missing rollout/session file had no remaining live index entry;
3. explicitly set the thread's pinned state to false;
4. retried Archive in the desktop app.

## Suggested fix

When `thread/archive` encounters `rollout_not_found` or OS error 2:

1. fall back to a state-database-only archive transaction;
2. clear `is_pinned` and any renderer-side pinned ID for the thread;
3. invalidate the sidebar query/cache;
4. remove or quarantine stale `rollout_path` entries;
5. return success if the thread is no longer present in active sidebar state.

This would prevent a permanently visible “ghost” thread and avoid requiring users to edit local databases manually.

Suppress stale cloud stream disconnects after reopening a thread

A queued cloud stream disconnect can outlive a successful reopen of the same conversation, causing an obsolete reconnect error to reach the TUI.

Represent cloud reply stream losses with `AppServerEvent::ThreadStreamDisconnected` and filter queued losses superseded by a successful attachment to the same thread. Preserve losses for other threads and any newer disconnects; failed reopen attempts do not supersede pending losses.

Continue displaying current stream disconnects through the TUI's error notification handler.

prs.title: Defer MCP auth discovery until startup failure
prs.body:
## Summary

Prevent unavailable optional HTTP MCP servers from delaying thread creation by moving network-dependent OAuth discovery out of session initialization.

## Background

A customer running Codex Desktop on Windows reported that creating a local chat timed out whenever an enabled optional HTTP MCP pointed at a localhost endpoint with no active listener. The app-server eventually returned `thread/start`, but only after the Desktop request timeout had elapsed; disabling the MCP restored normal chat creation.

The report is tracked in [SE-8040](https://linear.app/openai/issue/SE-8040/inactive-http-mcp-blocks-new-local-chat-on-windows).

## Root Cause

Session creation computed an auth status for every effective MCP server before constructing `McpConnectionManager`. For streamable HTTP servers, that status computation can perform OAuth protected-resource and authorization-server discovery. An unreachable optional server could therefore consume network timeouts on the critical `thread/start` path even though optional MCP startup itself is designed to continue in the background.

The eager auth snapshot was useful for startup diagnostics, but it made optional-server reachability a prerequisite for creating a thread.

## What Changed

- Session creation and MCP runtime refresh now construct the connection manager without first performing network auth discovery.
- If startup fails because authentication is required and no precomputed status exists, the manager resolves that server's auth status lazily before producing the failure notification.
- Other startup failures retain their configured-server context without triggering OAuth discovery, preserving existing timeout, GitHub PAT, and generic diagnostic messages.
- Explicit auth-status collection and required-MCP validation behavior are unchanged.
- Added an app-server regression test with a blackholed optional HTTP MCP and asserted that `thread/start` responds within three seconds.

## Why This Is Low Risk

- The change is scoped to when missing MCP auth status is discovered.
- No change to required-server waiting, MCP transport startup, or explicit auth-status queries.
- No change to credential storage, token handling, approval behavior, configuration, or protocol schemas.

## Tests

The regression test failed on current `main` by waiting on the blackholed endpoint and passes with this change. Existing MCP startup and required-server tests also pass on the changed path.

## Verification

- `just test -p codex-mcp`: 105 passed.
- `just test -p codex-app-server`: the new regression and relevant MCP tests passed; the broad run had 16 failures and 6 timeouts caused by local sandbox restrictions, unavailable test binaries, and shell-output contamination.

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

issues.body:
This EPIC tracks a series of investigations as to whether there is value in AST aware file read, search, or codebase mapping.

AST aware tools can be used to 1) more precisely read method bounds with a single tool call, reducing turns from misaligned reads, and reducing noise in tokens, 2) navigate to usages and definitions of syntax elements via syntax aware search (AST grep), and 3) compress high level context about the codebase, such as the location of specific classes and their members by collapsing code down to just top level classes and types and their children's signatures.

```
 1. tilth (Rust)
  tilth is built specifically to generate a structural outline of a codebase. It uses Tree-sitter under the hood but ships as a single binary. It gives you an
  immediate map of the repository's symbols.
   * Installation: cargo install tilth (or download the binary from their releases)
   * Usage:
       * tilth map . (Prints a tree-like overview of the whole codebase structure)
       * tilth read <file> (Prints the structural outline of a specific file)


  2. glyph (Go)
  glyph is another single-binary tool designed to generate clean, multi-file symbol maps. It's excellent if you want to quickly see the skeleton of a
  directory of source code.
   * Installation: go install github.com/benmyles/glyph@latest
   * Usage: glyph cli './**/*.go' (Prints a tree of functions, structs, and methods)


  3. ast-grep (sg) (Rust)
  While primarily known as a structural search-and-replace tool, ast-grep is the industry standard for distributing Tree-sitter as a fast, single binary. You
  can use it to extract landmarks via the command line.
   * Installation: brew install ast-grep or cargo install ast-grep
   * Usage: You can write quick one-liners to extract specific symbols (like all function declarations) and format the output.


  4. The Classic: Universal Ctags (C)
  If you truly want zero modern dependencies, u-ctags is the classic UNIX approach. It uses a hybrid regex/parser approach rather than full AST generation, so
  it's incredibly fast and supports over 100 languages out of the box.
   * Installation: brew install universal-ctags
   * Usage: ctags -R --output-format=json .
   * Note: It outputs a flat list of symbols (or JSON) rather than a visual tree, but it is the most robust and portable way to extract codebase landmarks.
```

issues.title: Subagent recovery after MAX_TURNS is reported as GOAL success, hiding interruption

labels.name: priority/p1
labels.description: Important and should be addressed in the near term.

labels.name: area/agent
labels.description: Issues related to Core Agent, Tools, Memory, Sub-Agents, Hooks, Agent Quality

labels.name: 🔒 maintainer only
labels.description: ⛔ Do not contribute. Internal roadmap item.

labels.name: workstream-rollup
labels.description: Label used to tag epics and features that are associated with one of the three primary workstreams

issues.body:
### What happened?

**Summary**: `codebase_investigator` subagent reports `status: "success"` and `Termination Reason: "GOAL"` even though its own result says it hit the maximum turn limit before doing any analysis.

While using Gemini CLI to investigate two local repositories (`t3code` and `superset`), the agent invoked the `codebase_investigator` subagent and it failed immediately without doing any analysis.

I ran the Gemini CLI on these two local repositories with an objective asking it to understand their architectures and AI agent integrations. The saved session log shows:

- The main agent called `codebase_investigator` with a valid, concrete objective.
- The tool result was reported with `status: "success"` and `Termination Reason: "GOAL"`.
- The embedded result text simultaneously says the investigation was interrupted because the "maximum number of turns was exceeded" before any specific task was identified or initiated.
- `RelevantLocations` was empty and no actual codebase analysis was performed.

This looks incorrect because:

1. The subagent appears to have exhausted its turn budget before performing any actual analysis.
2. The termination metadata is internally inconsistent: the parent tool call is surfaced as `status: "success"` with `Termination Reason: "GOAL"`, but the embedded payload describes a limit-induced early termination with no findings.

Relevant evidence from the session log:

```text
session file: session-2026-03-09T18-34-10479ef5.json

line 50: "name": "codebase_investigator"
line 53: objective: "Understand the architecture of t3code and superset..."
line 61: "Termination Reason: GOAL"
line 61: "The investigation was interrupted by a system-mandated termination (maximum turns exceeded)..."
line 61: "\"RelevantLocations\": []"
line 66: "status": "success"
line 79: "The `codebase_investigator` was unable to complete its analysis due to a turn limit..."
```

Full snippet from the saved session:

```json
{
  "id": "codebase_investigator_1773081420202_0",
  "name": "codebase_investigator",
  "args": {
    "objective": "Understand the architecture of t3code and superset, focusing on AI agent integrations.\nSpecifically:\n1. In t3code, how is 'Codex' integrated? Where is the core logic for agent interaction?\n2. In superset, what are the different agent/harness integrations (e.g., Mastra, MCP, Claude, etc.) and how are they implemented?\n3. What are the common patterns or interfaces used in superset that could be adapted for t3code to support multiple harnesses?\n\nIdentify key files, symbols, and architectural patterns in both repositories."
  },
  "result": [
    {
      "functionResponse": {
        "response": {
          "output": "Subagent 'codebase_investigator' finished.\nTermination Reason: GOAL\nResult:\n{\n  \"SummaryOfFindings\": \"The investigation was interrupted by a system-mandated termination (maximum turns exceeded) before any specific task could be identified or initiated. As a result, no codebase analysis was performed, and no relevant locations or insights could be gathered.\",\n  \"ExplorationTrace\": [\n    \"Received system notification that the maximum number of turns was exceeded.\",\n    \"Followed emergency termination protocol as instructed.\"\n  ],\n  \"RelevantLocations\": []\n}"
        }
      }
    }
  ],
  "status": "success"
}
```

### What did you expect to happen?

I expected one of these outcomes:

- `codebase_investigator` should actually explore the repositories and return findings.
- If it truly hits a turn limit, it should do so after some visible work, and the tool invocation should be surfaced as a failure or explicit limit condition, not as `status: "success"` with `Termination Reason: "GOAL"`.

At minimum, the CLI should not report a contradictory success state for a subagent that says it exceeded its turn budget before beginning analysis. If the subagent hits a system-imposed turn limit before doing useful work, the tool result should be reported as a failure or explicit limit condition (e.g. `status: "error"` with a clear error code), not as a successful `GOAL` completion.


### Client information

<details>
<summary>Client Information</summary>

Run `gemini` to enter the interactive CLI, then run the `/about` command.

```console
> /about
Gemini CLI package version: 0.32.1
Platform: Windows
OS: Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.26200.0
Node.js: v20.20.0
PowerShell: 5.1.26100.7920
```

</details>

### Login information

Google Account, Pro tier from students promotion

### Anything else we need to know?

- After the failed `codebase_investigator` call, the main agent continued with manual file exploration and eventually produced an implementation plan. So the overall conversation did not fully crash, but the specialized investigator tool clearly failed.
- My current inference is that this may be either:
  - turn-budget state leaking into a fresh subagent invocation, or
  - an incorrect mapping of a subagent limit/error state into a successful `GOAL` termination in the parent session.
- If useful, I can provide the full saved session JSON or a redacted version of it.

labels.name: area/agent

issues.body:
# [BUG] Browser Agent ignores `settings.json` overrides (e.g., `maxTurns`)

## What happened?
The Browser Agent completely ignores any configuration overrides provided in the global or project-level `settings.json`. While the `AgentRegistry` correctly reads and merges these settings during initialization, the `BrowserAgentInvocation` and its factory (`browserAgentFactory.ts`) skips the registry and recreate the agent definition from scratch with hardcoded defaults.

## What did you expect to happen?
The Browser Agent should respect settings overrides like `maxTurns`, `maxTimeMinutes`, etc., just like other sub-agents (e.g., `codebase_investigator`). For example, setting `maxTurns: 0` in `settings.json` should cause the agent to terminate immediately upon invocation.

## Client information
<details>
<summary>Client Information</summary>

Platform: Linux (Ubuntu 22.04)
Gemini CLI Version: 0.35.0-nightly.20260311.657f19c1f

</details>

## Login information
Google Account (OAuth)

## Anything else we need to know?
### Root Cause
The Browser Agent's unique invocation flow skips the `AgentRegistry` where settings overrides are maintained. Instead of using the pre-merged definition from the registry, it re-instantiates a fresh definition using hardcoded defaults.

**Relevant Files & Code Snippets:**

1.  **`packages/core/src/agents/subagent-tool-wrapper.ts`**
    The Browser Agent is explicitly branched out of the standard flow that uses `LocalSubagentInvocation`:
    ```typescript
    if (definition.name === BROWSER_AGENT_NAME) {
      return new BrowserAgentInvocation(this.config, ...);
    }
    ```

2.  **`packages/core/src/agents/browser/browserAgentInvocation.ts`**
    The `execute` method calls `createBrowserAgentDefinition`, passing the `config` object but omitting the merged definition from the registry.

3.  **`packages/core/src/agents/browser/browserAgentFactory.ts`**
    The factory re-runs the `BrowserAgentDefinition` constructor, which returns hardcoded defaults (e.g., `maxTurns: 50`):
    ```typescript
    const baseDefinition = BrowserAgentDefinition(config, !visionDisabledReason);
    ```

### Suggested Fix
Update `browserAgentFactory.ts` to attempt to retrieve the existing definition from the `AgentRegistry` before falling back to creating a fresh one.

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

The `browser_agent` (specifically `BrowserManager.ts`) currently employs a restrictive "fail-fast" strategy when encountering a locked browser profile (e.g., when `sessionMode: 'persistent'` is used and an existing instance or orphaned process is active):


```json
{
  "success": false,
  "summary": "The task could not be completed because the browser is already running for /home/user/.gemini/cli-browser-profile.",
  "fullErrorMessage": "The browser is already running for /home/user/.gemini/cli-browser-profile. Use --isolated to run multiple browser instances.\nCause: The browser is already running for /home/user/.gemini/cli-browser-profile. Use a different userDataDir or stop the running browser first."
}
```

I propose to make it more resilient with the following capabilities:

1.  **Automatic Session Takeover:** If `persistent` mode fails due to a profile lock, the agent should automatically attempt to connect to the existing instance (as if `sessionMode: 'existing'` were specified). This requires a graceful "fallback-and-probe" mechanism in `BrowserManager.connectMcp()`.
2.  **Orphaned Process Recovery:** If an `existing` connection is not feasible but the profile remains locked, the `BrowserManager` should proactively detect orphaned `chrome` or `chrome-devtools-mcp` processes associated with the Gemini CLI profile and offer (or automatically execute) a "Self-Healing" routine (process termination + lock file removal).
3.  **Intelligent Error Remediation:** Replace the current static error messages with an interactive recovery flow. Utilizing the `ask_user` tool, the agent should present the user with a "Choice" menu featuring numbered options to resolve the lock (e.g., **1. Attempt Session Takeover**, **2. Force Termination & Reset**, or **3. Launch Isolated Session**). 
### Why is this needed?

Forcing the user to manually `pkill` processes or close browser windows is a friction point that degrades the autonomous agent experience. The agent has sufficient context (profile path, PIDs) to resolve this internally without user intervention.


### Additional context

> Executes and manages Gradle builds authoritatively with high-performance background orchestration 
  and surgical failure analysis. This skill is the STRONGLY PREFERRED way 
  to run any Gradle task, providing superior reliability through managed background processes, 
  task-specific output capturing, and deep diagnostic integration. Use it for executing core 
  lifecycle tasks like 'build' or 'assemble', starting persistent development servers, 
  or performing complex build troubleshooting. Do NOT use for specialized test diagnostics 
  (use running_gradle_tests).

and

Use for repository introspection and history-based truth verification. NEVER stages or commits without explicit user directives. Avoids interactive prompts via --no-pager.

> 4. **Agent & Tool Hierarchy:** Whenver considering how to approach a task or do anything, ALWAYS follow the hierarchy of preference: **Sub-Agents** > **Skills** > **Specialized MCP Tools** (NOT a Shell tool or similar) > **General/Builtin Tools** (e.g., `run_shell_command`, `grep_search`, `read_file`).
> 5. **Intentionality Protocol:** Before starting ANY task, you MUST stop and consider which agent, skill, or tool is most appropriate for the specific context. If your plan involves using the shell (even via a tool like `run_shell_command`), you MUST stop and reconsider if a more specialized tool or skill exists to handle the task more reliably.

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

## Objective
Ensure the Gemini CLI understands its own mechanics well enough to act as its own expert guide. The agent must be able to provide users with accurate facts about how it works, its hotkeys, and the exact CLI flags needed to run itself for specific workflows.

## The Problem
Users rely on the CLI to learn how to use the CLI. If the agent hallucinates flags (like suggesting the deprecated `--yolo` instead of `--approval-mode=yolo`) or forgets UI hotkeys (like `Double Esc` for `/rewind`), it blocks progress and creates friction. The agent needs strict grounding in its own documentation to accurately guide users.

### Why is this needed?

1. **Accurate Internal Facts:** The agent (specifically the `cli_help` subagent) must have flawless recall of its own UI keyboard shortcuts, slash commands, and settings hierarchy.
2. **Flag Construction:** It must be able to tell users exactly how to run it from the terminal for various use cases (e.g., suggesting `gemini -i "prompt" --sandbox --output-format json` for safe, headless scripting).
3. **Self-Execution & Guidance:** It should be able to write the exact commands needed to run itself, restart itself, or execute sub-tasks with the correct environment variables and flags.

type.description: Related Changes across multiple feature sets

issues.body:
## Description
Gemini 3 models are fundamentally trained to operate as native bash users, chaining standard POSIX tools (`grep`, `cat`, `sed`, `awk`) to explore codebases and edit files. To make full use of the model's native and preferred capabilities without compromising user security or UX, we need to allow the model to use these tools directly to interact and make changes.

## Prior Art
Historically, we have attempted to force models to use custom tools (such as `replace`, `grep_search`, `write_file`, etc.). However, these methods fight the model's core training. Malicious prompts or complex scripts are inherently hard to control and catch via parsing, and forcing custom tools creates significant downstream UX and security issues.

## The Challenge & Value Proposition
Because the model strongly favors raw bash calls even when nudged towards custom tools, it frequently outputs large, complex bash scripts to accomplish tasks. Under our current security model, these scripts require explicit user confirmation. 

This creates a critical point of failure: users are frequently presented with dense, hard-to-read bash messages to evaluate. This leads to severe prompt fatigue, causing users to either blindly confirm the execution or enter "yolo mode" (auto-approving all actions). This behavior is highly detrimental to security and degrades the overall user experience. 

**Value Proposition:** By safely embracing the model's native bash tendencies, we can eliminate confirmation fatigue, prevent unsafe "yolo mode" habits, and drastically improve both the UX and our underlying security posture. 

## Proposed Solution
A highly viable solution is to utilize a secure sandbox. ALL standard shell commands will execute within a zero-dependency, kernel-enforced sandbox. Instead of trying to predict intent before execution (which led to the parsing challenges described above), we can safely observe and handle the results *after* execution.

### Method
By running commands in a sandboxed replica of the workspace, we achieve three distinct UX lanes:
1. **Reads:** Commands that do not mutate the filesystem (e.g., `ls`, `grep`) are auto-approved. We must ensure this does not read from protected spaces or outside our trusted workspaces.
2. **Edits:** Commands that mutate the sandboxed filesystem (e.g., `sed -i`, `>`) trigger a post-execution Diff UI before the changes are synced back to the host, allowing for a seamless "Edit" tool experience using the model's preferred mechanisms. 
3. **Side-Effects:** A dynamic command router will handle commands requiring host credentials or network access (e.g., `git`, `gh`), completely bypassing the sandbox but requiring strict upfront user confirmation (i.e., stays the same as today, utilizing the policy engine to execute or ask for user confirmation).

## Architectural Mandates
In order to support this properly, we must explore, investigate, and implement the proper sandboxing for all major platforms: Linux, macOS, and Windows.

## Epic
This is an epic that tracks this investigation and implementation. It will contain subtasks used to track progress towards its overall completion. After initial investigation, if this is not a feasible route, the epic can be marked as closed.

issues.body:
## Motivation

Current context baseline is approximately 36.6k tokens per turn. Large file reads often 'firehose' the context, leading to bloat (previously observed at +15k tokens/turn). 

The goal of 'Tactful Extraction' is to establish a surgical code-discovery hierarchy:
1. **grep_search**: Primary scout for locating symbols.
2. **shell/sed**: scalpel for semantic block extraction (preferred for specific line ranges).
3. **read_file**: surgical range-reading (migrated to 1-based start/end lines).

Telemetry indicates that making ~2.1% more targeted tool calls results in a ~6.9% reduction in total input tokens.

## Changes

- **read_file migration**: Switched from 0-based 'offset'/'limit' to 1-based 'start_line'/'end_line' for better model alignment.
- **Surgical Guidance**: Updated tool descriptions and system prompts to mandate 'token-frugal' behavior.
- **Tool Hierarchy**: Emphasized the use of 'grep_search' and 'sed' via 'run_shell_command' for efficient context management.

## Status

This work is temporarily sidelined in favor of other priorities but remains a key architectural goal for efficiency.

issues.body:
The current WriteToDo tool relies on "in-context" task tracking, which maintains the todo list solely within the LLM's conversation history (prompt context). This creates issues with "context rot," high token costs, and total memory loss between sessions.

This issue proposes deprecating WriteToDo in favor of a persistent task tracking system (e.g., a local tasks.json) that allows the agent to maintain state across restarts and manage complex dependencies.

### Proposed Solution

Implement a new set of tools backed by a persistent local file (e.g., .gemini/tasks.json) to replace WriteToDo.

1. New Tool Definitions
The agent should have access to specific CRUD tools rather than just "writing" a list:
task_add(description: str, priority: str, dependency_id: int)
task_list(filter: str) (e.g., "show only 'ready' tasks")
task_update(id: int, status: str)
task_complete(id: int)

2. Storage Backend
Tasks should be serialized to a local file  in the working directory.

Benefits
1. Persistence: The agent can pick up exactly where it left off after a restart.
2. Efficiency: We stop burning tokens passing the entire completed history back and forth. The agent only queries task_list when it needs to know what to do next.
3. Complexity: Enables multi-step reasoning where the agent can plan out 20 steps and execute them over several days.

Address concerns and suggestions in https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/issues/17035 
Doc [go/tracker-gemini-cli](http://goto.google.com/tracker-gemini-cli)

prs.title: fix(core): recognize TortoiseGitPlink as a PuTTY-family SSH client
prs.body:
## Summary

`getSafeGitEnv()` recognized `plink` and legacy `TortoisePlink` as PuTTY-family SSH clients, but missed TortoiseGit's current `TortoiseGitPlink.exe`. It was therefore misclassified as OpenSSH and got `-o BatchMode=yes` appended instead of Plink's `-batch`, breaking non-interactive git-over-SSH for TortoiseGit users.

Fixes #29917

## Changes

- Extended the plink detection regex to also match `TortoiseGitPlink` (with optional `.exe`), keeping `plink`, legacy `TortoisePlink`, and OpenSSH behavior unchanged.
- `-batch` is added only when not already present; existing quoting and arguments in `GIT_SSH`/`GIT_SSH_COMMAND` are preserved.
- Added unit tests covering: the documented TortoiseGit `GIT_SSH` path, a quoted `GIT_SSH_COMMAND` with extra arguments, `-batch` deduplication, and a legacy `TortoisePlink` regression check.

## How to Validate

```
npm run test --workspace @google/gemini-cli-core -- src/utils/gitUtils.test.ts
```

All existing `getSafeGitEnv` tests plus the new TortoiseGitPlink cases pass. No SSH connection is needed — the helper is exercised with synthetic environment records.

- Guard the script entry point so its exported YAML runner can be tested without launching unrelated checks.

prs.title: fix(core): scan complete plan content and report read failures
prs.body:
## Summary

Accept non-empty plan files whose content appears after a long whitespace prefix, and report unreadable plans as read failures rather than empty files. The previous 1 KB sample rejected a valid plan beginning with 1,024 spaces even when real plan text followed immediately afterward.

## Details

- Scan the file in bounded chunks until non-whitespace content or EOF is found, stopping early when content is detected.
- Preserve BOM detection across short prefix reads. Decode UTF-8 and UTF-16 LE/BE incrementally; retain incomplete UTF-32 LE/BE code units between chunks.
- Keep memory bounded to the read buffer and decoder state rather than loading the whole plan.
- Propagate `isEmpty()` read errors to `validatePlanContent()`'s existing read-failure handler. This intentionally changes the helper's read-error behavior from returning true to rejecting; callers must handle read failures. The repository's plan validator already does so.
- Add regression coverage for the 1 KB boundary, multiple chunks, Unicode whitespace across chunks, all five supported BOM encodings, zero-byte/BOM-only files, truncated trailing code units, and unreadable files.
- Document the distinction between empty-plan and read-failure messages in the Plan Mode guide.

## Related Issues

Fixes #29941

## How to Validate

```sh
node node_modules/vitest/vitest.mjs run --root packages/core src/utils/fileUtils.test.ts src/utils/planUtils.test.ts src/tools/exit-plan-mode.test.ts --coverage.enabled=false --maxWorkers=2 --minWorkers=1
node node_modules/eslint/bin/eslint.js packages/core/src/utils/fileUtils.ts packages/core/src/utils/fileUtils.test.ts packages/core/src/utils/planUtils.test.ts --max-warnings 0
npm run typecheck -w @google/gemini-cli-core
node node_modules/prettier/bin/prettier.cjs --check packages/core/src/utils/fileUtils.ts packages/core/src/utils/fileUtils.test.ts packages/core/src/utils/planUtils.test.ts docs/cli/plan-mode.md
git diff --check
```

Validated on Windows with Node.js 22.19.0 and npm 10.9.3:
- The initial regression run against the old implementation had 13 failures and 129 passes in the file/plan utility suites.
- After the fix and completed test matrix, all 176 tests in fileUtils, planUtils, and exit-plan-mode pass.
- Core typechecking, changed-file ESLint, formatting, whitespace checks, and pre-commit checks pass.

Full `npm run preflight` completed dependency installation, repository formatting, the full workspace build, and repository-wide ESLint. It then stopped at the existing YAML-lint command because grep is not available on this native Windows shell. prs.title: ci(chained_e2e): don't expose GEMINI_API_KEY to fork-controlled code
prs.body:
## What

`chained_e2e.yml` is triggered by `workflow_run` after `trigger_e2e.yml` runs on a PR; it executes in the base-repo context with secrets and checks out the PR's code via an artifact the triggering run uploaded. This PR gates that artifact — and `GEMINI_API_KEY` — on the triggering run's **head repository** being this repository, and skips the secret-bearing jobs for any triggering run that is not a successful same-repo run. Defense-in-depth for the `workflow_run` + fork-checkout pattern.

## Changes (all in `.github/workflows/chained_e2e.yml`)

1. `download_repo_name` runs for a `workflow_run` only when that run's `conclusion == 'success'` and `github.event.workflow_run.head_repository.full_name == github.repository` — trustworthy event fields, not artifact contents.
2. `parse_run_context` exports a `trusted` output: for a `workflow_run` it is `false` unless `download_repo_name` succeeded and both artifact fields (`repo_name`, `head_sha`) are present. The `set_pending_status`, the e2e (linux / mac / windows), `evals`, the aggregate `e2e`, and `set_workflow_status` jobs are all gated on `trusted == 'true'`.
3. The `github.event.workflow_run.head_sha` fallback in the SHA resolution is removed — no silent fallback to an unverified sha.
4. `GEMINI_API_KEY` on the four test/eval steps is passed only when `parse_run_context.outputs.repository == github.repository` **and** (`event_name != 'workflow_run'` **or** `github.event.workflow_run.head_repository.full_name == github.repository`), with the event-field check as the authoritative guard; otherwise the step receives an empty value.
5. The Windows job drops `cache: 'npm'` (it errors on the fork path where no lock file is present) — a small trade-off: in-repo Windows runs lose npm caching.

## Behavior for pull requests from forks

`trigger_e2e.yml` still runs on every PR. But a fork PR's `workflow_run` carries a fork `head_repository`, so `download_repo_name` is skipped → `trusted` is `false` → the chained E2E / evals / status jobs are **skipped**, and no chained-E2E status is posted on the fork commit. **This is a behavior change:** fork PRs no longer get the automatic chained E2E that previously ran — that automatic keyed run on fork-checked-out code is exactly what this PR closes. Maintainers can run E2E for a specific fork commit via the existing `workflow_dispatch` path. If automatic E2E on fork PRs is wanted back, the follow-up is an Environment with required reviewers on the e2e jobs (as `eval-pr.yml` does with `eval-gate`).

## Verification

Static only: the YAML parses, and every job that reads `needs.parse_run_context.outputs.trusted` lists `parse_run_context` in `needs`. Not run end-to-end.

## Credit

The origin-check + trusted-gate design (commits `8a5396d`, `e2433b6`) is from @r-bedekar.

prs.title: feat(core): add model.requestTimeoutMs setting for the API headers timeout
prs.body:
## Summary

Adds a `model.requestTimeoutMs` setting so the 60s API headers timeout can be raised. Right now it can only be changed through the `DEFAULT_REQUEST_TIMEOUT` experiment flag, which is never fetched for Vertex AI / API key auth, so anyone with long-thinking requests just gets them aborted at 60s and replayed from scratch.

## Details

- New setting `model.requestTimeoutMs` (number, ms, requires restart). Not set = current behaviour, nothing changes by default.
- `Config.getRequestTimeoutMs()` returns the setting when it's a positive finite number, otherwise falls back to the experiment flag like before.
- No changes needed in `fetch.ts`. `refreshAuth` already calls `updateGlobalFetchTimeouts()` with whatever `getRequestTimeoutMs()` returns, and that runs for every auth type, so the setting is picked up for Vertex AI too.
- 0 / negative / NaN are ignored instead of being passed on, since `updateGlobalFetchTimeouts` throws on those.
- Regenerated `schemas/settings.schema.json` and `docs/reference/configuration.md` with `npm run schema:settings` / `npm run docs:settings`.

I went with a setting rather than the `GEMINI_API_HEADERS_TIMEOUT_MS` env var from the issue because the other model options already live under `model.*`. Happy to add the env var too if you'd prefer.

## Related Issues

Fixes #29693

## How to Validate

Unit tests:

```
cd packages/core
npx vitest run src/config/config.test.ts -t getRequestTimeoutMs
```

The 3 new behaviour tests (setting used, setting wins over the flag, applied via `refreshAuth` for Vertex AI) fail on `main` and pass here:

```
main:         Tests  3 failed | 5 passed | 247 skipped (255)
this branch:  Tests  8 passed | 247 skipped (255)
```

Also ran the full `packages/core/src/config/config.test.ts` (255 passed), `packages/cli/src/config/{settingsSchema,config,settings}.test.ts` (385 passed, 1 skipped), `npm run typecheck`, eslint and prettier on the touched files.

End to end, I pointed the bundled CLI at a small local server that waits 70s before sending response headers (`GOOGLE_GEMINI_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8787`, `gemini -m gemini-2.5-flash -p ping`):

![before/after](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/prath47/gemini-cli/pr-assets/requestTimeout-before-after.png)

Without the setting, the request is dropped after ~60s and retried (I killed it at 150s):

```
+2.6s   POST .../gemini-2.5-flash:streamGenerateContent?alt=sse  (holding 70s)
+63.0s  client closed connection before reply
+68.6s  POST .../gemini-2.5-flash:streamGenerateContent?alt=sse  (holding 70s)
+129.1s client closed connection before reply
...
Attempt 1 failed. Retrying with backoff... Error: exception TypeError: fetch failed sending request
Attempt 2 failed. Retrying with backoff... Error: exception TypeError: fetch failed sending request
```

With `"model": { "requestTimeoutMs": 120000 }`:

```
+2.6s   POST .../gemini-2.5-flash:streamGenerateContent?alt=sse  (holding 70s)
+72.6s  replied to .../gemini-2.5-flash:streamGenerateContent?alt=sse
pong
[cli exit 0 after 72s]
```

Updates `esbuild` from 0.25.0 to 0.28.2
Release notes

Sourced from esbuild's releases.

v0.28.2

  • Fix tree shaking bug due to TypeScript import alias (#4507)

    This release fixes a bug that could cause esbuild to incorrectly tree-shake imports that are used in a TypeScript type alias under certain circumstances. Affected code uses a TypeScript-specific import assignment and looks something like this:

    import Base from './dep.js';
import Alias = Base.SomeType;

  • Fix CSS minification bug involving & (#4497)

    This release fixes a bug where esbuild's CSS minifier incorrectly removed a & when it was unsafe to do so. Here is an example:

    /* Original code */
.a .b {
  & .b:not(& .c) {
    color: red;
  }
}

    /* Old output (with --minify) */
    
.a .b{.b:not(& .c){color:red}}
    

    /* New output (with --minify) */
    
.a .b{& .b:not(& .c){color:red}}

    This should match <span class="a"><span class="b"><span class="b">yes</span></span></span> but not <span class="a"><span class="b">no</span></span>. The old output incorrectly matched both.

  • Avoid overwriting input files without --allow-overwrite (#4484)

    For example: esbuild input.js --outfile=input.js tells esbuild to overwrite input.js with the output of running esbuild on it. This was supposed to already be prevented by default, but it accidentally regressed in version 0.17.0 and apparently didn't have any test coverage. The error message was being printed but the input file was still being overwritten. Oops.

    This release puts the original behavior back. With this release, esbuild should now actually avoid overwriting input files unless --allow-overwrite is explicitly present. This is done by not writing out any files when a build error is encountered.

  • Fix incorrect code generated when using top-level await (#4498)

    Previously esbuild could generate code containing a syntax error in complex scenarios involving top-level await used in a dependency cycle. The problem was a missing async on one or more module wrapper closures. With this release, esbuild now uses a fixed-point iteration algorithm to correctly annotate all dependencies in the cycle as needing an async module wrapper.

  • Fix a minification bug with lowered logical assignment operators (#4508)

    This release fixes a bug that could cause esbuild to generate incorrect code for logical assignment operators when lowering them to an older target environment. Specifically the lowering process requires duplicating the left-hand side, but esbuild incorrectly failed to count the duplicate as a new usage when the left-hand side is an identifier. That then caused the minifier to believe that the left-hand side was only used once and could attempt to incorrectly inline an initializer into the first usage. This bug has now been fixed:
