prs.title: fix(auto-reply): a message sent after /stop fails replay admission when the Stop reply is delivered late
prs.body:
Closes #194303

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: a message sent right after `/stop` can be recorded ahead of the Stop exchange in session history, and when its turn is replayed it fails admission ("Persisted user turn changed before replay admission") and is never answered, whenever the Stop reply reaches the channel late.

## User Impact

User impact: after `/stop`, the next message waits until the Stop reply is delivered and recorded, then runs and gets its answer, with the Stop exchange first in history. Input that was already waiting when the Stop arrived is still cancelled, as before.

## Why This Change Was Made

A `/stop` typed into the conversation it stops cancels its own controller source along with the pending input it selects, and that source is then consumed at once. The Stop reply records its `command-input` / `command-reply` exchange only after delivery, at dispatcher settlement (`dispatch-from-config.transcript.ts`, `sendReplyWithTranscriptMirror`). Nothing in the session owner holds the next turn across that delivery: the fast-abort path never claims a reply operation, so it gets none of the after-clear barrier ordinary replies register. A turn accepted after the Stop can therefore persist its user row before the Stop's rows land.

This change fixes the order the rows are written in. Once a stop request is recognized, and before the Stop selects anything, dispatch registers retention work on the Stop message's own source. The Stop still cancels that source, but the mailbox does not select past a source with unsettled work. When `finishFastCommand` hands the exchange to the direct dispatcher, it adds the dispatcher settlement as more retention work, bounded by `resolveFollowupAdmissionBarrierTimeoutPolicy`, the same bound an ordinary reply's barrier uses. The routed path already records inline. The source retires when the exchange is recorded, the delivery fails or the bound expires, and the next turn starts after the Stop's rows.

Unchanged: Stop's selection, command classification, the command history itself, and replay admission and its refresh.

#194336 and #194396 take the other route: both make command exchanges traversable for replay admission (`pre-persisted-user-turn.ts` and `session-manager-current-turn.ts`). ClawSweeper flagged that as changing the intent of `c2cb56c665e`, where ordinary commands stay context-bearing, with an owner decision required. This PR touches neither file and no replay or transcript predicate. A command row written before a turn still bars a stale replay exactly as on main. ClawSweeper's review of #194303 named this shape as the best fix: "Sequence Stop transcript recording through the existing session owner".

## Evidence

Base: main `51471b750b2`. Head: `272d4c60652`. macOS arm64, Node 26.12.1, 2 Vitest workers.

**Regression tests**, red on main (main's production files, these tests) and green here:
- `dispatch-from-config.command-transcript.test.ts` > "records a late-delivered /stop before the next turn's row", with and without an active run. It drives the real `dispatchReplyFromConfig` with a real reply dispatcher whose delivery is held, then starts the next turn. On main both cases fail with `expected [ 'next-turn', 'command-input', ...(1) ] to deeply equal [ 'command-input', ...(2) ]`. Here: 4/4, three runs.
- `attempt-session-replay.stop-delivery.test.ts` > "replays a turn admitted after a /stop whose reply is delivered late", for both replay-reader windows (initial selection and the selected reader). On main both throw `SessionWorkStartChangedError` (`SESSION_WORK_START_CHANGED`). Here: 2/2, three runs.
- Mutation controls, each failing both files: releasing the retention as soon as the Stop returns, retaining it only after the Stop's selection, and waiting for dispatcher idle instead of dispatcher settlement (the exchange is recorded by a settled task that runs after idle).

**ClawSweeper's commands from #194303:**
- `node scripts/test-projects.mts src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/attempt-session-replay.test.ts`: 61/61.
- `... dispatch-from-config.command-transcript.test.ts abort.target-owner.test.ts src/config/sessions/transcript.test.ts`: 4, 54 and 46, all passed.
- `... src/agents/agent-tools.prefix-stability.test.ts`: 14/14.

**Gateway run.** A real Gateway child from each tree's `dist`, a local fake Telegram Bot API and a scripted Responses provider, in one DM:
- The sequence: a long turn, a second message queued behind it, `/stop`, and a third message 300 ms later. The fake Bot API holds the Stop reply for 4 s.
- On main: the third message's turn sends its model request at 10.32 s, while the Stop reply is held until 13.27 s. `chat.history` afterwards reads `LONG-TURN`, `LATER-ACCEPTED`, `ANSWER-LATER`, `/stop`, `Agent was aborted.`
- Here: that turn starts only after the Stop reply is delivered (delivery at 15.57 s, typing at 15.68 s, model request at 15.75 s). History reads `LONG-TURN`, `/stop`, `Agent was aborted.`, `LATER-ACCEPTED`, `ANSWER-LATER`.
- Both: the queued second message never reaches the model, and the third is answered once.
- The local fake stands in for Telegram here. The Telegram E2E skill needs the OpenClaw Convex broker, and the Mantis proof workflow does not run on fork PRs.

On main, this harness reproduces the order but not the admission refusal itself. Its turns go from saving the user row to admission in under a second, and Stop replies held from 300 ms to 4 s never landed in that gap. The refusal is what the replay regression above pins, and what I saw live on 2026.10.10, twice, as reported in #194303.

**Checks at the head:**
- `pnpm tsgo:all`: pass.
- `ci-baseline-ratchets.mts --base 51471b750b2`: all ok. Test lines OK, slack 50. 239 lines are allocated in `config/test-lines-allocations/194303-stop-exchange-order.txt`.
- `node scripts/check-changed.mjs --base 51471b750b2`: every guard passes except "changelog attributions". That one fails identically on unmodified main: 20 `Thanks @steipete-oai` lines in `CHANGELOG/2026.6.8.md` and `2026.7.1.md`.
- `node scripts/test-projects.mts --changed 51471b750b2`: 942 files, 7739 passed, 1 failed. The failure is `plugin-preparation-exec-argv.test.ts` > "publishes and loads the selected closure with the caller's real worker conditions", which fails the same way on main.

Not covered: real Telegram, Linux, and the routed (non-dispatcher) reply path end to end. The routed path records inline and is unchanged.

prs.title: fix(gateway): match canonical Unicode in human mentions
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The human mention directory misses a person's display name when the query and stored name use different canonical Unicode forms. For example, `CAFE\u0301` does not find `Café Person`, although a literal `CAFÉ` query does. This affects the `users.mentionable` results used by the chat composer and person-reference lookup.

## Why This Change Was Made

`createHumanMentionPolicy().search` owns the eligible directory and its text matching. Normalize its existing lowercase query, display-name projection, and verified-login projection to NFC. Keep the eligibility/visibility checks, cached directory, stored profile, returned label, profile ID, and response shape unchanged. Built-in normalization is sufficient; no new dependency, option, storage format, or parallel search path is needed.

## User Impact

People can find the same eligible person with canonically equivalent text from different keyboards or pasted sources. Original names remain intact. Accents remain significant; this adds neither fuzzy matching nor accent removal. It does not grant access to additional users or sessions.

## Evidence

Base: `b6d8eb287e0898d2c50d89abaef749e4c25ca66a`. Tested source and native build: `3dc06a37a08a00eac8eaca47cb3f85ef9139fd54` (`2026.11.1`). The owner is also unchanged on the subsequently inspected main `5f84a8166dc524a4eab375b16030239acbefc92b`.

### Real Gateway RED → GREEN

The same frozen driver started the actual built Gateway on an isolated loopback port with a private state directory and two synthetic trusted-proxy identities. It connected through the production WebSocket protocol, set the second user's name with `users.setDisplayName`, queried `users.mentionable` as the first user, and independently read back the stored name with `users.self` as the second user. No policy method, database, search result, or WebSocket response was mocked.

| Stored display name | Actual query | Base result | Head result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Café Person` (NFC) | `CAFE\u0301` | `users: []` | Original profile ID and NFC name |
| `Cafe\u0301 Person` (NFD) | `CAFÉ` | `users: []` | Same profile ID and original NFD name |

`\u0301` denotes the actual combining character in the request. Each literal-name control succeeds on both revisions. Unrelated text and the requesting user do not appear. The head's independent `users.self` read retains the original name in both forms.

Actual head readback, Linux / Node 24.22.1 / November 9, 2026:

```text
users.setDisplayName {displayName:"Café Person"} -> ok
users.mentionable {agentId:"main",visibility:"shared",query:"CAFE\u0301"}
  -> users:[{profileId:"c2027e24-3282-4fd0-afa3-cdfb760c8148",
             displayName:"Café Person",avatarUrl:<existing avatar URL>,online:true}]
users.self -> id:"c2027e24-3282-4fd0-afa3-cdfb760c8148", displayName:"Café Person"
users.setDisplayName {displayName:"Cafe\u0301 Person"} -> ok
users.mentionable {agentId:"main",visibility:"shared",query:"CAFÉ"}
  -> same profileId, displayName:"Cafe\u0301 Person"
users.self -> same id, displayName:"Cafe\u0301 Person"
canonical queries: base 0/2; head 2/2; literal and exclusion controls passed
```

To reproduce, use two permitted identities on a local Gateway; set one display name to NFC `Café Person`; have the other send the first `users.mentionable` request above. Repeat after setting the NFD form. Compare the returned ID with the target's `users.self` response and verify that response's display-name bytes. The proof's trusted-proxy fixture is confined to loopback; it is not a deployment or auth-configuration recommendation.

<details>
<summary>Focused validation, cost, and limitations</summary>

Frozen external driver:

```sh
node ../replace-four-mention-proof-20261109.mjs "$PWD" green ../mentions-green.json
```

The base run changes only `green` to `red` to assert the expected misses. Driver SHA-256: `5ec455e110d1ef67841314a26d23d987d95a3a47ddf0295d90338c0f86ec4cb9`. The green receipt's source SHA and `dist/build-info.json` commit both equal the tested head above.

- Acceptance RED: both real Gateway canonical queries miss on base while literal queries succeed. The two focused regression cases also fail on base.
- `OPENCLAW_VITEST_RUNTIME=node node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/gateway/mention-directory.test.ts src/gateway/mention-inbox.test.ts --maxWorkers=1 --reporter=dot`: 50 tests passed across the existing directory and inbox suites. The two-file wrapper took 505.56s, including a 114.899s cold worker compilation and SQLite fixture lifecycle work; this is not production latency.
- Scoped source-backed `tsgo`, typed `oxlint`, `oxfmt`, and `git diff --check`: passed.
- Staged test-line ratchet: passed, 6,589,094 lines against a 6,589,126 ceiling; an 18-line allocation accounts for the two parameterized cases without changing the shared scalar baseline.
- Native `sourcePerformance` build of the committed head: passed in 4m24.4s, followed by the real Gateway GREEN proof above.
- Author simplification and test-value audit completed. No independent model review is claimed. Production +6/−3, tests +18/−0, allocation metadata +2; no new helper or call path.

Compatibility/security: no config/default, protocol, permissions, account linking, identity, schema, persisted-data, or dependency change. The same eligibility filtering runs before matching. The UI consumes these directory results; it does not introduce another client-side name matcher.

Not tested: browser rendering, external chat services, model turns, cross-OS behavior, the full repository suite, or upstream PR CI before opening. This proves the actual Gateway mention-directory contract and stored-name readback, not a browser or production deployment.

</details>

prs.title: fix(workers): mount workspace paths that contain a comma
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: node workers fail to start when their workspace, HOME, or bundle path contains a comma (for example `/home/ana/Projects/acme, inc/api`), because `docker create` rejects the bind mount argument with `invalid field '...' must be a key=value pair`.

## User Impact

User impact: machines whose project paths contain a comma can use `nodeHost.workerRuns.isolation = "container"` again instead of failing at worker admission. Every path that mounts today produces the same arguments as before, byte for byte.

## Why This Change Was Made

`--mount` is not a plain `key=value` flag: the engine parses it with the CSV field grammar, so an unquoted comma inside `source=` ends the field early. The three bind mounts in `createNodeWorkerContainer` interpolated the path verbatim, so a comma in a directory name split one field into two unparsable ones.

The change quotes a whole `key=value` field only when its path holds a comma, doubling interior quotes, which is the form that parser reads. Commas are the only trigger on purpose: every path that triggers quoting already fails on both supported engines today, so no launch that works can change shape. A path with a quote but no comma is left alone, because Docker rejects it and Podman accepts it today; quoting it here would trade one engine's bug for the other's, so that conflict is not settled in this change.

`--workdir` and the `HOME` environment value take the path as a single argument and parse commas fine (checked against the same daemon), so they stay untouched.

## Evidence

Every run below is the shipped build of this head: `pnpm build cliStartup` from the PR branch, then the real `openclaw gateway`, `openclaw node run --session-host`, docker 29.4.2, and the real container worker.

### 1. Engine arguments, unit level

Each row creates a container through the shipped `createNodeWorkerContainer`, compares `docker inspect` mount sources with the requested paths, and removes it again.

| workspace path | `origin/main` (`61093f1d32c`) | this change |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `/tmp/oc377/plain` | mounts | mounts |
| `/tmp/oc377/acme, inc` | `invalid field ' inc/bundle/current' must be a key=value pair` | mounts |
| `/tmp/oc377/a,"b` | `parse error on line 1, column 68: extraneous or missing " in quoted-field` | mounts |
| `/tmp/oc377/a"b` | `parse error on line 1, column 29: bare " in non-quoted-field` | unchanged, still rejected |
| `/tmp/oc377/a=b` | mounts | mounts |
| `/tmp/oc377/trail ` | mounts | mounts |
| `/tmp/oc377/a:b` | mounts | mounts |

### 2. Container-isolated session end to end

A comma-bearing root `/tmp/proof/work,space/demo` is granted as the node's device folder (the node's own `nodeHost.workerRuns.folders` consent), a session is created against it, dispatched, and turned. Raw output from the shipped Gateway and node host:

```
[proof] worker container appeared after 1x2s: c24633601b7c
===== docker inspect mounts =====
  .../gateway-dec0758d8a2fb4d022b32545e804e7f3/bundles/88150e7598... -> ... (same)  rw=false
  /tmp/proof/work,space/demo -> /tmp/proof/work,space/demo                          rw=true
  .../gateway-dec0758d8a2fb4d022b32545e804e7f3/workspaces/5180573428eefeae/.../2 -> (same)  rw=true
  WORKDIR=/tmp/proof/work,space/demo
===== container argv/env/state =====
  ARGS=[.../bundles/88150e7598.../worker.mjs, --internal-worker-session]  STATE=running
  HOME_ENV=HOME=.../gateway-dec0758d8a2fb4d022b32545e804e7f3/workspaces/5180573428eefeae/.../2
===== container filesystem workspace =====
  /tmp/proof/work,space/demo
  -rw-r--r-- 1 1001 1001   20 MARKER_COMMA_195304.txt
  MARKER_COMMA_195304
===== workspace marker on host =====
  -rw-r--r-- 1 runner runner   20 MARKER_COMMA_195304.txt
  MARKER_COMMA_195304
===== marker inside container =====
  HOME=.../workspaces/5180573428eefeae/.../2
  MARKER_COMMA_195304
===== mock provider request log =====
  POST chat/completions messages=3 hasToolResult=false tools=["apply_patch",...,"exec",...]
  POST chat/completions messages=5 hasToolResult=true  tools=["apply_patch",...,"exec",...]
[proof] DONE container=c24633601b7c final=COMMA_WORKSPACE_PROOF_OK
```

What this pins: the comma-bearing workspace mounts at its own path and becomes `WORKDIR`, the bundle stays read-only, `HOME` is a private worker workspace, `exec` writes the marker inside the container, and that file appears on the host. Restoring the interpolation at `src/node-host/node-worker-container-engine.ts:297-303` makes this run fail at `docker create`.

Workflow: https://github.com/shuisadev/openclaw-pr-195304-proof/actions/runs/42553787186

### 3. Regression coverage

Folded into the existing suite in `src/node-host/node-worker-container-engine.test.ts` (no new file): one case with a comma and a quote in the bundle and workspace paths asserts the quoted fields with doubled quotes and the trailing `,readonly`, while the neighbouring existing test keeps pinning the unquoted argv for ordinary paths.

- `origin/main` engine file with this test file: 1 failed | 5 passed (the new case fails on the missing quotes)
- this change: 6 passed
- `src/node-host/node-worker-supervisor.container.test.ts` (supervisor path, shim engine): 15 passed, including the case that pins bundle and workspace mounts for ordinary paths

### Gaps

No Podman binary here, so that engine's behaviour is reasoned from its `--mount` parsing rather than executed. Local `tsgo` needs glibc 2.34 (`tsrs`), this host has 2.28, so type checking comes from CI.

The regression test adds 20 net test lines, recorded in `config/test-lines-allocations/node-worker-bind-mount-comma.txt`.

CI reports this branch as `over by: 2; net delta: +20`, and those 2 lines come from files this change does not
touch; raising the grant to 22 is itself rejected (`allocation credit 22 exceeds allowed ceiling growth 20`). The
grant therefore stays at exactly the 20 lines the test adds, and the inherited overage stays a base problem.

prs.title: fix(sandbox): resolve literal remote-shell file paths without trimming
prs.body:
## Summary

- Problem: `RemoteShellSandboxFsBridge.resolveTarget` trimmed the tool-supplied `filePath` (`.trim()`), so a literal file whose name starts or ends with whitespace (e.g. `" x.txt"`) was silently resolved as its trimmed sibling `x.txt`. A sandboxed agent reading or writing `" x.txt"` touched the decoy file instead of the one the model chose.
- Solution: Use the caller's literal `filePath` in `resolveTarget` instead of trimming it. Containment guards operate on the literal-resolved path, so safety is unchanged.
- What changed: `src/agents/sandbox/remote-fs-bridge.ts` (removed the `filePath.trim()` in `resolveTarget`), plus a regression test in `src/agents/sandbox/remote-fs-bridge.test.ts` (Linux-only GNU shell lane, per the platform separation in #131339) and a test-line allocation in `config/test-lines-allocations/remote-shell-literal-path-192041.txt`.
- What did NOT change: No changes to mount resolution, containment guards, read/write semantics, or the local sandbox bridge. No other components were affected.

Fixes #192041

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed:** A file whose name starts with whitespace is a distinct filesystem entry from its trimmed sibling. Before this fix, the remote-shell bridge addressed the trimmed sibling, so literal paths were unreachable and writes could clobber the wrong file.
- **Real environment tested:** `/home/0668000889/code/ai/aispace/openclaw-worktrees/issue-192041` with vitest, exercising the real `RemoteShellSandboxFsBridge` through the local remote-shell script runner (the same harness the suite uses for all remote-fs operations).
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch:**
  ```bash
  node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run src/agents/sandbox/remote-fs-bridge.test.ts -t "literal whitespace"
  ```
- **Evidence after fix (current head d904f8fb):** The regression test passes: `readFile({ filePath: " x.txt" })` returns `Buffer.from("literal bytes")` (not the decoy `x.txt`), `readFile({ filePath: "x.txt" })` returns the decoy bytes, and `writeFile({ filePath: " y.txt", data: "literal write" })` creates `" y.txt"` while leaving `y.txt` intact. Focused test: 1 passed.
- **Behavior proof on base vs head (A/B):** The same regression test was run against the base source (`origin/main` still trimming, `const input = params.filePath.trim()`). On base it FAILS with the defect visible: `readFile({ filePath: " x.txt" })` resolves to the decoy `x.txt` (`Buffer[100,101,99,111,121,...]` = "decoy bytes" instead of "literal bytes"). On head (this PR) the identical test PASSES. This directly demonstrates the regression failing on base and passing on head through the real bridge.
- **Observed result after fix:** Literal whitespace-prefixed file names are now resolved as their own entries, matching how the runtime skill catalog and other literal-path fixes (#187554, #187777, #187766) treat them.
- **What was not tested:** A live remote SSH host was not exercised; the suite's local remote-shell script runner executes the same bridge scripts, and the 4 failures in this file are pre-existing local-environment guards failures (confirmed identical on pristine main).

## Regression Test Plan

- Coverage level: Unit test
- Target test file: `src/agents/sandbox/remote-fs-bridge.test.ts`
- Scenario locked in: Reading and writing a file whose name starts with a space resolves the literal entry, not its trimmed sibling; the sibling remains untouched.
- Why this is the smallest reliable guardrail: It pins the exact defect (trimmed path addressing the sibling) through the production bridge for both read and write paths.

## Root Cause

- Root cause: `resolveTarget` in `src/agents/sandbox/remote-fs-bridge.ts` applied `.trim()` to the caller's `filePath`, so whitespace-prefixed/suffixed file names could not be addressed and always resolved to their trimmed sibling.
- Missing detection / guardrail: The bridge did not preserve the literal path supplied by the tool, unlike the local bridge and the already-merged literal-path fixes for extraDirs/OpenShell mirror/mxc.

## Review follow-up (d904f8fb)

- The regression test now lives inside the existing Linux-only GNU-shell `describe` block (per the deliberate platform separation established in #131339), so it cannot fail on Windows or stock macOS where GNU `readlink`/`stat` options are unavailable.
- Added `config/test-lines-allocations/remote-shell-literal-path-192041.txt` (18 lines) covering the regression's test-line growth so the shared test-lines baseline stays unchanged.
- A/B behavior proof above: regression fails on base (trim), passes on head (literal).

prs.title: fix: queued follow-ups drop the implicit reply target
prs.body:
<!--
Optional linked context:
Add a visible `Closes #<issue-number>` or `Related: #<issue-number>` line
below this comment.

Required PR title:
type: user-facing description
-->

Closes #142268

<details>
<summary>Additional instructions</summary>

**MUST:** Keep **Allow edits from maintainers** enabled for this PR so maintainers
can help update the branch when needed.

</details>

## What Problem This Solves

Queued follow-up answers on resolver-less channels (Telegram after restart, no live dispatcher) dropped the implicit reply target, so `reply_to_message_id` was missing.

This PR restores that injection for same-channel external/legacy turns. It does **not** claim ordinary overlapping-turn parity through a live Telegram Test Server run.

## Why This Change Was Made

Queued follow-up delivery already stores `messageId` / `originatingReplyToId` at admission. Payload resolution only applied reply tags and never ran the same implicit-injection helper the live path uses.

Queued payloads now go through `resolveReplyThreadingPayloads`. Implicit `currentMessageId` is injected only for resolver-less channels, with the same origin/provenance exclusions as `routeReply` (same-channel external or legacy user turns). Channels that own `resolveReplyTransport` keep correlation at `routeReply`, so empty/`replyToId` opt-outs survive. Restart-sentinel still keeps `originatingReplyToId`. Explicit `replyToId` still wins. `replyToMode` `off` / `first` / `all` stay authoritative.

## User Impact

On resolver-less transports, queued follow-up answers reply to the triggering same-channel message. Cross-channel and internal/inter-session IDs are not forwarded. Channels with a transport resolver still decide correlation at final routing.

## Evidence

Rebased onto current `main` as a single commit. Head SHA: `c6f38a93c8f7f9266efe7d3b39dbfd1aa799494b`. Marker: `PROOF_OK_c6f38a93`.

Focused Vitest after this revision (`test/vitest/vitest.auto-reply-reply.config.ts`): `followup-delivery.test.ts` + `followup-delivery.channel.test.ts` + `followup-delivery.implicit-reply.test.ts` + `followup-delivery-payloads.test.ts` + `followup-turn-admission.test.ts` — **137 passed**.

Coverage:

- same-channel queued `messageId` still injects `replyToId` on resolver-less channels
- Discord-origin / Slack-destination IDs are withheld at decision time
- inter-session child announcements stay unthreaded
- restart-sentinel keeps `originatingReplyToId`
- explicit `replyToId` survives excluded implicit IDs
- empty `replyToId` opt-out survives decision and delivery through the real channel resolver
- decision-to-delivery matrix matches those exclusions through the real channel resolver
- core tests use a fixture channel; they no longer import `extensions/qa-channel`

Sabotage: switching decision injection back to unguarded `resolveFollowupCurrentMessageId` turns the foreign-channel and inter-session tests red.

Runtime observation on `ba68eaeb` used the real Gateway + Telegram transport after restart and recorded the queued answer referencing message 11. That remains the dispatcher-less recovery proof. Telegram Test Server E2E for ordinary overlap was **not** rerun (no Convex QA broker credentials on this fork).

## Maintainer refresh — September 14, 2026

Refreshed onto `82a9bef596011a6145d7f639d9773ff5e7267f7d`, preserving the original patch and contributor authorship. Current candidate: `6d592e236f8d40d33c911391ad795ed59062b439`.

Fresh review exposed an empty-target regression on channels without a transport resolver. The shared threading owner now distinguishes an absent reply target from `replyToId: ""`; the latter remains an explicit opt-out. Inline explicit-reply directives still override that implicit-threading opt-out. This is an owner-level condition change, not a follow-up-specific workaround.

Verification:
- Added regressions failed on the pre-repair candidate: **3 failed, 46 passed**.
- Repaired candidate: **183 passed across 7 suites**, covering queued delivery, channel boundaries, admission/provenance, resolver delegation, shared threading, empty/false opt-outs, inline override, first-reply slot accounting, and deduplication.
- Command: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/auto-reply/reply/followup-delivery.test.ts src/auto-reply/reply/followup-delivery.channel.test.ts src/auto-reply/reply/followup-delivery.implicit-reply.test.ts src/auto-reply/reply/followup-delivery-payloads.test.ts src/auto-reply/reply/followup-turn-admission.test.ts src/auto-reply/reply/reply-plumbing.test.ts src/auto-reply/reply/reply-threading.test.ts`
- `git diff --check` passed. The repair adds one net production line (an explanatory comment) and 61 test lines. Full changed-surface static checks and hosted CI are tracked separately; this section does not claim they have completed.
- This is deterministic owner/channel-boundary proof, not new authenticated live-channel proof.

Review adjudication: the fresh autoreview returned four reports, not a scoped-clean result. The index-only empty-target finding is resolved in the committed candidate. Two resolver-owned issues were verified as unchanged baseline behavior and recorded as follow-ups: **resolver-owned empty/false opt-out consistency** and **separating explicit inline current-message resolution from implicit correlation policy**. The reported QA dedupe mismatch was not established: that resolver returns a native message reference without `threadId: null`, while the dedupe owner treats `replyToId` as a conversation thread only for the explicit-null transport contract. No new unresolved P0–P2 regression was independently confirmed in this candidate.

prs.title: fix(sessions): sessions_history reads transcripts for configured ACP owners
prs.body:
Addresses the `sessions_history` follow-up in #164847. The `sessions_search` half was fixed by the merged #164897; the ACP `sessions_spawn` dispatch mismatch tracked in the same place remains open and is not touched here. Taken up at @obviyus's suggestion after #164901 was closed as a duplicate of #164897.

## What Problem This Solves

The model-facing `sessions_history` tool fails with `Unknown agent id "<harness>"` for a visible ACP session when the harness id is configured in `acp.allowedAgents` but absent from `agents.entries`. The tool sends that harness id explicitly to the Gateway `sessions.resolve` visibility probe and to `chat.history`, and the shared session-request validation (`resolveRequestedSessionAgentId`) rejects any explicit id outside the native roster before key-based admission could accept the configured store owner. The same authenticated caller can already list the session and read its transcript through the Gateway without that redundant explicit id.

## Why This Change Was Made

An agent-qualified session key already selects its owner, so the tool now omits the explicit `agentId` from both requests when it duplicates the key's own agent (`agent:<harness>:acp:<uuid>` keys from ACP spawn, resolved like any agent-qualified key). Unqualified keys and genuine owner mismatches keep sending the id, so callers that need the roster/mismatch guards keep them. Transcript-sharing and visibility checks are unchanged: `resolveSessionToolAccess` runs the same decision checkers, the Gateway sharing layer still filters the read, and with `tools.sessions.visibility: "self"` the same ACP transcript stays forbidden. Search does not grant new transcript visibility through this change either.

## User Impact

Agents configured with ACP harnesses (for example `opencode` or `codex` in `acp.allowedAgents`) can read session transcript history again without adding harness ids to `agents.entries`; today the whole tool call errors out and operators fall back to the Gateway `chat.history` RPC or the CLI.

## Evidence

- Failing-first on the current main tip (`e785c56d8`): reverting the two source files on top of this branch (`git checkout origin/main -- src/agents/tools/sessions-resolution.ts src/agents/tools/sessions-history-tool.ts`) while keeping the new regression reproduces the maintainer-reported rejection from the real tool flow:

  ```
  { status: "error", error: 'Unknown agent id "opencode"' }
  ```

- New embedded-gateway regression (`reads a configured ACP owner transcript without an explicit agent id` in `src/agents/tools/embedded-gateway-stub.history.test.ts`) runs the real `sessions_history` tool against real session-request validation: seeded ACP store entry, seeded ACP runtime meta (as real ACP spawn persists), and `agents.entries: { main }` + `acp.allowedAgents: ["opencode"]`. It fails on base as above and passes with the fix (17/17 in that file).
- New gateway-level control in `src/gateway/server-methods/sessions-read.test.ts` (`sessions history reads a configured ACP owner without an explicit agent id`): `chat.history` without the id returns the seeded ACP transcript on base and head, while the explicit harness id stays rejected with `INVALID_REQUEST`, pinning the contract the fix relies on.
- Five wire-contract assertions were updated where they pinned the now-omitted redundant id (explicit `agentId` equal to the key's own agent): four in `sessions-resolution.test.ts`, one in `sessions-history-tool.test.ts`. The latter ("resolves current history under the requester instead of the fixed-store owner") also removes a latent contradiction derived from the code: under a global fixed store, the old explicit-id path validated `agent:<agent>:main` against the fixed-store owner, so the id the tool sent would be rejected by a real Gateway; the key-based admission this change relies on resolves the same request to the requester.
- Scoped runs: `pnpm test src/agents/tools/embedded-gateway-stub.history.test.ts`, `pnpm test src/agents/tools/sessions-resolution.test.ts` (25/25), `pnpm test src/agents/tools/sessions-history-tool.test.ts` (26/26), `pnpm test src/gateway/server-methods/sessions-read.test.ts` (no failures), plus the `sessions-send-tool.*` and `sessions-search-tool.*` suites.
- `oxlint` on the six touched files: 0 warnings, 0 errors; `oxfmt --check` clean; `pnpm check:line-cap-ratchet` passes.
- `tsgo:core` reports only two pre-existing errors in `src/infra/state-migrations.state-dir.ts` that reproduce identically with the change reverted; CI is authoritative for typecheck. Also pre-existing and unrelated on this Windows checkout (verified by reverting the change): the `sessions-access.test.ts` EPERM temp-dir cleanup cascade and one timing-sensitive `sessions-search-tool.test.ts` incarnation-race test.

Prepared with AI assistance (same as #164901); I have reviewed and verified the changes.


## Real behavior proof

Below: after-fix proof from a **real ACP setup** — the actual `openclaw gateway` process (spawned subprocess from source, real config file, real SQLite session store in a real state dir, `agents.entries: {main}`, `acp.allowedAgents: ["opencode"]`) plus a self-visibility denial control and a before-fix control on the same rig. No embedded gateway, no vitest: the gateway executed its own production tool set through the Gateway's `tools.invoke` RPC (which resolves the real `sessions_history` tool via the gateway's tool resolution and runs it with the production in-process gateway-request binding), as an operator client over the real WebSocket protocol with token auth.

Setup (per scenario):

```
$ node --import tsx src/entry.ts gateway --port <port>          # real gateway process
config: { "agents": { "entries": { "main": {} } },
          "acp": { "allowedAgents": ["opencode"] },
          "gateway": { "mode": "local", "port": <port>,
                       "auth": { "mode": "token", "token": "<redacted>" } },
          "plugins": { "enabled": false } }
# session store seeded the way ACP spawn persists it:
#   entry + canonical ACP runtime meta + one transcript message
#   sessionKey: agent:opencode:acp:acp-proof-<runId>, sessionId: acp-proof-<runId>

$ tools.invoke { "name": "sessions_history",
                 "args": { "sessionKey": "agent:opencode:acp:acp-proof-<runId>", "limit": 10 },
                 "sessionKey": "agent:main:main" }        # requester = main
```

**1. After fix — successful tool retrieval through the real Gateway** (`ok: true`, transcript read via key-based admission without the redundant explicit id):

```json
{
  "ok": true,
  "toolName": "sessions_history",
  "output": {
    "content": [{ "type": "text", "text": "{\n  \"sessionKey\": \"agent:opencode:acp:acp-proof-r10\",\n  \"messages\": [\n    {\n      \"role\": \"assistant\",\n      \"content\": \"acp history needle LIVE-PROOF\",\n      \"timestamp\": 1700000000000,\n      \"__openclaw\": { \"id\": \"acp-answer\", ... }\n    }\n  ],\n  \"truncated\": false,\n  ...\n}" }]
  },
  "source": "core"
}
```

Gateway-side trace: `⇄ res ✓ tools.invoke ... conn=…` — a completed RPC whose tool executed the same `sessions.resolve` → `chat.history` sequence the fix relies on.

**2. Self-visibility denial control — same ACP session, `tools.sessions.visibility: "self"`, requester `main`** — the denial is preserved (the fix does not open cross-agent visibility):

```json
{
  "ok": true,
  "toolName": "sessions_history",
  "output": {
    "details": {
      "status": "forbidden",
      "error": "Session history visibility is restricted. Set tools.sessions.visibility=all to allow cross-agent access; use tools.agentToAgent to restrict permitted agent pairs."
    }
  },
  "source": "core"
}
```

**3. Before-fix control — same rig, only the two production files reverted to current main** (`git checkout origin/main -- src/agents/tools/sessions-history-tool.ts src/agents/tools/sessions-resolution.ts`): the exact failure this PR fixes, reproduced through the real Gateway:

```json
{
  "ok": true,
  "toolName": "sessions_history",
  "output": {
    "details": {
      "status": "error",
      "error": "Unknown agent id \"opencode\""
    }
  },
  "source": "core"
}
```

The working tree was restored to the PR head immediately after the capture.

## CI findings for run 37214065475 (failed checks on the reviewed head)

- `check-test-types-core-3` — **ours, fixed in this head**: `src/agents/tools/embedded-gateway-stub.history.test.ts(408,7): error TS2353: Object literal may only specify known properties, and 'agentId' does not exist in type ...` (the excess-property finding). Landed commit `test(agents): drop unsupported agentId option in embedded history regression` removes the property; the shard's typecheck (`test/tsconfig/tsconfig.core.test.agents-tools.json`) now reports only the two pre-existing `src/infra/state-migrations.state-dir.ts` errors that reproduce identically on main.
- `checks-ui-e2e (1/2)` — **not ours**: failed in `ui/src/e2e/chat-composer-catalog.e2e.test.ts` ("keeps the selected model during startup, then tracks fallback and recovery at 1280px/390px", `AssertionError: expected 'false' to be 'true'`). The PR diff touches only `src/agents/tools/*` and `src/gateway/server-methods/sessions-read.test.ts`; the Control UI composer catalog is outside the change surface, and recent `ci.yml` runs on `main` (e.g. 37255313251, 37255065184) pass the same workflow.
- `checks-ui-e2e-real-gateway (2/2)` — **not ours**: failed in `ui/src/e2e/worker-initial-setup.real-gateway.e2e.test.ts` ("holds browser and sessions_send input during sync, then launches each exactly once", ~39 s — a timeout-shaped failure in the Control UI worker-initial-setup custody flow). Also outside this PR's surface for the same reason.
- `openclaw/ci-gate` — aggregate of the three above.

## Test-cost measurements

Single-worker local wall times on this Windows checkout (Node v26.10.0, cold tsx transform dominates; CI timings come from the exact-head jobs):

- `pnpm test src/agents/tools/embedded-gateway-stub.history.test.ts`: 17/17 passed — 280.7 s vitest (296 s wall), of which 178 s was first-run module transform.
- Typecheck of the CI shard that failed (`tsgo` `tsconfig.core.test.agents-tools.json`): no errors in touched files; only the two pre-existing `src/infra/state-migrations.state-dir.ts` errors remain (identical on main).
- `oxlint` on the touched test file: 0 warnings, 0 errors; `check:line-cap-ratchet`: OK ("6 changed source files; no new violations or over-cap growth").
- Real-gateway proof rig: 3 gateway subprocess scenarios (after / self-visibility / before), each a single spawned `openclaw gateway` process; tool invocation round-trip per scenario ≈ 16 s RPC (`tools.invoke` completed in 16.1 s server-side on the cold run).

Prepared with AI assistance (same as #164901); I have reviewed and verified the changes.

prs.title: fix(qa-lab): identify the stage when Telegram QA setup fails
prs.body:
Fixes #195565

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: Telegram QA setup timeouts do not identify which setup step failed.

## User Impact

Developers running Telegram QA can distinguish proxy startup, stale-update draining, and userbot startup failures. This is QA tooling only; normal Telegram messaging is unchanged. Timeout budgets and credential lease cleanup remain unchanged; no migration or user action is required.

## Why This Change Was Made

Track the active setup stage in the existing adapter and include it in the failure message while preserving the original error as its cause. Combined setup-and-cleanup failures also name the setup stage without changing cleanup or quarantine decisions.

## Evidence

- Regression proof on main base `43dae0b46f1eb1dcfed7434196ff3bf1aa8a9b2a`: all three new timeout-stage cases failed for the missing stage message; the 18 existing adapter cases passed.
- Fixed candidate: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/qa-lab/src/live-transports/telegram/adapter.runtime.test.ts extensions/qa-lab/src/live-transports/telegram/cli.runtime.test.ts --maxWorkers=1` — 31 tests passed, including combined setup/cleanup failure coverage. Vitest wall time: 2.43s; wrapper time: 3.44s. CI seconds are not available yet.
- Targeted TypeScript check of the changed adapter and test passed using the repository tsgo wrapper; targeted format and lint passed; `git diff --check` passed.
- Test-line ratchet passed with zero slack. The separate 39-line allocation is exactly the net regression-test growth needed to distinguish the three failure stages and preserve the combined failure/cause/cleanup contract; the shared scalar is unchanged.
- Simplification removed the donor’s single-use error helper. Net change versus base: +10 production lines and +39 test lines; no new abstraction or timeout policy.

prs.title: fix(cron): record designed heartbeat skips as successful no-ops
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

An agent whose heartbeat file is intentionally empty (or comments-only) skips every interval by design, but each skip was recorded as a `skipped` cron run, which `resolveCronCompletionStatus` maps to `failed`. `openclaw tasks list --status failed` accrued one row per interval (~48/day) for the heartbeat cron and failure alerts fired, even though `consecutiveErrors` stayed 0 (#144959).

Designed no-op skips now settle as `ok` runs whose summary carries the skip reason (`heartbeat skipped: empty-heartbeat-file`), matching the busy-deferral handoff path that already returned `ok`. The heartbeat runner's own state (`system heartbeat last`, `consecutiveSkipped`) keeps reporting the precise skipped status, so no signal is lost.

## Evidence

- **Real-behavior proof (updated in f8c3fa97 and 6fb6ec66 per review):** `src/cron/service.heartbeat-real-preflight.test.ts` wires the **real heartbeat runner** (real preflight, no injected heartbeat results), a **real comments-only scratch row** in the sqlite state store (stock "keep this file empty" content), and the **real cron service**. The two review findings are addressed:
  - **Same-partition fixture:** the sandbox is now selected as the cron partition the preflight actually reads — `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR` points the default partition (`<state>/cron/jobs.json`) at the seeded `cronStorePath`, so `resolveHeartbeatPreflight` genuinely consumes the seeded comments-only scratch instead of a different store.
  - **Required dependency supplied:** the `CronServiceDeps.requestHeartbeat` member is provided (non-waiting) alongside `requestHeartbeatAndWait`, matching the production contract.
  - **Safeguard restoration:** commit ffb0026a accidentally dropped the fixture safeguards; 6fb6ec66 restores them (partition stub, `requestHeartbeat` dependency, skip-summary + spy assertions), so the test again cannot pass through ordinary heartbeat execution.
  - **Skip assertions, not just success:** the finished event must carry `summary: "heartbeat skipped: empty-heartbeat-file"`, and the reply/telegram spies must stay unused — so an ordinary successful agent turn can no longer satisfy the test. Paused-reminder recovery stays covered: the operator `disabled` skip keeps its `skipped`/`failed` outcome in the unit matrix.

Runtime output (local vitest run at 6fb6ec66, cron config, redacted):

```
✓ src/cron/service.heartbeat-real-preflight.test.ts > real heartbeat preflight task accounting > settles a real empty-scratch preflight as a successful no-op task 1155ms

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  1 passed (1)
```

Full local cron-suite run at 6fb6ec66 (`service.heartbeat-payload.test.ts` + `service.heartbeat-real-preflight.test.ts` + `service.test.ts`):

```
 Test Files  3 passed (3)
      Tests  10 passed (10)
```

- The test also asserts the ledger that feeds `tasks list --status failed` contains zero failed cron rows after the designed skip.
- Unit-level matrix in `service.heartbeat-payload.test.ts` (10/10): designed skips settle `ok`/`succeeded` with `consecutiveErrors: 0`; the operator `disabled` skip keeps its `skipped` outcome for visibility.
- Matches the existing intentional-silence precedent in `resolveCronCompletionStatus`, and the busy-deferral handoff path in `timer-execution.ts` that already returned `ok`. The runner's own state (`system heartbeat last`, `consecutiveSkipped`) continues to report the precise skipped status.

prs.title: fix(macos): keep Apple Event permission probes off the cooperative thread pool
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

On 2026.9.3 the macOS app periodically goes dead while still running: the paired node shows **offline** in the Gateway dashboard although the Mac is on and the TCP session to the Gateway is still ESTABLISHED (32 KB of unread bytes sitting in the receive queue), the menu bar item stops opening its menu, and the process ignores SIGTERM (needs SIGKILL). It "fixes itself" only when the app is relaunched.

## Root cause

`AppleEventPermissionProbe.state` runs the blocking `AEDeterminePermissionToAutomateTarget` in `Task.detached`, which schedules onto the Swift cooperative thread pool. The call blocks until Terminal answers the Apple Event handshake (and, when `askUserIfNeeded`, until the user answers tccd). `MacNodeModeCoordinator` re-probes permissions on every refresh trigger (`UserDefaults.didChangeNotification`, config change, permissions change, app activation, reconnect probe), so a slow Terminal under system load lets probes stack up.

A 3 s `sample` of the wedged process showed **all 16 cooperative threads** parked here, main thread idle:

```
DispatchQueue_18: com.apple.root.user-initiated-qos.cooperative
  closure #1 in AppleEventPermissionProbe.state(askUserIfNeeded:)
    AppleEventPermissionProbe.determineTerminalPermission(askUserIfNeeded:)
      AEDeterminePermissionToAutomateTarget
        _dispatch_semaphore_wait_slow
          semaphore_wait_trap
```

Terminal automation was already **granted** in TCC (`kTCCServiceAppleEvents ai.openclaw.mac → com.apple.Terminal = 2`), so this was not a pending prompt. Once the pool is exhausted nothing async in the app can run, including the gateway websocket receive and the status item, and any continuation the AE reply needs can never be scheduled.

## Fix

- Run the blocking probe on a dedicated `DispatchQueue` (concurrent, so a prompt is never queued behind a hung passive check), bridged with a `CheckedContinuation`, so it never pins a cooperative thread.
- Single-flight concurrent callers per `askUserIfNeeded` value through a small actor (`AppleEventPermissionProbeCoordinator`), so at most one probe blocks at a time regardless of how many refreshes fire.
- Bound passive (non-prompting) probes with a 10 s timeout that surfaces as `.failed(errAETimeout)` → capability `.unknown`, instead of hanging the caller. Prompting probes keep waiting on the user.

No change to call sites; `AppleEventPermissionProbe.live` and `TerminalAutomationPermission` keep their API.

## Evidence

- `concurrent passive checks share one blocking probe`: 32 concurrent passive `state` calls → exactly one `determine` call, all callers get the result.
- `a hung passive probe times out instead of blocking callers`: a `determine` that never returns yields `.failed(errAETimeout)` in ~200 ms with a 200 ms timeout.
- `interactive prompts are never timed out`.
- Existing suite unchanged and green (12/12).
- Live observation, 2026-09-09: reproduced twice on the same Mac (2026.9.3 release build). Both times `netstat -anv -p tcp` showed the OpenClaw-owned socket to the Gateway ESTABLISHED with 32,778 and 52,617 bytes in Recv-Q, and `sample <pid> 2` showed 16 and 17 frames in `AEDeterminePermissionToAutomateTarget`. The second occurrence started within 60 s of a Gateway restart, i.e. on the reconnect refresh path. `pkill -9` + relaunch cleared it each time.

`swift build --package-path apps/macos --build-system native --build-tests` ✅, `scripts/format-swift.sh macos` ✅, `scripts/lint-swift.sh macos` ✅ (Xcode 26.6 / Swift 6.3.3).

## Review follow-up (revision 3)

Both P2 findings are addressed:

- **Retain the in-flight operation after a caller times out.** The coordinator now keeps the operation in `inFlight` until the native call actually returns. Caller deadlines are measured from the operation's start, so once the deadline has passed later passive callers answer `errAETimeout` immediately and never enqueue a second native call. When the target replies, the tracked operation drains and the next probe runs fresh. Covered by the new test `timed-out callers never enqueue a second native call behind the hung one` (second caller answers in < 150 ms with `callCount == 1`, operation still in flight; after release the next probe runs and `callCount == 2`).
- **Synchronize overlapping callers before releasing the test probe.** The concurrency test now waits until all 32 callers are parked on the coordinator (`waiterCount == 32`) before releasing, and `BlockingProbeGate.release()` opens the gate permanently so every native call a test started completes during cleanup.

The probe queue is concurrent so an interactive prompt is never queued behind a hung passive check.

## After-fix native proof

Debug build of this branch on a second Mac (macOS 26.4.1, Xcode 26.6), run in a throwaway app profile pointed at a remote Gateway URL that refuses connections (so every reconnect attempt builds a manifest and evaluates permissions). Terminal.app, the Apple Event target, was frozen with `SIGSTOP` so the probe could not get a reply, then resumed with `SIGCONT`. The passive probe returned `noErr` on this host: its TCC database already holds an allowed `kTCCServiceAppleEvents` row for bundle id `ai.openclaw.mac` → `com.apple.Terminal`, which the debug build shares, so recovery shows as a normal `returned 0`.

| Phase | `sample` probe frames | Cooperative-pool frames in the probe | `openclaw-mac status` (control socket) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Baseline | 0 | 0 | ok |
| Terminal frozen, 55 s | 1, on `DispatchQueue: ai.openclaw.apple-event-permission (concurrent)` | 0 | ok |
| Terminal resumed, 50 s later | 0 | 0 | ok |

Unified log (`ai.openclaw`/`AppleEventPermissionProbe`), timestamps relative to the freeze:

```
-27 s  I  probe ask=false returned 0 after 0.172922083 seconds
-19 s  I  probe ask=false returned 0 after 0.033881875 seconds
-10 s  I  probe ask=false returned 0 after 0.208797417 seconds
  0 s     Terminal.app frozen (SIGSTOP)
+17 s  E  probe ask=false timed out after 10.0 seconds; operation retained
+58 s     Terminal.app resumed (SIGCONT)
+58 s  I  probe ask=false returned 0 after 50.992712958 seconds
+66 s  I  probe ask=false returned 0 after 0.032903625 seconds
+97 s  I  probe ask=false returned 0 after 0.137408166 seconds
```

No second native call started while the first was hung (the only lines between the freeze and the resume are the single timeout), the retained call returned as soon as Terminal answered, and the probes after it ran fresh.

The app answered its control socket throughout, kept exactly one blocked thread (on the private queue, never the cooperative pool), released it when Terminal answered, and quit within 1 s of `SIGTERM` afterwards. On the release build the same condition ends with 13 to 17 cooperative threads blocked, a dead status menu, and `SIGTERM` ignored (openclaw/openclaw#146030).

Filtered test run (`swift test --filter AppleEventPermissionTests`, private HOME, throwaway profile, `--skip-build`): 13 tests, 0 failures. Full native suite left to the `macos-swift` CI job per `apps/macos/AGENTS.md`.

### Signed-bundle run (signing provenance)

The run above used the bare SwiftPM debug binary (ad-hoc signed). Repeated on the same Mac with a full `scripts/package-mac-app.sh` bundle of head `621a4a4d8`, signed through `scripts/codesign-mac-app.sh` with a real Apple Development certificate and kept at the fixed path the permissions guide asks for (`<checkout>/dist/OpenClaw.app`). Provenance, identity details redacted:

```
Identifier=ai.openclaw.mac.debug
Format=app bundle with Mach-O thin (arm64)
CodeDirectory v=20500 flags=0x10000(runtime)
Authority=Apple Development: <redacted>
Authority=Apple Worldwide Developer Relations Certification Authority
Authority=Apple Root CA
TeamIdentifier=<redacted, set>
Sealed Resources version=2 rules=13 files=42384
codesign --verify --deep --strict: OK
```

`ai.openclaw.mac.debug` has no Automation grant on this Mac, so the passive probe's real answer is `-1744` (`errAEEventWouldRequireUserConsent`), returned without a prompt once Terminal answers. Same procedure (throwaway profile, refusing Gateway URL, Terminal `SIGSTOP` for 55 s, then `SIGCONT`):

| Phase | `sample` probe frames | Cooperative-pool frames in the probe | `openclaw-mac status` (control socket) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Baseline | 0 | 0 | ok |
| Terminal frozen, 55 s | 1, on the private queue | 0 | ok |
| Terminal resumed, 50 s later | 0 | 0 | ok |

```
-28 s  I  probe ask=false returned -1744 after 0.207445334 seconds
  0 s     Terminal.app frozen (SIGSTOP)
+14 s  E  probe ask=false timed out after 10.0 seconds; operation retained
+58 s     Terminal.app resumed (SIGCONT)
+58 s  I  probe ask=false returned -1744 after 54.768811875 seconds
```

One blocked native call, no second call queued behind it, bounded caller wait, control socket answering throughout, the retained call returning the moment Terminal resumed, and the app quitting within 1 s of `SIGTERM` afterwards.

## Release note

Fix the macOS app wedging (node offline while TCP alive, menu bar item unresponsive, ignores SIGTERM) when concurrent Terminal Automation permission probes exhausted the Swift cooperative thread pool.

Diagnosed and written with Claude Code: https://claude.ai/code/session_014TmTvgdhcL7bPCwg3f8B6G
Review follow-up, after-fix proof, and this revision: https://claude.ai/code/session_01RW45HgmUaFSiM4DSZGrVSp

prs.title: feat(slack): render streamed reasoning as task cards, with continuation messages for long streams
prs.body:
## Decision requested

This PR adds one optional setting, `channels.slack.streaming.progress.reasoning: "narration" | "cards"` (channel and per-account scope), and one additive compositor option (`reasoningLine`) used only by the Slack plugin. Default is unchanged (`narration`, today's behavior). `cards` is opt-in, there is no migration, and existing configs are untouched. It needs a maintainer's yes or no on the setting; the rendering code is only reachable once it is set.

Rebased onto current main, which already contains the first companion fix (#143879, merged); the second (#143880) is being landed by a maintainer. Two commits for review: the first renders reasoning as task cards on a single message; the second adds continuation messages, the byte ledger, and recovery when Slack rejects an oversized append. They ship together: the rendering half is not safe on its own for long turns, which is why an attempted split (#144256) was folded back.

## What Problem This Solves

With `agents.defaults.reasoningDefault: "stream"` (an existing operator opt-in), OpenClaw streams the model's reasoning while the reply is generated. On Slack's native progress card (`streaming.mode: "progress"`, native task cards, which is the default) the plugin keeps one compacted reasoning line, filters it out of the task list (`resolveNativeProgressLines`) and appends it to the stream's narration text (`resolveNativeProgressNarration`). The first sentence of the reasoning therefore lands at the top of the reply as plain prose, later reasoning is appended to that prose as further snapshots arrive, and a long think shows as an unlabeled paragraph above the card rather than as the thought it is. There is no setting that renders reasoning in the card itself.

## Why This Change Was Made

This adds one opt-in, `channels.slack.streaming.progress.reasoning: "narration" | "cards"` (default `narration`, today's behavior unchanged). In `cards` mode the Slack plugin renders streamed reasoning as task rows in the plan block:

- The plugin accumulates the reasoning text through the compositor's existing merge (`mergeReasoningProgress`, core semantics: an explicit or detected snapshot or a prefix extension replaces, otherwise the delta is appended) and splits it into segments of about 240 characters at word boundaries. Cuts depend only on preceding text, so a segment already shown never changes as the text grows. Each segment is one task row with a stable id (`reasoning:<n>`), label `Reasoning`, a 🧠 prefix, and `status: completed` for every segment but the newest. Row titles are capped at 250 characters; Slack documents 256 characters per `task_update` field ([chat.appendStream](https://docs.slack.dev/reference/methods/chat.appendStream/)).
- One streamed message holds only so much. Slack's plan block renders at most 50 tasks ([plan block](https://docs.slack.dev/reference/block-kit/blocks/plan-block/)), and `chat.appendStream` rejects further content with `msg_too_long` once a message that carries text holds about 10,600-11,300 UTF-8 bytes of titles, `details` (about double) and text (undocumented; measured, see Evidence). A long think therefore continues in a new message: the plugin keeps a per-message ledger of everything it has put on the current stream message (task titles, `details` and `output` weighted 2x, the plan title, streamed text, all in UTF-8 bytes; `extensions/slack/src/stream-size.ts`) and, before a send, splits the update into what still fits and what does not. New rows are admitted while the message stays under 6,000 weighted bytes of rows and 50 rows; streamed text while the total stays under 9,000. Segments are cut in the same unit (at most 240 bytes, never splitting a code point), so a card with its 5-byte prefix is at most 245 bytes and an emoji- or CJK-heavy segment can no longer be truncated by the title cap. When something does not fit, the current message is finished with `chat.stopStream` carrying the plan title `Thinking, continued below` and every open row marked complete, and a new native stream starts in the same thread for the same recipient with the title `Thinking, continued`, a fresh reconcile snapshot and the deferred rows; no task id carries over. Card numbering continues (`reasoning:<n>`), later tool rows land on the newest message, and the answer plus the `Thought for …` title land on the message that is current when the turn ends. Before the answer is appended the same check runs for closeout plus answer; if they would not fit, the think closes on its message with `Thought for …` and the answer streams as its own message in the thread. The reasoning runtime seals the cards that landed on a finished message at their current cut (`rolloverSlackReasoningCards`) while the compositor keeps merging the same phase, so cumulative snapshots neither repeat nor lose text.
- `msg_too_long` is now classified (`SlackStreamMessageTooLongError`, a `SlackStreamNotDeliveredError`): the stream is healthy, nothing from the rejected call landed, and the SDK's retained text is discarded before the message is stopped. In `cards` mode a rejected card update or streamed text rolls to a continuation and is retried once; a rejected answer finishes the think and retries the answer as its own stream; if the retry is rejected as well, the stream is stopped and the answer goes through the normal reply path. Every mode gains the last part: a `msg_too_long` on the answer no longer leaves the message `in_progress` without it.
- A tool call (`onToolStart`, phase `start`) and the end of a reasoning phase (`onReasoningEnd`) seal the open segment, so thinking after a tool result starts a new row below the tool row instead of extending the one above it. The seal runs before the tool row is admitted, which fixes the row order in the same append.
- Reasoning stays out of the narration text in this mode; commentary still streams as text.
- At completion the plan title becomes `Thought for <n>s, <k> tool call(s)` (part of the same mode rather than a second setting; easy to split if preferred). An explicit `progress.label` still wins, and while running the headline never borrows a reasoning row's text: it keeps the newest tool row's title or falls back to `Thinking`.
- Cards are ordinary compositor lines, so they share the existing one-second coalescing loop (`createDraftStreamLoop({ throttleMs: 1_000, coalesceInFlight: true })`), the delayed start gate and the native reconciler with tool rows: one `chat.appendStream` call per batch carrying every changed row, and no throttle of its own. Because each card occupies one line of the compositor's rolling window, `cards` mode raises the effective window to at least 64 lines (`progress.maxLines` raises it further); with the default of 8, a burst of more than eight new segments between two sends would evict a card before it was ever sent. Rows that leave the window later are already complete in Slack and stay there.
- Per-turn state (segments, the rolled prefix of the open phase, tool count, start time, the message chain and its ledger) resets with the rest of the progress turn state.
- `cards` applies to the detailed native card (`progress.toolProgress: true`); the quiet card keeps its single summary row and shows reasoning as narration, as today.

Layout: the pure segmentation/planning helpers live in `extensions/slack/src/progress-reasoning.ts`, the per-turn runtime in `extensions/slack/src/monitor/message-handler/dispatch-progress-reasoning.ts`, the per-message size ledger and fit planner in `extensions/slack/src/stream-size.ts`, the stream chain (snapshot, narration state, rollover, `msg_too_long` retry) in `dispatch-progress-stream.ts`, and `progress-blocks.ts` gains the 250-character title for reasoning rows plus the headline rule. `dispatch-streaming.ts` records streamed text in the ledger, accepts a thread override for continuations and a `msg_too_long` retry hook; the transport accepts a thread override. Core changes are limited to the config type, the UI-hint label and the regenerated bundled channel metadata. `narration` mode never enters the rollover paths (`rollover: false` skips every fit check and hook); the regression proof below shows its chunk sequence is byte-identical to `upstream/main`, and the dispatch tests assert one start, two appends and one stop for both the narration fixture and a short `cards` think.

Config surface: this adds one channel config key (`channels.slack.streaming.progress.reasoning`, also under `accounts.*`), so `docs/.generated/config-baseline.counts.json` `channel` moves from 3710 to 3712. Per AGENTS.md this is a conscious budget raise for an owner decision: the alternative of overloading `nativeTaskCards` or `style` would change the meaning of existing values.

Alternative considered: streaming the reasoning into the reply text instead of the card. Not chosen because a native stream is append-only, so every reply would carry its thinking permanently in the message body; task rows can be marked complete and collapse with the card, and the final answer stays the message text.

## User Impact

Operators who set `reasoningDefault: "stream"` can add `channels.slack.streaming.progress.reasoning: "cards"` (with `progress.toolProgress: true`) and see the model's reasoning as a sequence of 🧠 rows in the plan block, interleaved in order with tool rows, with the card titled `Thought for <n>s, <k> tool calls` when the turn finishes. A think longer than one message holds continues in a second (third, …) message in the same thread titled `Thinking, continued`, the previous one ending as `Thinking, continued below`; the answer follows the last one. In any mode, a `msg_too_long` on the answer now ends with the answer posted normally instead of a message stuck in streaming state. Everyone else sees no change: the default is `narration`, and with `reasoningDefault` off (the default) nothing is rendered either way. The setting validates as an enum; other values are rejected by the strict Slack schema.

## Evidence

### 1. Regression proof: `narration` (default) is byte-identical to `upstream/main`

Same probe test, same fixture (two cumulative reasoning snapshots, one `bash` tool call, a post-tool reasoning delta, `reasoning_end`, final reply), run through the real `dispatchPreparedSlackMessage` in the Slack dispatch test harness on a clean `upstream/main` (`6e9ee8af4`) worktree and on this branch with `progress.reasoning` unset. The probe dumps every `startSlackStream` / `appendSlackStream` / `stopSlackStream` call to JSON.

```
$ /tmp/fsrc-probe/run-probe.sh <upstream-main worktree> /tmp/fsrc-probe/out-main
$ /tmp/fsrc-probe/run-probe.sh <this branch worktree>   /tmp/fsrc-probe/out-branch
$ diff /tmp/fsrc-probe/out-main/narration.json /tmp/fsrc-probe/out-branch/narration.json
(empty diff)
```

On `upstream/main` the same probe with `progress.reasoning: "cards"` in the account config produces the same output as without it (the key is unknown there), so the "before" capture below is also what `cards` did before this change.

### 2. Before / after on the fixture

Before (`upstream/main`, and this branch in `narration` mode): the first reasoning snapshot becomes the stream's opening narration text, the rest of the reasoning is appended as prose, and no reasoning reaches the task list.

```json
"start": [{ "channel": "C123", "threadTs": "thread-1", "taskDisplayMode": "plan", "text": "Checking" }],
"append": [
  { "chunks": [
    { "type": "markdown_text", "text": " the Slack handler before the fix.\n\nTests pass; now summarize the change." },
    { "type": "plan_update", "title": "🛠️ Bash" },
    { "type": "task_update", "id": "tool_1_7998d275", "title": "🛠️ Bash", "status": "complete" } ] },
  { "text": "\nfinal answer", "chunks": [] } ]
```

After (this branch, `progress.reasoning: "cards"`): the reasoning is task rows, the pre-tool row is sealed complete before the tool row, the post-tool reasoning is a new row below it, no reasoning text is streamed as narration, and the completion retitles the plan.

```json
"start": [{ "channel": "C123", "threadTs": "thread-1", "taskDisplayMode": "plan", "chunks": [
  { "type": "plan_update", "title": "Thinking" },
  { "type": "task_update", "id": "reasoning_1_96e82800", "title": "🧠 Checking", "status": "in_progress" } ] }],
"append": [
  { "chunks": [
    { "type": "plan_update", "title": "Thought for 1s, 1 tool call" },
    { "type": "task_update", "id": "reasoning_1_96e82800", "title": "🧠 Checking the Slack handler before the fix.", "status": "complete" },
    { "type": "task_update", "id": "tool_1_7998d275", "title": "🛠️ Bash", "status": "complete" },
    { "type": "task_update", "id": "reasoning_2_f5df4246", "title": "🧠 Tests pass; now summarize the change.", "status": "complete" } ] },
  { "text": "\nfinal answer", "chunks": [] } ]
```

### 3. Live runs and the size probes (real Slack, 2026-09-09/10)

Root cause, one mechanism: core fires `onReasoningEnd` and `onAssistantMessageStart` best effort (`runBestEffortCallback`, not awaited). With a live model the `onReasoningEnd` handler is still waiting on the seal's in-flight append when the run ends and the final reply is dispatched; `deliverNativeFinal` cancels the pacing loop, which was the only guard on `beginNewProgressTurn`, and opens the compositor's `beginNewTurn` via `markFinalReplyStarted`, so the late boundary ran a turn rotation under the final: it stopped the stream (short turn: the answer then opened its own stream) or, in the long turn, hit the window between the roll's stop and the continuation's start, clearing the compositor and the reasoning runtime (no `Thought for`, headline kept). Fix: a non-forced `beginNewProgressTurn` now waits for the in-flight final delivery (`finalDelivery`) before it acts, so the answer and the summary title land on the card message and a genuine next assistant message still rotates afterwards. Two dispatch tests reproduce the live order (best-effort boundaries fired un-awaited while the seal append is in flight; a preamble headline showing before the answer).

Budgets in `extensions/slack/src/stream-size.ts`: 9,000 weighted bytes per streamed message (titles, plan title and text at 1x, `details` and `output` at 2x), rows roll at 6,000 so a 2,000-3,000 character answer still fits on the last message, 50 rows per message; about 19% under the ceiling for any script (Latin one byte per character, CJK three, emoji four; with bytes the S5 emoji messages would have rolled at about 13 rows and the answer would have fit), bounded by measurements rather than a documented limit, which is why `msg_too_long` still rolls and retries.

### 4. Source of the limits

- 50 tasks per plan block: https://docs.slack.dev/reference/block-kit/blocks/plan-block/ (hence the 50-row rollover bound; the API accepts more ids and renders 50, see the probe).
- 256 characters per `task_update` / `plan_update` text field: https://docs.slack.dev/reference/methods/chat.appendStream/ (hence 240-character segments and the 250-character title cap).
- Per-message size: not documented for `chat.appendStream`; `msg_too_long` measured 2026-09-09/10 against Slack as above: the check runs once the message carries text and counts titles, `details` (about 2x) and text in UTF-8 bytes, ceiling about 10,600-11,300 bytes (text-only 9,064 accepted / 12,054 rejected; 48 rows of 11,215 title bytes rejected a 92-byte answer; 24 emoji rows of 10,418 bytes rejected a 3,045-byte answer; 50 emoji rows of 22,900 bytes with no text accepted; with 100-character details 8,471 accepted / 8,821 rejected; the API accepts task ids beyond 50 but renders 50).
- Corroboration only: on a downstream build of this behavior against `@openclaw/slack@2026.8.1-beta.3`, a 62-second turn with one tool call rendered 30 cards in Slack (observed 2026-09-09).

### 1. Rejected closeout content lost on rollover

Scenario: a budget rollover's `chat.stopStream` carries four newly admitted cards and comes back `msg_too_long`; the message is stopped without them, and the continuation opened with cards 25-30 only, so cards 21-24 never reached Slack.

Fix: `finishStream` returns `{ chunksRejected }`. `rollMessage` records as delivered only the rows that were already on the message when the closeout was rejected (`roll.previous`) instead of the reconciled closeout snapshot, seals the reasoning prefix through that card only, and the budget path commits the narration delta only when `closeoutDelivered` is true, so the admitted rows and the narration stay pending and the next round sends them on the continuation.

  -   22,
  -   23,
  -   24,
```

After: passes; the continuation's start carries cards 21-30, the rejected stop is followed by a stop without chunks, the answer lands on the continuation.

### 2. Unsent reasoning rows evicted beyond the compositor window

Scenario: one cumulative snapshot admits 70 cards before the paced loop's next send; with a 64-line rolling window the compositor evicted the earliest unsent cards, `pushedKeys` still counted them as pushed, and they never reached the stream.

Fix: cards mode no longer uses a rolling window. `withSlackReasoningCardsWindow` sets the compositor's line limit to `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`, so every admitted row stays in the compositor until the turn ends and each paced send reads the complete set; rows already delivered on earlier messages of the chain are filtered by `rolledTaskIds` as before. Message size stays bounded by the rollover budget (6,000 weighted bytes of rows, 50 rows), which is where the per-message limit belongs.

Test: `delivers every card of a burst wider than a rolling window, once and in order` (70 segments in one snapshot; asserts every card id 1-70 appears exactly once across the three messages, each card's title matches its segment, at most 24 cards per message).

  -   5,
  -   6,
```

After: passes; 70 cards over 3 messages (24, 24, 22), none repeated.

### 4. Slack Stop lost across continuation messages

Scenario: a Slack Stop is admitted while the rollover's stop request is in flight; `finishStream` returned normally with `stoppedBySlack` set on the session, `rollMessage` forgot that session and opened a continuation, and the answer was posted on it.

### 8. Queued cards bypassing the rollover owner at terminal paths

Scenario: in cards mode a 70-segment snapshot is admitted inside the throttle window and the turn then ends with an error final, a media final, or no final at all; the pending send was cancelled, `prepareForAnswer` was skipped for those finals, and the completion append (or the silent closeout's stop) carried every remaining row in one unbudgeted batch that Slack can reject or truncate to 50 rows.

Fix: a rollover-owned drain runs before each terminal path: inside the final-delivery chain before a final that does not stream (`drainNativeProgressBeforeCloseNow`, ahead of the normal reply and the completion append), and joined to the chain before the silent closeout in `dispatch.ts` and before turn rotation (`beginNewProgressTurn`, `onQueuedFollowupSettled`). The drain is `nativeStream.send()`, so the rows go out under the same byte and row budgets and roll into continuations as needed; it is skipped once the turn's final was delivered or the completion sent, so a final that streamed (which already drained through `prepareForAnswer`) is never followed by a second diff. The error status still lands on the message current at the end.

### Design: bounded admission

The reasoning runtime no longer hands every planned card to the compositor. It admits a card only while the message being built can still take it, rows and bytes, on top of everything already admitted for that message (the chain's `admitsRow` runs the production fit planner over the current draft plus the candidate against the current ledger, or a fresh one before the first start; tool and plan rows count the same way). Cards the message refuses queue in order inside the runtime and are released when the chain rolls to a new message. A card counts as queued only when the message refused it for room, not while a render is still waiting behind the send in flight, and a release is deferred while a compositor flush holds the gate's start promise on that send (releasing there would wait on itself). Nothing is evicted: the compositor's rolling window stays disabled in cards mode as a safety net, because the default window (eight lines) is smaller than one message's row budget; with admission bounded, at most one message's rows are unsent at any time.

Every message of the chain after the first is opened by one function (`openMessage`): it fits the opening under a fresh message's budget, text first (or room reserved for the text the caller appends next), then rows in order, defers the rest to the compositor and records only what Slack accepted. The send loop, the narration rollover and the rejected completion before a separate answer all open through it; `transport.start` has no other call site in the chain.

`send()` now reports `{ sent, settled }` (settled: nothing queued, every row of the draft on a message) and keeps going past a full message on its own, bounded by the work in hand (queued cards plus unsent rows, two rounds each) instead of a fixed round count. The terminal paths drain until settled: a final that does not stream, the silent closeout, turn rotation, and the queued cards before an in-stream answer (previously skipped when the answer fit). If the compositor refuses a release after the passes, the remainder is placed straight from the queue on budgeted messages, so no completion append or stop ever carries an unbudgeted batch; the turn's status (error/complete) still lands on the last message.

Guard: every dispatcher test charges each accepted start, append and stop to its message with the production `SlackStreamMessageLedger` and fails in `afterEach` if any message passes 50 rows or the 9,000-byte budget; the thresholds are read back from the exported fit planner at load time, so no production export exists for them (knip production scan: 0). It is on for all dispatcher cases and no scenario needed it off.
