prs.title: fix(android): stop reconnecting to a Gateway that never connected
prs.body:
Closes #194781 ## What Problem This Solves Fixes: Android keeps reconnecting to a Gateway address in the background, about every 20 seconds, after its first connection failed and the user moved on to a different address. ## User Impact A Gateway address that never completed a connection no longer gets a background session. Gateways that did connect still stay connected in the background after switching, as before. ## Why This Change Was Made Manual setup registers the typed target and makes it active before the first connection attempt (`MainViewModel.saveGatewayConfigAndConnect` → `connectGatewayLocked`). `GatewayRegistryStore.setActive` also added the Gateway to `connectedStableIds`, the list `reconcileBackgroundGatewayFleet` keeps connected in the background (#111932). So when the first attempt failed and the user switched to another address, the abandoned target became "enabled, not active" and got a background operator session that never stops. The registry now enrolls a Gateway in that list when it completes a connection (`markConnected`, which the operator session already calls on hello) instead of when it is selected. One owner holds the rule; the fleet planner and the Settings toggle are unchanged, and `setConnectionEnabled` still lets a user enable any saved Gateway explicitly.
Behavior details - A previously connected Gateway is already in the persisted list, so it keeps its background session; nothing is migrated or rewritten. - A Gateway the user disabled stays disabled until it connects as the active Gateway again, which matches the old `setActive` behavior. - Accepted edge case: a device that already has an abandoned target in its saved list keeps it until the user forgets that Gateway or turns its switch off in Settings. Cleaning existing lists would be a migration, not part of this fix. - iOS persists the active Gateway only after TLS trust is settled, so it does not reach this path (code reading, not run).
## Evidence **Real Gateway, Android 16 emulator** (`system-images;android-36;google_apis;arm64-v8a`), Play debug APKs of `upstream/main` and this branch. An isolated local OpenClaw Gateway (own profile, temp state, port `18555`, token auth) plus a host listener on `18443` that accepts TCP and never replies. Same steps on both builds, from cleared app data: onboarding → Set up manually → `10.0.2.2:18443`, Secure (TLS) → Test connection → trust prompt → Cancel → Back → `10.0.2.2:18555`, Unencrypted, Gateway token → Test connection → device approved → finish onboarding → Settings → Gateway. | main | this branch | this branch, after selecting `18443` | |---|---|---| | | | | - main: the never-connected `wss://10.0.2.2:18443` row has its background switch on, and `18443` received 11 connections between 02:10:48 and 02:16:41 while the app was paired and connected to `18555`. - This branch: the `18443` switch is off, and `18443` received no connection from the first setup probe (02:17:45) until I selected it in Settings (02:21:44). - This branch, after selecting `18443`: `18555`, which did connect, is now a background Gateway with its switch on, and the Gateway logged a new Android operator connection at 02:21:45. Multi-Gateway background connections still work for Gateways that connected.
Listener and Gateway logs ``` # 18443 stall listener 02:09:43 accepted # main: setup probe 02:10:48 accepted # main: after switching to 18555 (background session) 02:11:08 accepted 02:11:29 accepted 02:11:51 accepted 02:12:14 accepted 02:12:39 accepted 02:13:07 accepted 02:13:42 accepted 02:14:26 accepted 02:15:28 accepted 02:16:41 accepted 02:17:45 accepted # this branch: setup probe # no connections while paired to 18555 02:21:44 accepted # this branch: 18443 selected in Settings (probe) # isolated Gateway, Android clients (this branch) 02:20:23 client connected client=openclaw-android role=node 02:20:23 client connected client=openclaw-android role=operator 02:21:45 client connected client=openclaw-android role=operator # background session after selecting 18443 ```
**Scripted run, no Gateway**: the same steps against `18444` (plain HTTP) instead of a real Gateway, 60 s after switching: | | Connections to abandoned `18443` | |---|---| | main | 4 (01:33:29, 01:33:49, 01:34:10, 01:34:32) | | this branch | 0 | On main, a thread dump during one of those connections shows an OkHttp WebSocket call to `https://10.0.2.2:18443/` in `ConnectPlan.connectTls`, the background operator session rather than the fingerprint probe. Tests (Temurin 21.0.13, Gradle 9.7.1): `GatewayRegistryStoreTest` (8), `GatewayBootstrapAuthTest` (87), `NodeForegroundServiceTest` (54), `GatewayFleetSelectionTest` (4), `GatewayStoreMigrationTest` (5): 158 tests, 0 failed. - With `GatewayRegistry.kt` from main and the new tests kept: 2 failed. - `selectedGatewayThatHasNotConnectedIsNotKeptConnectedInTheBackground` drives `connectSwitchingGateway` for a registered target whose probe cannot read a certificate: expected `[]`, was `[manual|gateway.test|…]`. - `onlyAGatewayThatConnectedStaysConnectedAfterTheUserSwitchesAway`: expected `[paired]`, was `[abandoned, paired]`. - The existing background-session suites (secondary sessions, re-enable, forget, auth reset) pass unchanged. One existing registry test now records a completed connection before asserting the list, since selection alone no longer enrolls. - `./gradlew :app:ktlintCheck` passes. Production delta +5/-3; test delta +34/-0. Merge risk: two-way door; no stored data is rewritten, and reverting restores enrollment on selection. Blast radius is which saved Gateways get background sessions.

prs.title: fix(sandbox): avoid full template checkouts on source changes
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes a full sandbox template checkout on every selected source commit, even when the pnpm lockfile is unchanged.

## User Impact

Idle sandbox templates now advance their private source checkout and retain installed dependencies. Lockfile or Git-attribute changes still build a fresh template, and concurrent callers share one preparation. No new configuration or schema changes.

## Why This Change Was Made

Use the existing template owner's exclusive refresh operation. Keep exact commit identity: lifecycle scripts and local packages can depend on ordinary source files, so a lockfile-only key would publish stale installation output. Import the Git delta, preserve unchanged checkout files, rerun pnpm, validate, and publish. Remove obsolete private Git objects before another session receives the snapshot. Each refresh gets a distinct installer identity; the config-prefixed pnpm option prevents optimistic repeat install from skipping lifecycle scripts while preserving custom-image compatibility.

The existing coalescing works: mutation wait is inside template preparation; application is each caller's separate native clone. This change does not eliminate that clone or claim to fix slow native filesystem cloning.

Related overlap: #195433 changes the same checkout owner and tests for filtered fetches; preserve both behaviors when integrating. #193214 shares template tests but its production diagnostics owners are unchanged here.

## Evidence

Five counterbalanced before/after pairs after two A/A controls, on native APFS with 62,000 distinct synthetic payload blobs (1.10 GB logical), a real pnpm lockfile, and sandboxed pnpm 12.15.0:

| Source-change measurement | Before median | After median |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Prepare + apply | 10.066 s | 3.836 s |
| Complete owner operation | 10.079 s | 3.855 s |
| Checkout, inside prepare | 7.347 s | 0.711 s |
| Process CPU, including JS workers | 1.023 s | 0.791 s |
| Main-thread V8 allocation | 40.52 MiB | 48.63 MiB |

All five candidate prepare+apply samples were 2.799–4.026 s. All arms verified exact HEAD, clean tracked source, fresh lifecycle output and fresh local-package contents. Baseline retained two template generations; candidate advanced one in place. Both deliberately performed two installs across seed and source change.

**Limits and tradeoff:** A/A wall times were 11.395 and 23.989 s on this shared host. Allocation increased 20% by campaign median; one separate attribution probe did not reproduce a fixed increase (sampled allocation was nearly equal), so resource non-regression remains inconclusive. The fixture has synthetic compression (7.29 MiB packed Git) and a small dependency graph. Btrfs, full Gateway traffic and a large agent database are unqualified. These are owner-boundary results, not a production end-to-end latency claim.

The full sandbox/worktree suites passed on explicit Node (1,532 tests) and Bun (1,527 tests), with existing skips. Final owner/checkout/installer tests passed on both; the final command spelling also passed affected installer/lifecycle tests. Real-owner and real-Git regressions fail before the fix. Separate real-pnpm proof covers registry-only repeat installs, source-dependent lifecycle output, local dependencies, single-build concurrent waiters, lockfile rebuilding, and private-history removal. Fresh Codex review is scoped-clean.

`pnpm check:changed`: all checks passed except 20 historical changelog-attribution findings reproduced exactly on parent `465c110e4975690406b48709d58a581756c85b82`. Commit `266a7aa0fe69` / #194364 introduced this finding set; its parent had a different 26-finding failure. This is an unresolved main regression, not a passing gate. The final option-spelling edit has separate affected-test, formatting and lint verification.

The reproducible driver is `scripts/perf/sandbox-template-commit-measure.ts`. Production growth is 57 lines for refresh, builder identity and private-history cleanup; the scoped allocation is exactly 109 lines for this PR’s net test growth. Main separately owns the 19-line #195382 debt; the ratchet passes with zero slack. Owner and independent Git boundary coverage remain. No changelog edit: release-note context is in this body.


CI follow-up: rebased onto `ac26a0d7f1f8`, including upstream type fix `3fa60aed`. The test-line ratchet and previously failing root-other typecheck pass locally; focused checkout/template suites pass all 14 tests on both Node and Bun. Targeted formatting/lint and fresh Codex review are clean.

Allocation follow-up: rebased onto `826999cd5f76` and removed the duplicated inherited credit. `node --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs scripts/check-test-lines-ratchet.mts --base origin/main --no-merge-base` passes: 6,586,850 lines, equal ceiling, zero slack. Fresh Codex review is clean.

prs.title: fix(cli): expose the scoped manual-selection permission in the full model inventory
prs.body:
Closes #194738

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: `openclaw models list --all --json` reported an authenticated but policy-blocked model as `available: true` with no separate manual-choice permission field, so an agent using the inventory to pick a reviewer hit a local `sessions_spawn` rejection ("model not allowed") that the inventory could have predicted.

## User Impact

User impact: the full CLI inventory now carries `manualSelectionAllowed` beside `available`, so readiness (runtime/provider facts) and override permission (the agent's model policy) are separately visible, exactly as the gateway protocol documents the field. Models without a projected permission show `null` (unknown) instead of implying "allowed", and the rendered table is unchanged.

## Why This Change Was Made

The gateway already projects `manualSelectionAllowed` for clients that declare the `model-selection-policy` capability, and `ModelsListParams`/`BuildModelsListResultParams` already carry the opt-in — the CLI simply never requested or surfaced it. The CLI's `models.list` connection now declares the capability, the offline local-catalog read passes `includeManualSelection` directly (the operator's own policy computation), and the row projection keeps the field beside availability.

## Evidence

- New regression in `list.prepared-catalog.test.ts`: a gateway response where one model carries `manualSelectionAllowed: false` and another omits it renders rows with `false` and `null` respectively — and the test asserts the CLI's request advertises the `model-selection-policy` capability, which is the piece that makes the gateway project the field at all. `node scripts/test-projects.mts src/commands/models/list.prepared-catalog.test.ts` — 16/16 passing.
- Independent review round 1 found a P1: the capability was declared on the offline `runWithLocalStateOwner` path while the reported scenario (a running Gateway) goes through `readSelectedGatewayModelCatalog`, whose `callGateway` call had no caps — fixed by declaring the cap there; the dead `runWithLocalStateOwner` plumbing was removed, and the test now pins the request shape so the gap cannot reappear.
- `pnpm check:changed`: all lanes pass except the pre-existing red lanes on current `main` untouched by this diff (`changelog attributions`, and the `dead export scan` flagging `extensions/google/provider-policy.ts`). The 21 net added test lines have a matching `config/test-lines-allocations/models-list-manual-selection.txt` record.
- Not exercised: a live Gateway with a real model policy over RPC; the mocked-response regression stands in.

prs.title: fix(agents): rate-limit replies say "try again in a few minutes" when the harness reported a reset time hours away
prs.body:
Closes #195184

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: when a native harness such as Muse reports a usage limit with a reset time, the user still reads "Please try again in a few minutes", even when the provider says the limit resets hours or days later. Plugins had no way to hand the host a reset time, so the host's reply copy could not use it.

## User Impact

User impact: a rate-limit failure whose provider reported a reset time now says how long to wait, for example `⚠️ The AI service needs a short break. Please try again in ~3 h.` (seconds, minutes, hours or days). Replies without a reset time are unchanged, provider text never reaches the user (the raw diagnostic stays in the operator log), and the host still owns the wording. The Muse harness passes its typed `quota.resetsAtMs` through as `retryAfterMs`.

## Why This Change Was Made

A thrown harness error can now carry a numeric `retryAfterMs` (milliseconds until the limit lifts), the name the failover signal and the Gateway's 503 envelope already use. `resolveRateLimitResetAt` reads it from a `FailoverError` or from a raw error's cause chain, and the shared reply facts (`resolveReplyFailoverFacts`) expose it as `rateLimitResetAt`, separate from saved-login cooldowns (`soonestCooldownExpiry`) and retry exhaustion.

The copy owners then render the wait from it instead of the generic notice: `renderRateLimitReplyCopy` in its direct branch (which returned before reaching the cooldown copy), `renderRateLimitOrOverloadedCopy` after the existing provider-hint check, the embedded runner's incomplete-turn and terminal-preparation copy (the path `agent --local` and Gateway turns actually take), and the auto-reply error handler, where a known reset time now outranks the generic quota-429 facet the same way recorded retry exhaustion already does. One wait formatter serves all of them. Muse sets `retryAfterMs` from `TurnError.quota.resetsAtMs`, the follow-up left open in #195148.

## Evidence

From source on `main` at 54b059c478 (merged into this branch), macOS, Node 26.7.0. Shipped `openclaw.mjs agent --local` entry point, the real `@muse-code/sdk` MSP transport, and the repository's `extensions/muse/src/test-support/fake-muse.mjs` as the Muse binary (its `quota` prompt reports `limitKind: tierLimit`, `resetsAtMs` = 2030-01-02T03:04Z). Fresh state directory, `meta/muse-spark-1.3` routed through the `muse` runtime, first turn `hello`, second turn `quota`.

Before (`main`):
```
$ openclaw agent --local --json --message quota
      "text": "⚠️ The AI service needs a short break. Please try again in a few minutes.",
```

After (same setup plus this change):
```
$ openclaw agent --local --json --message quota
      "text": "⚠️ The AI service needs a short break. Please try again in ~1151 days.",
$ openclaw agent --local --message quota
⚠️ The AI service needs a short break. Please try again in ~1151 days.
```
Operator stderr keeps the diagnostic in both cases (`[plugins] Muse Code: Muse usage limit reached (tierLimit); resets at 2030-01-02T03:04:00.000Z. fixture quota exhausted`); none of it appears in the reply. The `hello` control turn still answers `started: hello`.

An earlier revision of this branch changed only the copy renderer and the coercion site; the same CLI run still printed "a few minutes", which is how the incomplete-turn and facet paths above were found. The final revision was rerun end to end as shown.

Tests:
- `pnpm test` on `src/agents/failover/user-copy.test.ts`, `src/agents/failover-error.test.ts`, `src/auto-reply/reply/agent-runner-failure-reply.test.ts`, `src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/incomplete-turn-resolution.test.ts`, `src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/terminal-preparation.test.ts`: 142 passed. `extensions/muse/harness.test.ts -t surfaces`: 4 passed (the quota row now asserts `retryAfterMs`).
- New cases: reset-time copy for 45 s / 90 min / 3 h / 10 days plus a past reset falling back to the generic notice, for both `renderRateLimitReplyCopy` and `renderRateLimitOrOverloadedCopy`; `coerceToFailoverError` keeps `retryAfterMs` as `rateLimitResetAt` and `resolveRateLimitResetAt` reads it through a wrapper's `cause`; the terminal reply for a `FailoverError`, the raw harness error and a wrapper around it, through both `buildKnownAgentRunFailureReplyPayload` and `buildExternalRunFailureReply`. With the production files reverted to `main`, the copy, coercion and reply cases fail and the Muse quota row fails; all pass with the change.
- Test-line budget: 70 added lines, allocated in `config/test-lines-allocations/harness-rate-limit-reset-copy.txt`.
- `pnpm tsgo:core`, `pnpm tsgo:extensions`, `pnpm tsgo:extensions:test`, `oxfmt --check` and `oxlint --type-aware` on the changed files: clean.

Not covered: the three `cancels only its own catalog check on a shared host` cases in `harness.test.ts` time out after 120 s on this macOS host both with and without this change; the rest of that file passes. The red `check-test-types-core-5` job on the earlier heads is `test/chat-history-legacy-refusal-notice.e2e.test.ts(46,45)` from main's 86cb0bde5b, which also fails on `main` at 75c2c49cec. Local autoreview / local ClawSweeper were not run.

prs.title: fix(discord): replies show an empty or broken code block when it starts at a message split
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: a Discord reply shows an empty code block, or loses its code formatting, when a fenced code block starts right at the point where the reply has to be split into a second message.

With the default limits (2000 chars, 17 lines), a reply with a 14-item list followed by a fenced block is split so the first message ends with the opener and a synthetic closer and nothing between them (`buildDiscordTextChunks`, the send path, on `main`):

```
"...14. Step number 14\n```bash\n```"   <- empty code block in Discord
"```bash\nnpm install\nnpm test\n```\nDone."
```

When the opener lands one to three characters short of the 2000-char cap instead, the opener line itself is cut in half:

```
"aaaa...a\n``"
"`ts\nconst x = 1;\n```\nafter"   <- `ts is prose, and the closing ``` opens an unclosed block
```

## User Impact

User impact: Discord replies with a code block near a message boundary no longer show an empty code block or render the code as text and the rest of the message as code. The opener now starts the next message together with its code.

## Why This Change Was Made

The range helper already keeps a fence opener with its body (`cutBoundary`), but `flush` only used it when the chunk overlapped an inline code span. A plain-text chunk ending on or inside an opener line went through `boundary`, which doesn't know about fences. `flush` now always uses `cutBoundary`.

## Evidence

- New `it.each` case in `extensions/discord/src/chunk.test.ts` (opener after 1990-1994 chars of text). On `main` all five fail; for 1993 the received chunks are `"aaa…\n``"` and `` "`ts\nconst x = 1;\n```\nafter" ``, for 1990 the first chunk ends with `` "\n```ts\n```" ``. They pass with the fix.
- Before/after on 6,000 generated replies (prose, lists, quotes, inline code, emoji, well-formed `` ``` `` / `~~~` blocks) at 2000 and 500 chars: 466 outputs differ, and every difference removes a chunk ending in an empty fenced block (466 before, 0 after). No chunk goes over the limit and no chunk has an unbalanced fence, before or after.
- `pnpm test:extension discord`: 258 files, 2,683 tests pass. The touched test file runs in under 0.1 s of test time. `pnpm tsgo:extensions`, `pnpm tsgo:extensions:test`, `oxfmt --check` and `oxlint --type-aware` on the touched files: clean.
- Test-line budget: 12 added lines, recorded in `config/test-lines-allocations/discord-fence-opener-boundary.txt`.
- Gap: not checked against a live Discord bot. The strings above come from `buildDiscordTextChunks`, which the Discord send helpers post as one message per chunk.

prs.title: feat(agents): hide picker-hidden agents from user-facing pickers
prs.body:
Related: #166678

## What Problem This Solves

Internal worker agents must be configured as full `agents.entries` entries to stay spawnable as `sessions_spawn` targets, so every user-facing agent picker (sidebar roster, agent switcher, New Session target picker) lists agents that are never meant to be chatted with directly. The only way to remove one from the picker today is to delete its entry, which breaks spawning.

## User Impact

Operators can set `agents.entries.<id>.picker.hidden: true` to keep those agents out of chat-facing agent pickers and switchers. Hidden agents remain valid `sessions_spawn` targets and stay listed by `openclaw agents list`, marked `(hidden)`. Administrative and automation surfaces keep them selectable.

## Why This Change Was Made

This is the config flag proposed in #166678. The UI distinguishes the two roster predicates: `listSelectableAgents` and `findSelectableAgent` remain the administrative/automation projection (system rows only), while chat-facing surfaces use the new `listChatAgents`/`chatAgentsList` helpers (`kind === "system"` and `hidden` excluded). That fixes the first review's Settings finding: `SettingsAgentSelector` still offers picker-hidden agents for management. Docs explicitly state the initial scope is the Control UI; native apps (macOS, iOS) do not yet consume this flag.

## Evidence

**Visual proof** (mocked Control UI via `pnpm dev:ui:mock`, Chromium, agent switcher menu open, `scout` with `picker.hidden: true`):

- Before: switcher rows `[Show all, Molty, Forge, Scout, Bloom]`
- After: switcher rows `[Show all, Molty, Forge, Bloom]` — Scout gone, no other change

Captured locally at `/tmp/opencode/picker-before.png` and `/tmp/opencode/picker-after.png` (GitHub API cannot attach images; uploads were posted in the issue thread).

**Focused tests**, all green on this head:

- `src/config/zod-schema.agents.test.ts` — accepts `picker.hidden`, rejects unknown picker keys / non-boolean values, and asserts the default stays visible when omitted
- `src/gateway/session-utils.picker-hidden.test.ts` — projection carries `hidden: true` for hidden agents, omits it for visible agents, and legacy rosters without `picker` still project
- `packages/gateway-protocol/src/schema/agents-models-skills.test.ts` — `AgentSummarySchema` accepts `hidden`, rejects a non-boolean flag
- `src/commands/agents.commands.list.test.ts` — text output marks `- worker (hidden)` while JSON keeps the row
- `ui/src/lib/agents/display.test.ts` — `listSelectableAgents` keeps picker-hidden rows for administration; `listChatAgents` excludes them; `findSelectableAgent` still resolves hidden agents so existing sessions stay reachable
- `ui/src/components/settings-sidebar.test.tsx` — Settings switcher still offers a picker-hidden agent and selects it
- `ui/src/components/app-sidebar-session-navigation-logic.test.ts` — the sidebar switcher excludes picker-hidden agents while a hidden agent's existing session stays resolvable by id

**Targeted gates** (`pnpm check:changed`, first run): typecheck all, typecheck core tests, typecheck UI, format, config docs baseline, mock-export ratchet, and all architecture/ratchet checks pass. `pnpm build` exits 0 locally.

The config surface deliberately grew by 2 (the new key), so `docs/.generated/config-baseline.{counts.json,sha256}` are regenerated in this PR per the config-surface bar. Test-line allocation in `config/test-lines-allocations/194280-picker-hidden.txt` records exactly this change's net test growth; the shared scalar is unchanged.

Two `check:changed` checks fail, pre-existing on clean `origin/main` (`changelog attributions`, dead export scan in `extensions/codex`). PR CI job failures are in infra/generated paths: `pnpm build qaRuntime` fails resolving generated `extensions/deep-research/browser/index.tsx -> ./client.js` (only `client.ts` is tracked) and the Node-test shards fail in the same build step, while the local full build passes; `checks-fast-baseline-ratchets` is the same inherited main debt (main alone reports `over by: 32; net delta: 0`). No failure in this run points at the changed contract.

## What Problem This Solves

## User Impact

## Why This Change Was Made

Define fixture output streams as own properties and give the watch fixture an explicit null stdin. This follows the fixture pattern in https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/195058 and removes the test dependency on upstream https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/pull/44933. | file | case | stock before | fork | stock after | node | control | wall s |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `test/scripts/ios-release-gateway.test.ts` | 13 package selection/install cases | Fails: readonly output stream | Pass before/after | Pass | Pass before/after | Original failures reproduced | 3.57 → 2.10 |

prs.title: feat(telegram): roll Telegram's native dice from the message tool
prs.body:
Closes #137110

## What Problem This Solves

An OpenClaw bot cannot take part in a Telegram dice roll. Sending 🎲 as text posts a static
emoji: no animation, no roll, no value. Telegram's `sendDice` is the only way for a bot to
trigger the real thing, and it was unreachable — the message tool exposed no action for it.

The distinction matters because Telegram picks the outcome server-side. Nobody in the chat,
agent or operator, can influence or fake it, so a roll everyone watches land is credible in a
way a number the agent typed is not.

## Why This Change Was Made

`dice` joins the core action vocabulary with target mode `to` and no conversation read — it
is an outbound send to an explicit target. That vocabulary is closed by design ("Plugins add
names through a core PR; runtime registration is intentionally unsupported",
`src/channels/plugins/message-action-names.ts`), so a third-party plugin cannot add this and
the core entry is the intended path.

Scoped tool schemas prune parameters the selected actions do not use and merge the surviving
groups into one flat object. Dice therefore gets its own `diceEmoji` key rather than reusing
the reaction group's `emoji`: sharing that name would retitle the reaction parameter for
`react` whenever both actions are enabled. The group is also part of the full schema, so the
six faces are advertised in both scoped and unscoped tool surfaces.

The Telegram runtime wraps `sendDice` and returns `messageId`, `chatId`, `emoji` and the
rolled `value` in the same tool result, so the agent learns the outcome without a second
round-trip. Input is validated against Telegram's documented allowlist before the API call,
after stripping the emoji presentation selector (⚽️ vs ⚽) the same way the plugin's reaction
path does — that form is what most keyboards and models emit.

No new configuration key. Dice rides the existing `sendMessage` gate: permission to post in a
chat already governs it, and a roll is an ordinary outbound message to a chat the bot may
already post in, so a dedicated toggle would guard nothing. `sticker` is gated because it also
enables `sticker-search`, which reads external sticker packs; dice has no such surface, which
puts it with `edit`, `delete`, `reactions` and `topic-create` — all enabled without a toggle.
Disabling `channels.telegram.actions.sendMessage` withdraws dice too, and a test asserts that.

Accepted tradeoff: the returned `emoji` echoes the validated request rather than
`result.dice.emoji`. Telegram's contract returns the requested face, and reading it back
would add a branch for a state the API does not produce; the rolled `value`, which the API
alone decides, is read from the response.

Inbound dice are a separate defect and ship in their own PR (#137112); this one is outbound
only.

Opened so the product decision on #137110 has a concrete diff to judge rather than a
description. The gate shape here follows the recommendation in that issue's review — dice under
the existing send gate, no new configuration key. If maintainers decide against the capability,
closing this costs nothing.
`sticker` and `poll` have `openclaw message` subcommands and `dice` does not; CLI parity
is a small follow-up rather than part of this change, since most action names have no
subcommand either.

## User Impact

Telegram operators can have their agent roll Telegram's native animated dice — 🎲 🎯 🏀 ⚽ 🎳 🎰 —
and act on the result in the same turn, with no configuration to discover or enable. Operators
who have disabled Telegram sending are unaffected: dice is withdrawn along with `send`.

## Evidence

- **Live**: run on a live gateway against a real Telegram bot.
  `{"action":"dice","diceEmoji":"🎲"}` returned
  `{"ok":true,"messageId":"944","emoji":"🎲","value":6}`, a real animated roll landed in the
  chat, and the agent reported the value in the same turn with no chat re-read between the
  call and the reply. The model picked the `diceEmoji` key unprompted, from the schema
  description alone. That run predates the gate change below; the send-gate coupling is
  covered by a test rather than by that session.
- **Live**: ⚽ with the presentation selector (`U+26BD U+FE0F`) was accepted and reached
  `sendDice` as the bare face, returning `{"emoji":"⚽","value":1}`. That form was rejected
  before this change.
- **Live**: the stale-key case behaves as documented — `{"action":"dice","emoji":"🎯"}` with
  no `diceEmoji` rolls 🎲, since `emoji` remains a legal key belonging to reactions in the
  same flattened object. This is why the separate key is load-bearing rather than cosmetic.
- **Live, earlier revision**: an earlier form of this action ran for a week on a live
  instance before the rename and the selector handling.
- `pnpm check:changed` — exit 0 (oxlint 0 errors, `tsgo:all`, assertion/max-lines ratchets,
  Knip dead-export scan, import cycles, plugin boundaries, generated-metadata check).
- `pnpm test:extension telegram` — exit 0.
- `pnpm test:contracts:channels` — 13 files, 32 tests passed.
- Focused: dice send tests (default face, all six faces, presentation selector, rejection
  before the API call, missing dice payload) and schema-scoping tests, including a regression
  test that `emoji` keeps its reaction description when `react` and `dice` are both in scope.
- Gate coupling: `ties dice availability to the send gate` asserts dice is offered under an
  ordinary config and withdrawn when `channels.telegram.actions.sendMessage` is `false`.
- `pnpm config:channels:check` — exit 0 as its own job, confirming the generated bundled
  channel metadata matches the schemas now that no dice key exists.
- `autoreview` (skill) — `scoped-clean`, no accepted findings.

Note on the telegram lane: three cases in `bot/body-helpers.inbound.test.ts` (inline-code
whitespace normalization) fail on this branch, and they fail identically on a clean
`upstream/main` checkout with the file byte-identical to upstream. They are unrelated to dice —
not Node-version specific (same on 24.20.0 and 26.8.1) and not locale specific (same under
`C.UTF-8`). Nothing in this PR touches that file or its subject.




## v2

Rebased onto current `main` first: `annotateSourceDelivery` was refactored there after the
review, which absorbed part of the second repair and made the rest smaller.

- `dice` is declared `GUARDED_ACTION` in `CHANNEL_MESSAGE_ACTION_DEFINITIONS`
  (`src/channels/plugins/message-action-names.ts`), so a roll addressed by `to` clears the same
  cross-context check as every other recipient-visible send. As a plain targeted action it
  carried no `crossContext` fact, and the guard returns early for such actions, which is why the
  gap was silent rather than a build error. Deliberately not `"marker"`: that decoration writes
  into `params.message`, which dice never sends.
- A successful roll now sets `messageToolOnlySourceReplyDelivered`. The fact was neither
  produced nor trusted, so the repair has two halves:
  - Produced: `source-reply-mirror.ts` carried the "which actions address their conversation by
    target" rule twice — once inside `isCurrentSourceConversation`, once in the `default` arm of
    `isDeliveredCurrentSourceReply`, where it compared `params.action` raw while the switch head
    compared it normalized. Both now read one `TARGET_ADDRESSED_ACTION_NAMES` set that includes
    `dice`, since a roll addresses its conversation by target exactly like a send. Net zero
    production lines in that file (+11/-11), one duplicate policy gone. Transcript mirroring
    shares the predicate and needs no second gate: a roll carries no text or media, so it drops
    out on the existing empty-payload check.
  - Trusted: `isDeliveredMessageToolOnlySourceReplyResult`
    (`src/agents/embedded-agent-message-tool-source-reply.ts`) re-derived eligibility from an
    action-name list (`["reply", "thread-reply", "poll"]` plus the send names) even when the
    producer had already recorded the route, so it still rejected dice after the marking landed.
    It now reads the recorded fact. This is more permissive in exactly one direction: a result
    the producer stamped `current-source` is trusted regardless of action name, and only results
    that passed the target comparison carry that stamp — nothing that did not deliver visible
    content to this conversation can reach it. The `allowExplicitSourceRoute` path, where no such
    stamp exists, still requires the name list.
- Mirrorable payload eligibility is now separate from current-source delivery classification.
  The message tool's argument object is flat, so `{action: "dice", message: "You rolled a six"}`
  passes validation; Telegram ignores `message`, but `mirrorDeliveredSourceReplyToTranscript`
  reads text and media straight out of `actionParams` and would have recorded assistant text no
  recipient ever saw. A `MIRRORABLE_SOURCE_ACTION_NAMES` set (currently `send` alone) gates the
  mirror, while `TARGET_ADDRESSED_ACTION_NAMES` keeps covering delivery classification. The same
  hole already existed for `poll` — its params can carry `message` too — so the regressions cover
  dice text, dice media and poll text; all three fail without the gate.
  Both halves are in core rather than in `extensions/telegram/src/channel-actions.ts` where the
  finding was reported: a channel plugin cannot classify itself into a core delivery decision,
  and the classification has to hold for any channel that grows an equivalent send.
- `silent` is read in the dice handler and forwarded to `sendDiceTelegram`, matching the schema
  the action already advertises.

Named follow-up, not changed here: `sticker` is likewise absent from `MESSAGE_TOOL_SEND_ACTIONS`
and the reply-name list, so it does not set `messageToolOnlySourceReplyDelivered` either. Whether
that is the same gap or deliberate — a sticker may not answer the question, so the fallback reply
is wanted — is a product call this PR does not make. Stickers behave exactly as before.

### Dependency contract

The review recorded that it could not inspect the `sendDice` contract (dependency sources absent,
DNS blocked). From the installed tree:

- `grammy@1.46.0`, `node_modules/grammy/out/core/api.d.ts:470` —
  `sendDice(chat_id: number | string, emoji: … | "🎲" | "🎯" | "🏀" | "⚽" | "🎳" | "🎰", other?, signal?): Promise<Message.DiceMessage>`.
- `@grammyjs/types@5.0.0`, `methods.d.ts:927-935` — payload is `chat_id`, `message_thread_id?`,
  `emoji?` restricted to the same six faces, and `disable_notification?`, which is what `silent`
  maps to. This is the upstream source of both the allowlist and the silent option.
- `@grammyjs/types@5.0.0`, `message.d.ts:878-883` — `Dice` is `{ emoji: string; value: number }`,
  with value ranges documented as 1-6 for 🎲 🎯 🎳, 1-5 for 🏀 ⚽ and 1-64 for 🎰. The roll is
  server-decided, which is why `value` is read from the response while `emoji` echoes the
  validated request.

### v2 evidence

- Regressions, each verified by reverting its own fix and rerunning:
  - cross-context denial for `dice` (`src/infra/outbound/outbound-policy.test.ts`) — without the
    policy entry: `expected [Function run] to throw an error`.
  - current-source marking for a target-addressed send
    (`src/infra/outbound/message-action-execution.reply-action.test.ts`, plus the negative case
    for another conversation) — without the set entry:
    `expected { ok: true, …(2) } to match object { sourceReplyRoute: 'current-source' }`.
  - the classifier accepting a recorded route it does not enumerate by name
    (`src/agents/embedded-agent-message-tool-source-reply.test.ts`, plus the unconfirmed negative)
    — without the fix: `expected false to be true`.
  - `silent` forwarded to `sendDiceTelegram` (`extensions/telegram/src/action-runtime.test.ts`)
    — without the fix: `expected undefined to be true`.
- `pnpm check:changed` — exit 0.
- `pnpm tsgo` — exit 0.
- Vitest over `src/infra/outbound`, `src/agents/tools`, both source-reply suites,
  `src/gateway/chat-display-projection.test.ts` and `extensions/telegram` — the only failures are
  the three pre-existing `body-helpers.inbound.test.ts` whitespace cases noted above. Both that
  test and the module it covers are byte-identical to `upstream/main` on this branch.
- `autoreview` (skill) — `scoped-clean`, no accepted findings.

Repair commit alone: production +20/-9 (net +11), tests and test support +114/-3. The
`source-reply-mirror.ts` half is net-neutral (+11/-7 replacing a duplicated action list with one
set). Whole branch versus `main`: production +285/-62, tests +185/-3, docs +16/-1.

Test-line budget: `config/test-lines-allocations/telegram-dice-action.txt` allocates the
branch's net +182 test lines. They hold the contracts no cheaper layer proves: the dice
authority gates, silent and topic delivery at the Telegram sender, cross-context and delivery
classification in outbound policy, and source-reply ownership in the agent.

The branch is a linear series of six commits on current `main`, with no merge commits.

### Live proof

Captured against a real Telegram bot on `dfa0fb6`, an earlier head of this branch. Later
revisions rebased and compressed it without changing the behaviour on the proven paths. The run used a gateway built from this
branch, agent model `openai/gpt-5.6-sol`. Chat identifiers are redacted as `<chat-a>` (the
conversation the run is bound to) and `<chat-b>` (a different configured chat).

**Cross-context egress.** With `tools.message.crossContext.allowWithinProvider: false`, a
direct message-tool call from the session bound to `<chat-a>`:

```
toolCall   message {"action":"dice","target":"telegram:<chat-b>","diceEmoji":"🎲"}
toolResult Cross-context messaging denied: action=dice target="telegram:<chat-b>"
           while bound to "telegram:<chat-a>" (channel=telegram).
```

Nothing reached `<chat-b>`. Before this change `dice` carried no `crossContext` fact, so the
guard returned before it ever compared targets.

**Terminal delivery.** With `messages.visibleReplies: "message_tool"`, a roll in the bound
conversation:

```
toolCall   message {"action":"dice","diceEmoji":"🎲","final":true}
toolResult {"ok":true,"messageId":"…","emoji":"🎲","value":4,
            "sourceReplyRoute":"current-source"}
```

`sourceReplyRoute: "current-source"` is the marking this PR adds; the operator observed
exactly one message in the chat — the animated roll — with no fallback text after it.

**Silent.** The call carried the option and the roll was delivered:

```
toolCall   message {"action":"dice","diceEmoji":"🎲","silent":true}
```

The forwarding is covered by the sender-boundary regression above and by
`extensions/telegram/src/send-special.ts:183`, which maps `silent` to the
`disable_notification` field `@grammyjs/types` declares for `sendDice`.

**Forum-topic roll.** Captured on the current head `6b6731dd31c` with a Gateway built from
this branch in an isolated state directory, agent model `litellm/deepseek-v4-flash`, and
`messages.groupChat.visibleReplies: "message_tool"`. `<forum>` is a forum supergroup; the
request was a user message in its topic 14 that mentioned the bot and asked for a roll there.

```
session    agent:main:telegram:group:<forum>:topic:14
toolCall   message {"action":"dice","diceEmoji":"🎲"}
toolResult {"ok":true,"messageId":"727","chatId":"<forum>","emoji":"🎲","value":5,
            "receipt":{"threadId":"14"},"sourceReplyRoute":"current-source"}
delivery   {"createdThreadIds":["14"],"status":"settled","sourceReplyDelivered":true}
```

The call named no target or thread: the roll landed in the topic the request came from, and
the receipt in the result reports that topic. The tool result ended the turn (`terminate: true`,
stop reason `toolUse`); the model was not called again, no assistant text was produced, and the
Gateway sent nothing after the roll. The operator observed the animated die, face 5, in topic 14
with no message after it.

Follow-up, not changed here: the trajectory recorder labels this turn
`non_deliverable_terminal_turn` (`status: error`). `finalizeEmbeddedAttempt` in
`src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/attempt-finalize.ts` counts a tool-use turn as delivered
only through `messagingToolSent*` evidence, which neither `poll` nor `dice` records. The runtime
terminal check, `hasAttemptTerminalState` in `attempt-terminal-evidence.ts`, also accepts
`didDeliverSourceReplyViaMessageTool`; delivery and fallback follow that check, so only the
trajectory label is affected. A turn that ends with `poll` takes the same path.

An earlier attempt at the cross-context case did not exercise the guard: the model routed
around it with `sessions_send`, asking the session already bound to `<chat-b>` to roll in its
own conversation, where no cross-context target exists. The proof above is the direct call.

prs.title: fix(lmstudio): guard model discovery with the embedding SSRF policy
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

LM Studio catalog refresh and dynamic model preparation fetched the configured base URL with platform fetch. That path follows redirects and sends the provider API key. Embeddings in the same plugin already build a guarded policy from the base URL and `allowPrivateNetwork`. Discovery now uses that policy. An omitted setting still allows a private local LM Studio. An explicit denial sends no request.

## Evidence

Head `35ec16b1f7e` on macOS Darwin arm64, Node v26.12.1. The shipped catalog owner is `extensions/lmstudio/provider-discovery.ts`, which calls `discoverLmstudioProvider` in strict mode. Dynamic preparation is `prepareLmstudioDynamicModel`. Both ran against a loopback HTTP server that speaks the LM Studio models JSON shape. The bearer value is a synthetic local marker and is not shown.

```console
OK: catalog allow=omit models=1 requests=1 auth=bearer custom=present
[security] blocked URL fetch (lmstudio-model-discovery) reason=Blocked hostname or private/internal/special-use IP address
OK: catalog allow=false models=0 requests=0 auth=none custom=none
OK: catalog allow=true models=1 requests=1 auth=bearer custom=present
OK: dynamic allow=omit model=proof-local requests=1 auth=bearer custom=present
OK: dynamic allow=false model=missing requests=0
OK: dynamic allow=true model=proof-local requests=1 auth=bearer custom=present
OK: redirect first=1 auth=bearer custom=present second=1 secondAuth=absent secondCustom=absent
```

The redirect was from the configured origin to another port on the same loopback host. The first hop carried the bearer and the custom `X-Proof-Client` header. The followed hop received the models request with both absent.

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed:** Shipped LM Studio catalog refresh and dynamic preparation reach a loopback models server when the private-network setting is omitted or true, send no request when it is false, and do not forward the bearer or custom credential on a cross-origin redirect.
- **Real environment tested:** macOS Darwin arm64, Node v26.12.1, head `35ec16b1f7e` in `/tmp/oc-191529`. The listener was a local HTTP server, not the LM Studio app.
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch:** Called the plugin catalog `run` and `prepareLmstudioDynamicModel` for an omitted setting, `allowPrivateNetwork: false`, and `allowPrivateNetwork: true`. Then repeated the allowed catalog call against a server that returned a redirect to another loopback port.
- **Evidence after fix:** terminal output from those production calls:

```console
OK: catalog allow=omit models=1 requests=1 auth=bearer custom=present
OK: catalog allow=false models=0 requests=0
OK: catalog allow=true models=1 requests=1 auth=bearer custom=present
OK: dynamic allow=omit model=proof-local requests=1 auth=bearer custom=present
OK: dynamic allow=false model=missing requests=0
OK: dynamic allow=true model=proof-local requests=1 auth=bearer custom=present
OK: redirect first=1 auth=bearer custom=present second=1 secondAuth=absent secondCustom=absent
```

- **Observed result after fix:** Omitted and allowed discovery each returned `proof-local` after one request. Explicit denial opened no socket. The redirect destination received one request and neither the bearer nor the custom header.
- **What was not tested:** A config file written by published OpenClaw v2026.11.1 and then opened by this head. A LM Studio desktop process. A server on another machine.

## Summary

Catalog refresh and dynamic preparation use the embedding SSRF policy. The local default still allows a private LM Studio. An explicit denial is blocked before HTTP. A cross-origin redirect does not carry the bearer or the custom header.

The test-line ratchet on this branch is still red. The base tree is already over its ceiling, this branch adds lines, and `check-test-lines-ratchet` refuses to forgive that inherited debt. Raising the allocation above the lines this branch adds is rejected. The restored discovery regressions stay.

prs.title: fix: Codex sign-in import fails on busy Linux hosts when process cleanup exceeds 2 s
prs.body:
Closes #195425

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: `openclaw models auth login --provider openai` fails with "The Codex credential reader could not stop. No credential was imported." on a busy Linux host (~950 processes).

## User Impact

User impact: Linux users on busy or large hosts can import a Codex sign-in again. Hosts that were already fast see no change; the longer budget is only a ceiling for a stuck probe.

## Why This Change Was Made

Stopping the credential reader takes several full `/proc` snapshots under one shared deadline. At ~950 processes one snapshot took about 1.6 s, so the old 2 s budget expired, cleanup was reported `uncertain`, and the import was rejected. The budget is now one shared constant of 10 s (it was duplicated in two files). The rule that `uncertain` cleanup rejects the import, even when the root has exited, is unchanged: it protects descendant cleanup for a credential-bearing process, and an existing test asserts it.

## Evidence

- New test `completes a full snapshot of a busy host within the default containment budget` simulates 950 processes at ~3 ms each (about 2.9 s). Against the old 2 s constant it fails with `Process inspection exceeded its deadline`; with this change it passes.
- `extensions/codex/src/app-server/transport-process-snapshot.test.ts`: 31 passed, 6 skipped (platform-specific).
- `extensions/codex/src/migration/provider.auth.test.ts`: 28 passed (includes the uncertain-cleanup rejection cases).
- `oxfmt --check` and `oxlint` clean on the changed files.
- Before the fix, locally raising both constants to 15 s made the real login succeed on the affected host.

Related: #161341 reports the same message on Windows, which has a different cause (no process-tree cleanup) and is not addressed here.

prs.title: fix(agents): keep exec approval followup observation deadline on the monotonic clock
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When an async `exec_approval_followup` run completes on the gateway, OpenClaw keeps observing it for a bounded 6-minute window before deciding whether to resume the originating session. That observation window is budgeted on the wall clock (`Date.now()`) but consumed by the monotonic timer that backs the gateway `agent.wait` RPC. When the system wall clock is adjusted (NTP step, VM clock sync, or a laptop waking from hibernation), the two clocks diverge and the observation window is distorted.

- **Problem**: `waitForAgentFollowupRun` seeds `observationDeadline = Date.now() + timeout` and reads `remainingMs = deadline - Date.now()`, passing that budget into a gateway wait consumed on the monotonic clock (`performance.now()` / `setTimeout`). Budget computed in one clock domain, spent in another.
- **Solution**: align the whole observation budget to the monotonic clock — seed `observationDeadline` and read `remainingMs` / `retryDelayMs` with `performance.now()`, matching the monotonic consumer.
- **What changed**: `src/agents/bash-tools.exec-approval-followup.ts` (3 deadline reads `Date.now()`→`performance.now()`; per-wait budget rounded up with `Math.ceil` for the gateway `agent.wait` integer `timeoutMs` schema); the deadline regression test now controls the monotonic clock.
- **What did NOT change**: the transport retry/backoff policy and the observation lifecycle (reason `"deadline"`, `transportErrors` accounting) are untouched.

## Why This Change Was Made

The observation deadline is a pure process-local closure (never serialized/persisted/cross-process), so a monotonic clock is the only correct source. The gateway consumer already computes its own monotonic `DispatchDeadline`; passing it a wall-clock-derived remaining budget is a cross-clock-domain mismatch. Switching the three reads keeps the seed and every remaining-budget read on the same (monotonic) domain, zero external contract change.

- **Best fix**: yes — one canonical owner, no new parser/policy branch.
- **Alternative**: keep `Date.now()` and rely on the per-wait `Math.min` cap; rejected because the cap only bounds a single wait, not the total observation window, nor the `retryDelayMs <= 0` exit from a forward wall jump.
- **Risk**: low — `Math.ceil` on the remaining budget never shrinks the observation window and always yields an integer accepted by the gateway validator.

## User Impact

Exec approval follow-ups for async commands now complete on a stable, clock-skew-proof observation window. Under NTP/hibernation clock steps, a healthy agent run is no longer prematurely declared complete (dropping slow terminal output), and a finished run is no longer observed far beyond its deadline.

## Evidence

**1. Shipped exec-host public-entry clock-skew proof, both directions.** Driven through the exec-host **public shipped entry** `sendExecApprovalFollowupResult` (`bash-tools.exec-host-shared.ts`) — the exact function `exec-host-node.ts` / `exec-host-gateway.ts` call after an approved async exec. It registers the handoff, then `sendExecApprovalFollowup` runs through the **production** `GatewayRecoveryRuntime` the Gateway registers at startup — **no** `registerGatewayRecoveryRuntime` override, **no** internal-function call. Both the `agent` dispatch (production `recovery.dispatchAgent` → real in-process `agent.run`, accepted against a synthetic-provider run that stays pending) and the wait (production `recovery.waitForAgent` → shipped wait transport) are unmodified shipped code. A 30 s wall step (−30 s / +30 s) is injected inside `waitForAgentFollowupRun` via a `Date.now` proxy; a pass-through probe on `recovery.waitForAgent` records the round-1 budget handed to the wait transport. (Observation budget shortened 6 m→20 s as a disclosed control; the per-wait cap cannot mask it.)

```console
# BACKWARD (−30s rewind)
[proof] production recovery runtime present = true (Gateway auto-registered)
[proof] recovery.waitForAgent budget timeoutMs=20000 -> shipped wait transport   # post-fix: BOUNDED
[proof] recovery.waitForAgent budget timeoutMs=49999 -> shipped wait transport   # pre-fix: INFLATED +30s
# FORWARD (+30s jump)
[proof] recovery.waitForAgent budget timeoutMs=20000 -> shipped wait transport   # post-fix: BOUNDED, observation proceeds
[proof] outcome=undefined elapsed=2652ms / NO agent.wait dispatched             # pre-fix: observation ENDED IMMEDIATELY (drops slow output)
```

| leg | skew | production-recovery budget (round 1) | window |
|---|---|---|---|
| post-fix | −30 s | 20000 | bounded |
| pre-fix | −30 s | 49999 | inflated +30 s |
| post-fix | +30 s | 20000 (proceeds) | bounded |
| pre-fix | +30 s | none (ends immediately) | drops slow output |

Keeping the budget on the monotonic clock makes the shipped wait budget immune to wall-clock steps in both directions. The accepted run stays the sole delivery owner (`direct_deliveries=0`; no competing direct delivery), and the integer `timeoutMs` passes the shipped `validateAgentWaitParams`.

**2. Integer-boundary proof (P2).** `performance.now()` is fractional; the `agent.wait` schema requires an integer `timeoutMs`. `sendExecApprovalFollowup` was driven through a recovery runtime whose `waitForAgent` re-runs the shipped validator on the exact params. Same fractional remaining budget (59999.75 ms), before vs after the one-line `Math.ceil`:

```console
before: [waitForAgent] timeoutMs=59999.75 -> shipped validator: REJECT
after : [waitForAgent] timeoutMs=60000   -> shipped validator: ACCEPT
```

`Math.ceil(59999.75) === 60000` never shrinks the budget; `Math.max(1, ...)` keeps the positive minimum.

**3. Regression.** Pre-fix the new test fails (`Number.isInteger(59999.75)` false); post-fix it passes, full suite green (18/18).

**What was not tested**: the divergence itself (NTP/hibernation) is injected by the proof; direct-delivery and session-resume paths are unchanged and covered by existing suites.

**Collision check**: `origin/main` still has the wall-clock reads (bug live); sibling PR #181942 touches the same three reads for the same defect; both open.

prs.title: fix(logging): retain kernel stall reports without CPU profiles
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Linux main-thread stall warnings lose already-collected kernel observations when CPU recording is unsupported, disabled by a profiling conflict, or fails. Node 24's supported runtime path is affected.

## User Impact

Operators retain wait-channel, syscall and scheduler evidence even without a CPU profile. Kernel-only reports explicitly say `cpuProfile=unavailable`, preserve the stall interval, and remain within the existing 2 KiB log limit. This repairs attribution; it does not shorten the underlying stall.

## Why This Change Was Made

The flight recorder drained the independent kernel observer before returning early for unavailable CPU recording. Preserve that observation through the existing formatter, including capture failures. No new collection, timer, configuration, schema or cache. Production delta is +4 lines for the independent report path and unavailable-CPU marker.

## Evidence

- Two regressions fail before the repair because the report is missing. Focused local recorder/observer proof: 22 passed, 3 platform/runtime skips; 37.23 s Vitest wall time including compilation (41.70 s wrapper).
- Real Linux Node 24.22.1 observer, two A/A controls and five A/B pairs: baseline emitted no reports; all five candidate arms emitted an 803-byte report with three actual `/proc` futex observations. Reporting wall median 0.0565 → 0.1004 ms; the injected 3.6 s stalls remain unchanged. [Testbox run](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/42525551552).
- The same Linux run passed 21 tests with 1 skip, including the native futex regression now enabled on Node 24 (3.824 s). The lease is stopped. A full-Gateway Linux follow-up was blocked by the wrapper's stale-task receipt check; that check was not bypassed.
- Full-context Codex autoreview, P0–P2, against parent `51b8257b29b8` plus this change: no actionable findings. The +16 test lines have an exact allocation record; they cover evidence loss on unsupported and failed CPU capture, while reusing the native Linux test.
- `pnpm check:changed` completed: every stage passed except changelog attributions, which reproduces 20 identical violations on unchanged parent `51b8257b29b8`; the rule change is `266a7aa0fe69` (#194364). This is an unresolved main regression, not a passing gate.

It reproduces as the sole diagnostic on the exact integration main parent `c1e55e24b3cb` (root stripe 4/4, 13.3 s). prs.title: fix: avoid oversized cache restores for Apple assets
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

macOS qualification can spend minutes restoring the repository-wide pnpm store before installing Apple asset dependencies, consuming its unchanged native-test deadline.

## User Impact

No user-visible behavior changes. This removes the general Node/pnpm cache restore from the Apple asset setup invocation only; native tests, assertions, deadlines, pinned tools, frozen dependency installation, and independent Apple/Swift caches remain unchanged.

## Why This Change Was Made

The existing setup action explicitly supports `cache-mode: off`. In frozen candidate `92f709539e5a`, normal CI run 42513226675/job 128830875193 spent 270.049 seconds restoring a 3,881,440,298-byte pnpm cache before a narrow renderer/protocol install. The job later hit its 30-minute cap after an 872.15-second cold Swift compilation, with no evidenced Swift assertion failure.

Main also installs the root dependency graph in the tests phase for native policy fixtures; the packages phase and the frozen candidate asset installation are narrower. Cold downloads can cost more or depend on the registry. **Net savings for main’s broader tests installation and complete cold macOS completion are not yet proven.** This is not a claim that removing the observed cache cost alone fixes the whole qualification budget. If hosted evidence shows a broader-install regression, retain the existing cache policy there and restrict this optimization to the narrow installation scope.

## Evidence

- Independent source review found no actionable issue: both setup actions accept off; tool bootstrap, frozen install flags/filters, independent Apple/Swift cache policy, native partitions and assertions are preserved.
- Required native workflow guard suite: **1,295 tests across 10 files passed**, including all ci-workflow guards, Swift cache lifetime, and native launch ownership (206.84s).
- Workflow formatting and git diff whitespace check passed.
- `check:workflows` was attempted locally and in a disposable toolchain; host Python venv support and container proxy CA trust prevented acquiring pinned linters. The actual, unchanged workflow-lint CI gate remains required.
- Original failed job: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/42513226675/job/128830875193
- Hosted cold main install and complete native runtime timing remain a proof gap; no timeout increase or test omission is included.

prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

A change confined to the Windows CI test lists in `package.json` currently selects consumers of every `openclaw` SDK export. A completed backup-fix PR with one such list edit ran 106 Blacksmith Node jobs.

## User Impact

CI can retain the relevant source tests, manifest readers, policy checks, smoke tests and newly listed Windows tests without running unrelated SDK consumers. Missing history, malformed lists, metadata changes and other script edits retain the existing conservative behavior.

## Why This Change Was Made

Reuse the semantic package-script classifier and share the existing Windows inventory parser with the selector. Only a validated change to `test:windows:ci:1` or `test:windows:ci:2` bypasses root package-consumer expansion. New targets are admitted explicitly, including unchanged files newly added to the Windows inventory. The native PR wrapper includes the shared parser.

## Evidence

- Regression: two narrowing cases fail on the base; all 28 selection cases pass with the fix, including add/move/remove, metadata, other scripts, malformed/duplicate lists and missing/unreadable base history.
- The first CI run exposed a missing parser in the compiler-coverage fixture. Its copied input list is fixed; all six affected cases pass on blacksmith, github and hybrid profiles.
- 86 sibling checks pass for changed lanes, Windows inventory and dependency selection; native wrapper closure passes. Targeted typecheck, lint, format and test-line ratchet pass.
- Read-only planner replay of [PR #193685](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/193685), using its exact ten changed files over common revision `44662c4c196431fdabf9ae3b1ddae62368f6857d`, the original base manifest and an isolated Git index: 2,962 → 181 selected targets (-93.89%); 105 → 21 planned Node jobs (-80%). Both plans resolve without fallback. Every removed target belongs to root package-consumer expansion; all independently selected targets and the newly added Windows test remain.
- This is a common-revision reconstruction, not an exact historical whole-tree or runtime benchmark. The [recorded run](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/42515751607) had $3.220 of Blacksmith Node list-price usage; post-change runtime and dollar savings have not been measured. Job reduction is not a proportional billing claim.

The 81-line allocation covers the existing selector suite's parameterized boundary regression. Scheduled/full validation, isolation and required CI gates are unchanged.

prs.title: fix(codex): avoid replaying consumed native results after cold resume
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

A resumed native Codex parent can consume child results without emitting raw receipt notifications. Retiring that parent then loses the receipt owner and can admit the same completion again. Codex's resume listener explicitly disables raw events ([source](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/6aaac694803004a63c6f393d153c96d22521a6b9/codex-rs/app-server/src/request_processors/thread_processor.rs#L4372)).

## User Impact

Cold-resumed parents can recognize a child result they already consumed, avoiding duplicate completion handoffs when native raw receipts are absent. Missing or ambiguous proof preserves normal completion delivery.

## Why This Change Was Made

Before releasing a settled parent's existing custody, reconcile exact consumption facts from its canonical local rollout. A typed child-completion intent identifies the child turn; only a later consumed native `agent_message` with the exact owned parent turn, trusted alias and immutable result can acknowledge it. Complete child history must also prove that every other turn has a distinct known result. Intent alone, identical outputs and incomplete history preserve normal delivery.

The entire observation has one hard **30-second total** deadline covering lifecycle checks, RPCs and filesystem reads. It retains observation custody, grants no execution authority, and rechecks lifecycle/source/runtime/candidate ownership before acknowledgement. Timeout, cancellation, revocation and late async resolution fail closed. Remote transports and unsafe or unproven files retain normal delivery.

## Evidence

Validation on parent `eb4ebb59f` (receipt-ingress/alias fix) and head `73de4409e`:

- Actual monitor regression: with raw receipt events omitted, the base admits a consumed child result again; the fix does not.
- Monitor negatives cover intent-only history, duplicate child output, remote transport, yielded parent, revoked lifecycle and source, and total-budget timeout with late resolution.
- Registration guard regression proves closed execution remains closed while bounded observation retains only current lifecycle/connection checks.
- Canonical-reader cases cover wrong owner/turn/child/path, missing or ambiguous facts, complete-LF boundaries, invalid UTF-8, bounded tail windows, hardlinks, symlinks and path escapes; complete child-history cases cover ambiguous earlier and later turns.
- **74 focused monitor/receipt/input-scope tests passed**, as did production extension and extension test typechecks, formatting, lint and commit checks. Independent Codex source review found no actionable P0–P2 findings; the reviewer did not execute project code. Final guard-call/type refinements were checked by typechecks, focused tests and author review.

These are deterministic source-level checks using synthetic native records and notifications. They do not establish live-model or production acceptance for this source revision. Previously deployed runtime validation is separate evidence and is not presented as proof for this port.

Depends on #194748 (receipt ingress and trusted aliases). The additional source is necessary for canonical same-descriptor provenance, a complete bounded snapshot, exact child-history uniqueness and lifecycle-safe retirement; the existing generic live-receipt ambiguity rules remain unchanged. Existing receiver eligibility and registration execution guards are extracted unchanged to keep their original files within the source line-growth gates.


### Follow-up: failed or interrupted parent turns

At `cc5c155d1`, receipt retirement requires a successfully completed parent turn; failed, interrupted, or unrecognized terminal statuses retain the normal delivery fallback. This also applies when the terminal event precedes turn binding, and success is rechecked after asynchronous history reads. Four synthetic regressions fail on the previous head and pass with this change. The three focused monitor/receipt suites passed (35 tests); formatting and targeted lint passed. Live Gateway / native Codex cold-resume validation remains outstanding.


### CI test-line allocation

CI reported test-line growth of 29 lines above its exact merge-base allocation. At `01f6053a7`, a separate 29-line allocation covers the failed/interrupted parent regressions; the global ceiling and tests are unchanged. On the same CI merge tree, the ratchet reproduced 6,583,248 / 6,583,219 before the allocation and passed 6,583,248 / 6,583,248 after it. New exact-head CI is pending.

prs.body:
Depends on [#194814](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/194814) and [#194755](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/194755); both are included in this integration head. Upstream budgets are unchanged.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes missing first-folder creation and conversations appearing to disappear after moving them into a collapsed chat folder.

## User Impact

Users can create their first project folder from the agent chat toolbar and immediately see accepted menu, drag, or batch moves in the destination. Successful empty-folder creation also makes its grouped view visible.

## Why This Change Was Made

Keep creation and moves with the organizer's existing scoped operations and lazy dialog loading. The toolbar uses the authoritative access check. Reveal a collapsed destination only after a current accepted move; a batch reveals it when at least one member succeeds. Rejected members retain their error feedback, and a fully rejected batch leaves the destination collapsed. Browser tests use the accessible button name; the existing 22px geometry, labels and permission checks remain intact.

## Evidence

- Functional UI head `f9b66066`: 14/14 bundled browser cases (5 creation, 5 physical-session menu/DnD/batch, 3 agent/owner scope, 1 retained-folder reload) and 184/184 tests across 11 affected owner/layout suites. Coverage includes pending admission, read-only denial, failed-save recovery, main/new agents, captured physical session identities, rejected/partial batches, and persistence after reload.
- UI and strict E2E types, lint, formatting, allocation and fresh independent integration review passed. All functional CI jobs also passed on the newer `636fc28d` merge graph; the 4 B size overage and its aggregate gates were its only failures.
- Proposal-only head `41995f7e` changes no UI/runtime source. Existing budget contracts pass 50/50 (21.45 s). Exact CI candidate/base replay reproduces the old 4 B violation and no violations with the proposed cap, asserting that Chat gzip is the sole changed budget. Targeted lint/format and fresh review pass.
- Current-head CI passed for `41995f7e` (57 successful checks; 41 intentionally skipped checks); performance-owner acceptance remains pending. Captures use synthetic sidebar data and a mocked Gateway. The retained creation captures originate from ancestor `de74d3ad`; final creation behavior is covered by the five final browser cases.

### Follow-up: preserve personal folder settings

The existing browser test was extended with another hidden folder and both grouped and flat preferences: it failed on the prior head and passes with this fix (5 scenarios total). `pnpm tsgo:ui`, formatting and the commit checks pass. These are synthetic Gateway tests; installed-version and exact-head live Gateway acceptance remain separate. The earlier boot-budget exception was removed in the subsequent merge; see the current measurement below.


### Upstream conflict resolution and performance

Merged upstream `13ab261c53b4af8e2fd02972dd8ed3b4d5e69825` at `6d7810f51`. The performance-budget conflict was resolved using upstream limits, without increasing the cap. The deterministic same-toolchain comparison measured chat boot JS 1,296,615 → 1,296,298 bytes gzip (-317), New Session 802,673 → 802,486 (-187), and startup JS 90,798 → 90,809 (+11), with unchanged request counts. The 11-byte startup increase requires performance-owner evaluation; no owner acceptance is claimed. Five bundled-browser scenarios and `pnpm tsgo:ui` pass after the merge. A normal local build produced a non-deterministic advisory chat-budget overage; CI remains the exact-head authority.


### Previous integrated head (historical)

At `b0201ec3e`, the final #194814 follow-up is merged along with the type-only import fix. The integrated test-line allocation is 263 lines; against pinned upstream `13ab261c`, the ratchet passed exactly at 6,583,624 / 6,583,624. The three affected bundled-browser files and UI typecheck passed after integration; independent picker checks cover 53 unit cases and the seven previously affected browser cases. Owner evaluation of the +3 B New Session metric remains pending. GitHub exact-head CI and live end-to-end qualification remain separate. Earlier measurements and approvals below are historical snapshots, not claims about this head.

`1f616c721` includes #194814 `9b69e34af`, the controller-guard repair and assertions that wait for the asynchronous agent selection. Twelve integrated bundled-browser cases and UI typecheck passed; the dependency independently passed 172 unit cases and three additional browser cases. An equivalent integrated source measured chat +128 B gzip (8 B headroom) and New Session +214 B within existing caps; performance-owner evaluation remains required. Exact-head CI and live end-to-end acceptance remain separate.

`12a7169ab` corrects the documented signed-in owner default to All owners and the empty-group default/Reset to Never. prs.title: docs(channels): document four missing mattermost configuration keys
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`extensions/mattermost/src/config-schema-core.ts` defines `MattermostAccountSchemaBase` with several runtime-read configuration keys, but `docs/channels/mattermost.md` has missing documentation for four of them: `markdown.tables`, `contextVisibility`, `responsePrefix`, and `textChunkLimit`. Users configuring Mattermost via the docs cannot discover these options or their accepted values and defaults.

## Why This Change Was Made

These four keys are all live: the Mattermost channel resolves them at runtime and has regression tests for them. The channel guide simply omits them. Adding them makes the Mattermost reference complete for the shared channel schema and matches the wording already used for the same keys in sibling channels (e.g. `contextVisibility` and `responsePrefix` in the shared channel config).

## User Impact

Users can now look up the correct shape, allowed values, and runtime defaults for Mattermost's table rendering (`markdown.tables`), supplemental-context visibility (`contextVisibility`), reply-prefix (`responsePrefix`), and message chunking (`textChunkLimit`) settings without reading source. No behavior changes.

## Evidence

**Schema** — `extensions/mattermost/src/config-schema-core.ts` (`MattermostAccountSchemaBase`, lines 99–122) declares all four keys:

```typescript
markdown: MarkdownConfigSchema,                    // line 99
contextVisibility: ContextVisibilityModeSchema.optional(),  // line 102
textChunkLimit: z.number().int().positive().optional(),     // line 118
responsePrefix: z.string().optional(),                       // line 122
```

**Runtime type** — `markdown.tables` uses the shared `MarkdownConfigSchema` in `src/config/zod-schema.core.ts` (line 489), whose `tables` leaf is `z.enum(["off", "bullets", "code", "block"])`. `contextVisibility` uses the shared `ContextVisibilityModeSchema` in `src/config/zod-schema.core.ts` (line 449): `z.enum(["all", "allowlist", "allowlist_quote"])`.

**Default** — `markdown.tables` resolves to the Mattermost plugin's `defaultMarkdownTableMode: "off"` (`extensions/mattermost/src/channel.ts:568`); `resolveMarkdownTableMode` prefers the loaded plugin default over its generic `"code"` fallback (`src/config/markdown-tables.ts:45`). `contextVisibility` falls back to `"all"` at runtime (`src/config/context-visibility.ts:46`). `textChunkLimit` falls back to `4000` (`monitor-event-plan.ts:108`, `slash-http.ts:632`). `responsePrefix` has no default.

**Consumer** — `markdown.tables` is resolved in `extensions/mattermost/src/mattermost/send.ts:250` (`resolveMarkdownTableMode`) and the plugin default is registered in `extensions/mattermost/src/channel.ts:568`. `contextVisibility` is resolved in `extensions/mattermost/src/mattermost/monitor-auth.ts:166` (`resolveChannelContextVisibilityMode`). `responsePrefix` is resolved in `extensions/mattermost/src/mattermost/monitor-turn.ts:258` (`resolveResponsePrefix`), expanding `auto` to the routed agent's `identity.name` via `resolveIdentityNamePrefix` (`src/agents/identity.ts:34`), bracketed (e.g. `[Support]`), with no prefix when no agent identity name is set. `textChunkLimit` is read in `extensions/mattermost/src/mattermost/accounts.ts:124` and applied as a fallback limit in `monitor-event-plan.ts:108` and `slash-http.ts:632`.

**Test** — `markdown.tables` default is covered in `src/config/markdown-tables.test.ts:26` (`resolveMarkdownTableMode({ channel: "mattermost" })` → `"off"`) and in `extensions/mattermost/src/mattermost/send.test.ts:29`; `contextVisibility` in `extensions/mattermost/src/mattermost/monitor-posts.thread-history.test.ts:304/316` and `monitor.inbound-system-event.test.ts:686-906`; `responsePrefix` and `textChunkLimit` in `extensions/mattermost/src/mattermost/monitor.inbound-system-event.test.ts:181/350`.

**Docs toolchain**
- `pnpm format:docs:check` — 1,411 files, clean

**Proof boundary** — this is a documentation discoverability fix; the Mattermost implementation is unchanged. No runtime behavior proof applies.

**Exact head** — `910cabea3e2527e014b5cd529912f9d8cf5fe5f9`

prs.title: docs(telegram): document ingest and disableAudioPreflight group options
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`extensions/telegram/src/config-schema.ts` defines two per-group/per-topic options for handling messages that do not mention the bot, but `docs/channels/telegram/access-control.md` does not document either of them. Users configuring group behavior via the docs cannot discover `ingest` or `disableAudioPreflight`.

- **Problem**: Two real, runtime-consumed Telegram group options are undocumented.
- **Solution**: Document both options with config examples in the "Mention behavior" tab of `access-control.md`.
- **What changed**: `docs/channels/telegram/access-control.md` (2 fields added).
- **What did NOT change**: No code or behavior changes. Documentation only.

**Missing fields**:
1. **`ingest`** (`boolean`, default: `false`) — deliver mention-skipped group messages through the internal `message:received` hook without starting an agent turn. Available at both group and topic level.
2. **`disableAudioPreflight`** (`boolean`, default: `false`) — skip the preflight audio transcription that otherwise runs when a mention-required group receives audio without text. Available at both group and topic level, inherited topic → group.

## Why This Change Was Made

Both options control how Telegram group traffic behaves when `requireMention` is on, which is the default access-control mode. `ingest` decides whether mention-skipped messages are additionally delivered to the `message:received` internal hook (they are already retained in group history by default). `disableAudioPreflight` lets operators avoid the preflight transcription of audio-only group messages that never trigger a turn. Documenting them makes the documented group configuration surface match the runtime config schema.

## User Impact

Users who configure `channels.telegram.groups.<id>` or `channels.telegram.groups.<id>.topics.<topic>` can now discover and use `ingest` and `disableAudioPreflight` from the docs instead of guessing from the schema. The examples match the existing `requireMention`/`requireMentionInBotThreads` configuration style already documented in the same tab. No behavior changes — this is documentation only.

## Evidence

**Schema** — `extensions/telegram/src/config-schema.ts` declares both fields on the topic schema (lines 88–89) and the group schema (lines 102–103):

```typescript
// TelegramTopicSchema
ingest: z.boolean().optional(),
disableAudioPreflight: z.boolean().optional(),

// TelegramGroupSchema (buildGroupEntrySchema)
ingest: z.boolean().optional(),
disableAudioPreflight: z.boolean().optional(),
```

**Runtime type** — both are `z.boolean().optional()`, resolved as `=== true` at read time, so the effective default is `false`.

## What Problem This Solves

The shared config reference (`docs/gateway/config-channels/community-chat.md`) states that Discord preview streaming defaults to `off` in two places. ## User Impact
