prs.title: docs(runtime): propose the shell-grammar binding row for the #11994 follow-up
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`.
- **What changed and why:**
  - #11994 reads POSIX commands in bash's grammar when bash runs them. Review there found that the policy cannot see which shell runs a command: the shell tool resolves `[runtime].shell` on the `PATH` a connected TUI forwards, while the policy can only inspect what it resolves itself. #11994 now applies bash's grammar only to an absolute configured path to bash with no possible container sandbox, and records the shell on `SecurityPolicy` from the same helper the runtime factory uses. That is safe, but it leaves two owners of the shell choice (Greptile's finding on #11994) and gives a bare `bash` the portable rules.
  - The fix that removes both limits is for the policy to check a command in the grammar of the program the runtime will spawn, without keeping its own copy of the shell. `RuntimeAdapter::shell_program()` already reports that program before resolution, so no `zeroclaw-api` change is needed. The shell tool, the shell-backed skill tool and the cron run-time recheck would pass it, and the effective `PATH`, to the policy before validation. The policy resolves the program without building anything, and `SecurityPolicy::native_shell` goes away.
  - **Policy stays ahead of building (#9182).** The command is built only after the policy accepts it, so a refused command never reaches the runtime's builder. Before spawning, the policy confirms the built command's program: if it checked the command in bash's grammar and the built program is not bash, it refuses.
  - That changes four holding-crate files, which needs a recorded exception under ADR-016. This adds one row for it, after the last row. Every existing row is unchanged.
  - **Amended after the first approval:** the first wording (5ef4a8dac2) had these callers build the command before validating it, which reverses #9182. 8c6bc005d9 changes the row to the order above, with the same files and limits. It needs re-approval.
- **Scope boundary:** The table in `crates/zeroclaw-runtime/AGENTS.md` only. No code. The row keeps the policy, the grammar, the container-sandbox decision and executable resolution in `zeroclaw-config`. It permits no `zeroclaw-api` or `Sandbox` trait change, new tool, approval, sandbox or allowlist authority, config key, retained state, or user-facing text.
- **Blast radius:** Merge eligibility of the #11994 follow-up's runtime changes under ADR-016.
- **Linked issue(s):** Related #11994, Related #11822, Related #10557, Related #9182

### What this does, simply

ZeroClaw's runtime crate is a holding crate: new work there needs a recorded Core Team decision. To check a command in the right shell's grammar, the policy needs to know exactly which shell will run it, and only the runtime knows that, at the moment it builds the command. This row asks permission for the shell tool, skill tool and cron runner to tell the policy which shell they will run before it checks a command, and to show it the program they built before the command runs. The policy keeps every decision, and still checks every command before anything is built; the runtime only reports its shell and what it built.

### The planned follow-up

- `zeroclaw-config` (no exception needed): `SecurityPolicy::shell_target(dialect, shell_program, effective_path)` resolves the runtime's shell program without building anything and returns the grammar to check in. It is bash only when the resolved file is named `bash` and no container sandbox is possible (Docker runs its image's program at the configured name). `SecurityPolicy::confirm_shell_target` checks the built program afterwards. The `*_for_target` checks read the target. With no program, the grammar is portable. `SecurityPolicy::native_shell` and the recorded copy are removed.
- `src/tools/shell.rs`: work out the target from `shell_program()` and the forwarded `PATH`, validate, build only after the policy accepts, confirm the built program, then wrap and spawn.
- `src/tools/skill_tool.rs`: the same order around `build_shell_command`.
- `src/cron/mod.rs`: a `validate_shell_command_for_target` helper. Job creation keeps the portable grammar, which is stricter, never looser.
- `src/cron/scheduler.rs`: the run-time recheck works out its targets from `shell_program()`, validates, builds, then confirms.
- Focused regressions:
  - A bare `bash` that resolves to bash on the effective `PATH` gets bash's grammar.
  - A bare `bash` that resolves to another shell, a relinked launcher, a Docker or `auto` sandbox, and the Docker runtime keep the portable grammar.
  - A refused command is never built, and #9182's scheduler test stays unchanged.
  - A built program that differs from the predicted bash is refused before it runs.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** Yes, for scope: check that the row names every runtime path the follow-up above touches, and nothing broader.
- **Expected on this branch (after):** One added row with four cells; every existing table line unchanged.

### How I tested

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** The repository checks on the changed file.
- **Commands run and tail output:** `git diff --stat origin/master` shows `crates/zeroclaw-runtime/AGENTS.md | 1 +`, with no line removed. Every row in the table has four cells. The row's paths are the runtime callers that validate a POSIX command and then build it for spawning (`rg 'validate_command_execution_for_shell|forbidden_.*for_shell|forbidden_path_argument\('` outside `zeroclaw-config`).
- **If any command was intentionally skipped, why:** No build or tests: no code changes. `scripts/ci/docs_quality_gate.sh` covers only `docs/book/src/**` and skips this file.

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? Yes, if Core approves: the row permits the named reordering in the holding crate. It grants no runtime authority. The follow-up only makes the policy read the program that will actually run, checked before building and confirmed before spawning. Where that program is unknown, the policy keeps the stricter portable rules.
- New external network calls? No
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? No
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? No
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? No

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? Yes
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? No
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? No

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)

Revert the commit. If the follow-up has merged by then, the code it covers stays; reverting withdraws the permission for further additions under this row.

prs.title: fix(cli): publish authorization edits from config set and config patch into the running daemon
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`
- **What changed and why:**
  - `zeroclaw config set` and `zeroclaw config patch` saved `config.toml` and printed "updated" while a running daemon kept enforcing the previous authorization policy until someone reloaded it. When an edit writes or changes an authorization input (`[users]`, `[permission_profiles]`, `[oidc]`, `security.trust_daemon_uid`) and this configuration's daemon is running, the CLI now commits the edit through the daemon's own RPC config path (`config/set`, or `config/set-many` for a patch). The daemon's admitted config commit (`begin_config_commit`, then `save_and_publish_config`) already validates the policy, saves the file and publishes the new configuration and the next accepted authorization revision under the process-wide config writer lock, so the policy is in force before the CLI reports success and established connections re-resolve at their next operation. Nothing is reloaded and no connection is dropped. A `--comment` travels with the edit and the daemon writes it under the same lock, so the CLI does not touch `config.toml` after the daemon saved it.
  - The CLI only talks to the daemon that belongs to its configuration directory. That daemon counts as running while its heartbeat file beside `config.toml` is recent and names a live process. Before anything is written to the socket, the peer must be this account or root and, where the kernel reports it, the peer process must be the one the heartbeat names; otherwise the pid the daemon reports at `initialize` must match. With no confirmed daemon the CLI contacts no endpoint (an exported `ZEROCLAW_SOCKET` included), but it does probe the configuration's ownership lock: if another process holds it (a daemon still starting, before its first heartbeat, a standalone `zeroclaw gateway start`, or a `zeroclaw agent` session), the edit is saved and reported pending instead of passing silently. On Windows the CLI does not verify a named pipe's server, so it never sends an authorization edit there and reports it pending.
  - A refusal is judged by phase. When the daemon refuses the caller at the handshake (a uid outside the roster, the deny-all state), the CLI keeps its direct write and reports the edit as **pending reload**; that is the lockout-recovery path. When the daemon identifies the caller and then refuses the edit (its principal lacks the config-write grant), the command fails and nothing is saved. Pending is also reported, with the reason on stderr and as a `daemon` member in the `--json` envelope, when the daemon runs another release, fails the handshake, cannot be reached, is not this configuration's daemon, or for writes its config methods do not take (clearing a secret, creating a keyed-list row, a patch over the 256-entry batch cap). Before a pending local save, the CLI retains the effective-policy check for a daemon that shares its environment and also validates the actual persisted baseline and final TOML produced by the canonical writer, after environment masking, secret-reference restoration and dirty-path merging. Each check refuses an edit that turns its working policy into one that does not compile; an already-broken policy remains repairable in steps. Validation of the saved policy uses the writer's real merged bytes, including non-dirty file values changed since CLI staging. When the daemon rejects the edit, or is asked and never answers, the command fails and nothing is saved. A `config patch` that the daemon would apply fails before the daemon is asked if it carries any `test` op, whatever path it checks, because the `test` would be checked against the CLI's on-disk copy while every write in the patch lands on the daemon's live configuration.
  - Whether an edit is an authorization edit is decided by path (`is_auth_input_path`) or by a change in `auth_inputs`, the comparison the daemon's own publication makes, so re-asserting a value that is only on disk still reaches the daemon. The CLI owns `is_auth_input_path` privately in `src/config_publication.rs` and consumes canonical `auth_inputs` from `zeroclaw_runtime::rpc::auth`. Its guard test walks every configuration property and fails when changing a property moves `auth_inputs` without `is_auth_input_path` covering it, so adding a new authorization input cannot leave the path list behind. The CLI also owns its private heartbeat reader and freshness check, using the runtime writer's canonical state-file path and flush interval, and the daemon's refusal to overwrite a secret with a placeholder is one function (`refuses_secret_placeholder`) that both the daemon and the CLI call. Edits outside the authorization inputs never contact the daemon and their output is unchanged. `config init` never commits authorization entries through the daemon: while one runs it reports such an entry as pending, and refuses one that cannot compile until filled in (`users.<name>`, `oidc.<alias>`).
  - The authentication guide documents the full contract next to the `--json` reason codes, and no longer describes dashboard writes as reload-bound (since the supervised gateway and RPC share one authority and one live configuration, a stale statement this PR corrects deliberately); the config lifecycle and gateway API pages summarize it and link there.
- **Scope boundary:** No change to what the daemon accepts, publishes or writes, and no new RPC method. The CLI never triggers a reload. Edits outside the four authorization inputs keep their reload-bound semantics. `config migrate`, the alias helpers and the model helpers are unchanged. A standalone `zeroclaw gateway start` (like `zeroclaw agent`) holds the ownership lock without writing a heartbeat, so an authorization edit made while it runs is reported pending (`owner_unconfirmed`); it publishes its own config-API edits and picks up CLI and hand edits at its restart. `config set` still does not run the full `Config::validate()` when no daemon runs (tracked separately). The ownership lock is probed, not held: holding it from `config set` would make a daemon that starts at that moment refuse to run. The identity-checked client stays in the CLI for now; moving it into `zeroclaw_runtime::rpc::local` so `route_agent_mutation` and the shared RPC client crate can use it is #11324. Verifying a Windows named pipe's server process so Windows can publish live is #11325.
- **Blast radius:** an additive `Config::save_dirty_with_validation` callback in the existing config writer, used by pending CLI authorization saves; ordinary save methods retain their behavior. The callback receives the actual original/final documents and refuses before the atomic writer creates a backup or temporary file. It replaces the separate saved-policy preview/cache while retaining the existing effective-policy guard. Also the `config set`, `config patch` and `config init` arms in `src/main.rs` and two new modules beside it; in the runtime, the existing `auth_inputs` made public (`rpc/auth.rs`), `refuses_secret_placeholder` extracted from `stage_config_set` with identical behavior and `CONFIG_SET_MANY_MAX_ENTRIES` made `pub const` (`rpc/dispatch.rs`), and the existing heartbeat writer interval `STATUS_FLUSH_SECONDS` exposed (`daemon/mod.rs`, writer unchanged); the new heartbeat reader and auth-path classifier stay private to the CLI consumer; English Fluent keys only; four book pages. Built on #10621, which landed first: agent-targeting paths keep its routing through `route_agent_mutation`, and authorization paths, which it does not route, take this PR's. They use separate one-shot clients for now: `call_local` neither verifies which process serves the socket nor separates a refusal at the handshake from a refused request, a rejected edit and an unanswered request, and this issue needs those distinctions (#11324 tracks consolidating them).
- **Linked issue(s):** Closes #10876. Closes #11323 (implements the decision recorded in this PR's review: an identified principal's refused edit fails; the save-and-pending fallback stays for refusals at the handshake). Related #11324, #11325, #11202, #10621, #11186, #10320, #10892.

### What this does, simply

ZeroClaw's roster and permission profiles decide who may do what over the daemon's RPC socket. The daemon recompiles that policy whenever a config write goes through it, which is what zerocode's config editor and the web dashboard do. The command line did not: `zeroclaw config set users.alice.permission_profiles reader` rewrote the file and said "updated" while the daemon, which had never been told, kept alice's old, wider grants until someone reloaded it.

Now the command hands such an edit to the running daemon, which applies and publishes it before the command says it succeeded. If the daemon identifies the user and refuses the edit, the command fails and saves nothing. If the daemon cannot be reached, or cannot identify the user at all (the way out of a lockout), the command still saves the file as before but says plainly that the daemon is still enforcing the previous policy and that the change waits for the next reload or restart. It refuses to save an edit that would leave a working policy unable to load. Edits to anything other than the authorization sections behave exactly as they did.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** Yes, one A/B if you want to see it by hand; the same scenarios are automated in `tests/component/config_auth_publication_cli.rs`.
- **Interface(s) exercised:** `cli` against a supervised daemon's local socket.
- **Setup / preconditions:** a config with `[security] trust_daemon_uid = false`, `[permission_profiles.admin] admin = true`, `[permission_profiles.reader] grants = { sessions = ["read"], config = ["read"] }`, and `[users.me] uid = <your uid>, permission_profiles = ["admin"]`; `zeroclaw daemon` running from it.
- **Steps to run:** keep a zerocode session (or a raw socket client) connected and confirm `config/set` is permitted; run `zeroclaw config set --no-interactive users.me.permission_profiles reader`; retry `config/set` on the open connection; then run `zeroclaw config set --no-interactive permission_profiles.reader.admin true`.
- **Expected on this branch (after):** stderr says the change was applied to the running daemon; the open connection's next `config/set` is refused (`-32012`), a fresh connection binds as the reader, and `config.toml` holds `["reader"]`. The reader's attempt to grant itself admin then fails with a non-zero exit and leaves `config.toml` unchanged.
- **Prior behavior on `master` (before):** the CLI prints only "updated"; the open connection keeps admin and a fresh connection still binds as admin until `config/reload` or a restart; the second command saves `admin = true` for the next restart.

### How I tested

#### Review follow-up: `f3060f7a7cdba2aae42fae37b23c4e138934f5d0`

This head adds one commit on `1068365f74` for JordanTheJet's re-review notes, with no behavior change. In the authentication guide's Recovery section, the sentence on a roster principal without the config-write grant no longer reads as an authorization guarantee: the daemon still identifies that principal and refuses the edit, so the command fails and saves nothing, but the refusal does not guard the file, and the file's owner can still change `config.toml` directly, effective at the next reload or restart. The guide's named-pipe note now says the CLI does not yet verify which process serves a pipe, so on Windows `config set` and `config patch` save each authorization edit themselves and report it pending (`unverified_endpoint`). In `src/config_publication.rs`, the ownership-lock probe in `daemon_presence` now says at the call that its side effects are accepted, the same ones an offline alias mutation has: a daemon launched in that instant fails to start, and a missing lock file or directory is created.

On this revision, `cargo fmt --all -- --check`, `cargo clippy -p zeroclaw --all-targets -- -D warnings`, `cargo doc -p zeroclaw --no-deps`, and the comment hygiene, docs quality and docs links gates (all four book pages) pass. The Rust change is a comment, so the test runs recorded for `1068365f74` below cover this head's code. Hosted checks on the new head remain required.

#### Current master merge: `1068365f74ba5591bef16091bcb5d014021ec152`

This head merges master `afd6cf912e413c36a8ba7b23c55bb66d48e52782` into `3d9f95d880` after the PR left the merge queue on a conflict. The conflicts were all in documentation: master's #11268 aligned the gateway policy publication docs while this PR was open, and described `zeroclaw config set` authorization writes as disk-only, which this PR changes. Its new table rows, wording and shared-authority detail are kept, and only the claims this PR makes false are dropped: the "including authorization sections" clauses in the config-lifecycle table, the lifecycle "Saved vs applied" paragraph and the runtime-state persistence table (a clean merge that needed the same correction), and the sentence that CLI authorization writes apply at the next reload. The gateway and RPC sharing sentence takes master's wording. The authorization section keeps this PR's contract, with master's points on shared authority, publication before success and the pending-reload flag folded in. The five code files this PR shares with master merged without conflicts; master did not change the heartbeat format or the `config/set` staging rules the CLI relies on.

On this revision (macOS arm64, rustc 1.98.0), with `<cli-only>` the `cargo run -p xtask --bin generate -- features --selection cli-only` set that CI's CLI-only job builds:

```text

cargo test -p zeroclaw-config --lib
# 1984 passed; 1 failed: policy::tests::unix_foreign_null_spellings_get_no_filesystem_exception, the known macOS case-insensitive APFS EEXIST that #11646 fixes; policy.rs is identical to master.
cargo clippy -p zeroclaw-config --all-targets -- -D warnings
cargo test -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib -- rpc::auth:: rpc::dispatch::tests::refuses_secret_placeholder
# 34 passed; 0 failed.
cargo test -p zeroclaw --bin zeroclaw -- daemon_rpc:: config_publication:: config_set_ config_init_ config_patch
# 61 passed; 0 failed; 64 passed under <cli-only>.
cargo test -p zeroclaw --test component config_auth_publication -- --test-threads=1
# 33 passed; 0 failed, using real daemon/CLI boundaries; 33 passed under <cli-only> too.
cargo test -p zeroclaw --test component config_patch_cli
# 25 passed; 0 failed.
cargo test -p zeroclaw --test architecture
# 86 passed; 0 failed.
cargo clippy -p zeroclaw --all-targets -- -D warnings     # default and <cli-only> features
cargo doc -p zeroclaw -p zeroclaw-config --no-deps
cargo check -p zeroclaw --no-default-features

```

Hosted checks on the new head remain required.

#### Earlier master merge: `3d9f95d8804dc3cfe912f2c0c80ac24baf9fa457`

This head merges master `88872e986627772c3e3dd68622c27dacf40366d0` (the app's host-side merge `f1468f34c0`) and then the pushed head `09981ee44f`, so the branch moved forward without a rewrite. The one conflict was in `Config::save_impl`, where master's #11218 now builds the saved document from `(doc, retired)` (the retired-keys policy and the written-spelling checks) while this branch validates the exact document before the atomic write. Master's construction is kept, and `validate` runs on the final TOML just before `write_config_atomically`, receiving the file read at the start of the save, or `None` when there was none. In `save_dirty_with_validation`, master's incremental save now carries a V1 or V2 file through the structural migration and replaces `existing` with the rewrite; the callback still receives the file as it stood on disk, which its contract promises and which the persisted-policy check migrates the way a load does. The new test `save_dirty_with_validation_sees_a_v2_file_as_it_stood` covers that case and fails against the plain auto-merge.

On this revision (macOS arm64, rustc 1.98.0), with `<cli-only>` the `cargo run -p xtask --bin generate -- features --selection cli-only` set that CI's CLI-only job builds:

```text

cargo test -p zeroclaw-config --lib -- save_dirty
# 35 passed; 0 failed, including the new test.
cargo clippy -p zeroclaw-config --all-targets -- -D warnings
cargo test -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib -- rpc::auth:: rpc::dispatch::tests::refuses_secret_placeholder
# 34 passed; 0 failed.
cargo test -p zeroclaw --bin zeroclaw -- daemon_rpc:: config_publication:: config_set_ config_init_ config_patch
# 61 passed; 0 failed; 64 passed under <cli-only>.
cargo test -p zeroclaw --test component config_auth_publication -- --test-threads=1
# 33 passed; 0 failed, using real daemon/CLI boundaries; 33 passed under <cli-only> too.
cargo test -p zeroclaw --test component config_patch_cli
# 25 passed; 0 failed.
cargo test -p zeroclaw --test architecture
# 84 passed; 0 failed.
cargo clippy -p zeroclaw --all-targets -- -D warnings     # default and <cli-only> features
cargo doc -p zeroclaw -p zeroclaw-config --no-deps

```

The full `cargo test -p zeroclaw-config --lib` ran on the merge just before the new test was added: 1954 passed and 1 failed, `policy::tests::unix_foreign_null_spellings_get_no_filesystem_exception`, the known macOS case-insensitive APFS `EEXIST` that #11646 fixes; `policy.rs` is identical to master and Linux CI does not hit it. The new test is the only change since, so the root crate results above hold for this head. Hosted checks on the new head remain required.

#### Earlier writer-boundary repair: `09981ee44fd430777b46d7892a9fa2c97981e792`

This additive follow-up preserves `1bef746eac25dab099a36227239eec9d24e26bf7`'s two-policy contract and fixes a separate merge race. The file initially contains `me.uid=1000` and `bob.uid=3000`; the CLI stages `bob.uid=2000`. While the CLI waits for the daemon handshake, another writer changes the non-dirty `me.uid` to `2000`. If the handshake refuses the unbound caller, the pending-save fallback previously checked its stale saved-policy preview and then merged the new file into duplicate `2000` uids. No environment override is needed. A mixed patch could also save its unrelated changes and report success.

The saved-policy check now runs inside the existing writer on its actual original and final TOML. The effective-policy guard is preserved, so a valid saved policy cannot excuse a collision in the CLI environment. Refusal leaves the file and dirty set unchanged and preserves the structured `validation_failed` response for the whole patch. Materialization can perform preparation before validation; the guard runs before the atomic writer's backup/temp/rename effects. This does not add locking against arbitrary external writers after materialization, change daemon publication, or change no-daemon saves.

Local validation used macOS arm64 and consistent Homebrew Rust/Cargo 1.97.1:

```text
cargo test --locked -p zeroclaw --test component config_auth_publication_cli -- --test-threads=4
# 33 passed; 0 failed, including real CLI processes at daemon, ownership-lock and scripted Unix-handshake boundaries.
cargo test --locked -p zeroclaw --bin zeroclaw -- daemon_rpc:: config_publication:: config_set_ config_init_ config_patch
# 61 passed; 0 failed.
cargo test --locked -p zeroclaw-config --lib -- save_dirty save_ env_override onepassword
# 64 passed; 0 failed.
cargo clippy --locked -p zeroclaw-config --all-targets -- -D warnings
cargo clippy --locked -p zeroclaw --bin zeroclaw --test component -- -D warnings
cargo clippy --locked -p zeroclaw --tests -- -D warnings
cargo fmt --all -- --check
bash scripts/ci/docs_quality_gate.sh
bash scripts/ci/docs_links_gate.sh
```

All checks passed. The final revision differs from the first fully tested candidate only by boxing one test fixture's save future to satisfy the additional test-target Clippy check. CLI units, both CLI lint selections, formatting and whitespace were rerun on the final commit; component/config tests, config Clippy and docs evidence cover byte-identical retained surfaces. The failed lint was corrected without suppression.

The three merge-race component cases, with tests only applied to source `1bef746eac25dab099a36227239eec9d24e26bf7`, produced two intended unsafe-write failures and one passing compatible-edit control. The order is established by receiving the actual CLI initialize request before changing the file, with no timing sleeps or production hooks. Writer tests also verify exact checked/written bytes, masked overrides, preserved non-dirty edits and no backup/temp or dirty-state change on refusal. Parser/drop, missing-file, stepwise-repair and dual-policy controls are covered.

The final repair and evidence received an independent review. Hosted checks on the new head remain required. Full-workspace local, native Windows, live-provider, CLI-only feature-set and plugin-matrix tests were not rerun for this follow-up; no dependency files changed. Earlier feature-specific evidence below belongs to its named revisions.

#### Earlier env-override repair: `1bef746eac25dab099a36227239eec9d24e26bf7`

This commit addresses [Greptile's env-override finding](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/pull/11313#discussion_r4433686859). A save writes back the value each `ZEROCLAW_*` override replaced, so while overrides set authorization inputs, the compile check before a pending local save now also compiles the configuration masked the way `save_dirty` masks it, and refuses, saving nothing, an edit that turns that policy from compiling into not compiling. The check of the policy the CLI sees is unchanged, and without overrides on authorization inputs the policy is still compiled once. Only `src/config_publication.rs` and one paragraph of the authentication page change. The new unit test `classify_local_save_judges_the_policy_config_toml_holds_without_env_overrides` covers the reported case (it fails with the new check disabled) and a control edit that is still saved and reported pending.

On this exact revision (macOS arm64, rustc 1.98.0), all of these passed. `<cli-only>` is the `cargo run -p xtask --bin generate -- features --selection cli-only` set that CI's CLI-only job builds:

```text

cargo test -p zeroclaw --bin zeroclaw -- daemon_rpc:: config_publication:: config_set_ config_init_ config_patch
# 58 passed; 0 failed.
cargo test --locked -p zeroclaw --no-default-features --features <cli-only> --bin zeroclaw -- (same filters)
# 61 passed; 0 failed.
cargo test -p zeroclaw --test component config_auth_publication -- --test-threads=1
# 23 passed; 0 failed, using real daemon/CLI boundaries; 23 passed under <cli-only> too.
cargo test -p zeroclaw --test component config_patch_cli
# 25 passed; 0 failed.
cargo test -p zeroclaw --test architecture
# 81 passed; 0 failed.
cargo clippy -p zeroclaw --all-targets -- -D warnings     # default and <cli-only> features
cargo doc -p zeroclaw --no-deps
cargo check -p zeroclaw --no-default-features
```

```text
$ zeroclaw config set --no-interactive permission_profiles.reader.admin true

--- stderr

--- exit 1

== 5. daemon stopped (its heartbeat file is still on disk): output as before this change
$ zeroclaw config set --no-interactive users.me.permission_profiles admin --json
```

</details>

- **Action or changed state and observed result:** step 2 narrows the caller through the CLI and the already-open connection is refused on its next `config/set`; steps 3 and 4 are that caller, now a reader the daemon identifies, trying to grant itself admin: the command fails, `config.toml` stays byte-identical and the live policy does not move; step 5 is unchanged output once the daemon has stopped.
- **If any command was intentionally skipped, why:** `cargo fluent check` builds xtask in release with fat LTO; every new key is rendered through the real Fluent path by unit tests instead (`notices_carry_their_evidence`, `commit_failures_name_the_reason_and_the_property_to_check`). `daemon::tests::a_live_config_write_reaches_the_daemon_pricing_refresher_without_a_reload` is skipped in the runtime filter: on master `f151c2e00d` without this change it fails the same way when it runs alongside the other `daemon::` tests, and it passes alone, so it is a pre-existing race between tests that share the process-wide pricing setting. The macOS-only unused import in `crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/service/mod.rs` predates this branch and affects only that crate's test build.

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? No. The CLI connects to the daemon's owner-only local socket, which it could already reach as the same account, and presents no credential; the daemon authorizes the connection by peer credential against its accepted policy exactly as it does for zerocode, including `selector_config_write` and the recheck under the write lock.
- New external network calls? No.
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? Yes. A value given to `config set` for `oidc.<alias>.client_secret` (or a secret inside a mixed `config patch`) now travels over the local socket to the daemon when the daemon commits the edit, as zerocode's config editor already sends it. It is written only after the peer uid and peer pid checks pass, never over a Windows named pipe, it is not logged, and the CLI's `--json` envelope keeps the `{path, populated}` shape for secrets.
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? No. Tests use the running test uid and synthetic names.
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? No.
- If any `Yes`, describe the risk and mitigation: the risk is a plaintext secret reaching an endpoint that is not this configuration's daemon. The uid check keeps it from another account's process; the pid check keeps it from another daemon of the same account (`config_set_refuses_to_publish_through_another_daemon`); with no running daemon for this configuration nothing is contacted (`config_set_ignores_another_daemon_when_this_configuration_has_none`); Windows never sends. A principal the daemon identifies cannot get around its verdict through this command: `config_set_refused_to_the_bound_principal_saves_nothing` proves a reader's attempt to grant itself admin exits non-zero, leaves `config.toml` byte-identical and leaves the live policy unchanged. That refusal is not a file permission: the account that owns `config.toml` can still change it directly, by hand or with a `config set` that cannot reach the daemon and is saved as pending (`unreachable`), and that applies at the next reload or restart, so file ownership stays the boundary, as it was before this PR. Only a refusal at the handshake keeps the file write, which the same OS account could already make by hand; that is the lockout-recovery path (`config_set_refused_at_the_handshake_is_saved_and_pending`, `config_set_repairs_a_deny_all_daemon_through_the_file`), and the CLI says the edit is not in force.

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? No, in four cases, all only while this configuration's daemon is running. (1) An authorization edit the daemon refuses for a principal it identified, for example a reader granting itself admin, now exits non-zero with nothing saved, where it used to save and exit 0; an edit refused at the handshake (a uid outside the roster, the deny-all state) still saves and exits 0, reported as pending with reason `refused`. (2) An authorization edit that would turn a compiling policy into one that does not (for example `config set users.bob.uid 1002` for a new entry with no `permission_profiles`, or `config init users.bob`) now fails with nothing saved instead of saving a state the next reload would turn into deny-all. (3) A `config patch` with a `test` op, on any path, fails when the daemon would apply it. (4) A `config patch` that touches the authorization sections is applied by the daemon as one batch, so its other paths also take the RPC apply boundary instead of waiting for a reload. With no daemon running, `config set`, `config patch` and `config init` are unchanged.
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? Yes: exit status as above; a stderr notice on authorization edits while a daemon runs (none with `--json`); and an optional `daemon` member in the `--json` envelopes of `config set`, `config patch` and `config init`: `{"applied": true}` or `{"applied": false, "pending_reload": true, "reason": ...}` with the reasons `refused`, `version_mismatch`, `handshake`, `unreachable`, `other_daemon`, `unverified_endpoint`, `owner_unconfirmed`, `not_replayable`, `offline_command` (documented in the authentication guide). Existing members are unchanged.
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? No.
- If backward compatibility is `No` or either surface/floor question is `Yes`: exact upgrade steps for existing users: none. Scripts that create a roster or OIDC entry field by field with `config set` or `config init` while the daemon runs should send the fields in one `config patch`; scripts that relied on a refused CLI edit still landing at the next restart should make the edit as an account with the config-write grant.

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)

- **Fast rollback command/path:** after landing, revert the landed PR commit and reconcile dependent work. Reverting only `09981ee44fd430777b46d7892a9fa2c97981e792` restores the preceding saved-policy preview and its demonstrated dirty-merge race while retaining the earlier effective-policy behavior. No schema/data migration is introduced by this repair.
- **Feature flags or config toggles:** None.
- **Observable failure symptoms:** an authorization `config set` that reports `pending_reload` with reason `other_daemon`, `owner_unconfirmed` or `unreachable` while the daemon is healthy; a `config set` that waits up to about 38 s on a stuck daemon before failing with an unknown outcome; `RPC authorization denied` audit lines on the daemon for a CLI caller. `grep 'did not answer an authorization edit'` in the CLI's trace output catches the unknown-outcome case.

milestone.description:
v0.9.0 prioritizes opt-in OIDC dashboard sign-in, principal isolation, schema V4 and a CLI-only build option.

The standard build keeps the working in-process dashboard. Sign-in stays off by default, preserving the existing pairing flow. Release gates are real-provider sign-in evidence; the five principal-isolation repairs (#11234, #11220, #11225, #11230, #11266, with #11198 tracked); schema V4 (#11218); and a build-time CLI-only option that omits gateway/web assets and directs dashboard users to the standard build.

Scoped dashboard chat has a November 3 go/no-go, with sign-in alone as the fallback. November 10 is the earliest target, subject to the gates, not a committed date.

Standalone zeroclaw-gw, full gateway IPC route/parity work, cross-process webhook handling and two-process desktop packaging move to v0.9.x. Channel listeners remain in core under existing documented exceptions. These deferrals do not complete the remaining gateway roadmap.

Source of truth: #7432 (https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/issues/7432), current release allocation. Existing implementation trackers keep their detailed work. Feature acceptance, current-head review/CI, recorded placement decisions and the v0.8.7-tag hold on breaking work remain in force.

prs.title: feat(gateway): scoped dashboard chat through the core, on a shared RPC client
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`. It builds on #11964 (the daemon retires orphaned remote sessions) and #12232 (tools that can't act as the caller are withheld from non-administrators); both have merged, and the branch has master `7666a52abf` merged in (6e00b1de6c, after #12270 landed). Current head: `6e00b1de6c`.
- **One PR in place of three.** This replaces #11165 (the RPC wire contract), #11186 (the RPC client and the in-process transport) and #11986 (scoped dashboard chat). It is cut fresh from master, with every review point on the three answered (listed below). The RPC pieces exist for the chat and are only used by it, so they land together. A runtime placement row approved in #11963 asks for exactly that: the in-process adapter must not merge ahead of its use.
- **Commits:**
  - **The RPC foundation (11):**
    - f25e96ea39 refactor(rpc): extract the wire contract into `zeroclaw-rpc-proto` with an OpenRPC drift check (from #11165);
    - 492ef50e4b feat(rpc): add `zeroclaw-rpc-client` and the in-process gateway transport (from #11186);
    - 44ac94d165 test(rpc): strengthen connector retirement regressions (by @Aarlington);
    - f67fa1c8fb fix(rpc): bound a request by its encoded frame before it is queued (by @IftekharUddin);
    - bc8818d167, f19359c8ed, 12966a5143, 0caf0cc94b, b3a4cf7a91, f284c7cc39 and 331d3abf0b: review follow-ups (a message, a doc, tests and their formatting).
  - **The chat (11):**
    - 28258e7010 feat(rpc): bind in-process connections to the provider their bearer came from;
    - 37ba342c46 feat(gateway): scoped dashboard chat through the core;
    - 195834a5ad feat(web): one conversation per chat socket for accounts chatting through the core;
    - a0e10317de docs(security): describe scoped dashboard chat and its limits;
    - then the review fixes: a2edf767bf, 654832760d, 1bb86b50a7, 32f33446df (by @IftekharUddin), 0bd93712ba, 63918008f7 and ed3d47bc79 (by @IftekharUddin).
  - **After opening (CI and review):**
    - cd0a6f1fa5 names the runtime's `zeroclaw-rpc-proto` edge in the composition consumer's retained-dependency policy;
    - 0919b0fe1a keeps a first message pending until it is sent (from the automated review);
    - da97348acd marks the generated OpenRPC document `linguist-generated`;
    - 6533ac3742 pins the stuck-write test's socket buffers to 64 KiB, because host TCP autotuning could hold the 7 MiB turn end.
  - **After #12232 landed:**
    - 762e37391a merges master, bringing in #12253 and #12232, with no conflicts;
    - 5c1753601a adds a gateway test: a member chat whose profile has `tools:execute` with wildcard tool and agent selectors is not offered `sessions_list`, `sessions_history` or `sessions_send`.
  - **Review rounds, 11-06 to 11-08:**
    - a473465de1, 6ac73ac8ac, f06e60c5aa and c5cdcd19e4 (by @IftekharUddin): scoped chat and config access in the web app, dashboard principal and session reads, the lost-result guidance, and integration with the landed orphan retirement;
    - f7fc03fd07: stop acting for a chat whose session ended mid-renewal (the sign-out gap @Audacity88 raised);
    - ce044b9f0d and 84ea4c77ab: keep a renewal or cleanup handshake cut short by sign-out charged until it ends (from @Aarlington's review);
    - 7473bb0264: merges master `641b766030`;
    - a8d68cab3a and f1b31d12e5: offer Retry when the scoped chat or the agents page can't load the agent list;
    - 630564be2a and d21b3bcbb5: refuse an agent that can't take turns (disabled, or without a model provider or risk profile; a runtime profile stays optional), from @IftekharUddin's disabled-agent finding;
    - 1525c9e97d: check the agent again once the chat's connection is verified (@Aarlington's handshake follow-up);
    - 6e00b1de6c: merges master `7666a52abf` after #12270 landed. The only conflict was `web/package.json`'s `test:auth` line, where both PRs add tests; it keeps both lists (16 entries). Nothing else changes.
- **Limit to know first: a scoped account's conversation ends with its socket.** Reloading the page, leaving the chat or signing out ends it, and the dashboard can't reopen it. This is deliberate for this release (details under the scope boundary below).
- **What changed and why:**
  - **The RPC wire contract has one home.** Its method table, params and result types, notifications and frame limit move from the runtime into `zeroclaw-rpc-proto`, a crate with no async I/O. The runtime re-exports them, so the wire is unchanged.
    - `cargo generate openrpc` writes `docs/book/src/architecture/zeroclaw-rpc.openrpc.json` from it.
    - The drift check fails when the document and the code disagree.
  - **A client for the daemon's RPC, and an in-process way to reach it.**
    - `zeroclaw-rpc-client` does the handshake, calls, notifications and reconnects, over the local socket or over a duplex inside the daemon.
    - The daemon's `InprocConnector` hands the supervised gateway such a duplex. Each connection authenticates as a socket client does, with no authority from being in-process, and is treated as remote for every local-only check.
    - A daemon reload seals the connector, drains its connections and releases the generation's context.
  - **Non-administrator accounts can now chat in the dashboard.** The daemon runs the chat as that account, under its grants, and keeps the conversation as that account's own. Administrators keep today's in-process chat and its history.
  - **Each chat socket is one conversation.**
    - The socket opens a daemon connection of its own through the in-process connector, presenting the token the account signed in with.
    - It creates one conversation there.
    - The conversation is closed (never deleted) when the socket closes, when the account signs out, shortly before its token expires, when it loses access, and at a daemon reload.
    - No other socket reopens it. So nothing about a conversation is shared between sockets: not its connection, not the identity the daemon holds it under, not its approvals.
  - **The daemon treats that connection as remote**, so it assigns the conversation's id, and only the connection that created a conversation can use it.
  - **At most four chats per sign-in, and 32 per account across its sign-ins.**
    - A conversation still being created, or not yet closed after its chat ended, counts. Signing out and in again therefore frees nothing until it is closed.
    - The chat holds its place from the start of its daemon handshake until it is done, including while the daemon is still verifying the token after the gateway stopped waiting.
    - A creation the chat stopped waiting for (after 10 minutes) stays counted until the daemon answers it. A conversation created after all is closed when the answer lands and then no longer counts.
    - A conversation whose close failed, or whose creation lost its connection before the answer, stays counted until the next reload, since its fate is unknown.
    - A chat past either limit is accepted, told `CONVERSATION_LIMIT` and closed with `4409`; no other tab's conversation is closed.
  - **The chat follows the account's current grants.** Every chat frame, and a periodic check while the socket is idle, requires the session grants a chat needs and its agent under the current policy. A policy that narrows either closes the socket with `4403` before anything else is acted on.
  - **A conversation the daemon finishes creating after its socket left is still closed.** The creation runs in a task of its own and waits as long as the daemon takes (MCP servers can make that longer than a request's usual deadline). Whatever it creates that nobody took, or creates after sign-out, is closed.
  - **The token goes only to the provider that issued it.**
    - Every connection a chat opens is bound to the sign-in's provider, as it was configured at sign-in: `InprocConnector::connect_bound`, verified with `authenticate_bound` in the daemon.
    - If the provider is repointed at another issuer or client, the chat is refused and the token is not sent there.
  - **Messages are bounded before they are read.** The chat socket refuses a frame, or a fragmented message as it is assembled, over the RPC frame limit (8 MiB). A prompt that fits the socket but not the encoded frame (escapes count) is refused by the client before it is queued, so the turn ends with `CORE_REFUSED` and the conversation carries on.
  - **A chat that ends stops its reply.** The browser leaving, sign-out or a reload closes the conversation at once, which cancels a turn under way. A turn end the socket can't deliver ends the chat the same way.
  - **The identity provider is asked once per chat.** Each chat's connection verifies the token once. The agent list is kept per sign-in for 30 s, under one policy generation only, and the account's current read grant decides on every request.
  - **Writes to the browser never hold up the end.** Every write gives up at sign-out or a reload, or after 10 s on a browser that stopped reading.
  - **A close survives a lost connection, a lapsed binding, or a send the client refused locally.** It is tried again on a new connection, with the chat's own identity and the token the chat kept.
  - **The chat is offered only to accounts that can use, read and close a conversation** (`sessions` create, read, execute and update). Its agent uses only the tools the account is granted.
  - **Dashboard chat for scoped accounts (web).** This applies to an account without the operator dashboard, or any session with `features.core_sessions`.
    - Opening the chat opens no socket. The first message does.
    - The composer stays disabled until the socket's `session_start` says the conversation exists, and only then does the first message go out. So nothing can be sent ahead of it, and a refusal at the conversation limit keeps the message for Retry.
    - If the socket closes before `session_start` for any other reason, the message goes back to the composer, ahead of anything typed since, and the send error is shown.
    - At the limit, the banner with its Retry is the only notice.
    - There is no history to load, no conversation list and no resume. The stop button aborts by the id from `session_start`.
    - Any close ends the conversation. The socket never reconnects, and the transcript stays on the page followed by a notice. The next message starts a new conversation on a new socket.
    - New conversation (`/new`, `/clear`) closes the current one and deletes nothing.
    - Administrators and paired browsers keep stored conversations as before.

### What this does, simply

**Someone who signs in to the dashboard without administrator rights can now chat** with the agents they're allowed to use. The agent runs as them: it uses their permissions, and nobody else's dashboard sees their conversations. If their permissions are narrowed while a chat is open, the chat closes.

**A conversation lasts as long as its chat.** Each chat window is one conversation. Closing or reloading the page, signing out, or a daemon restart ends it. The transcript is kept, but the dashboard can't reopen it.

**Each sign-in can have four chats open at once.** A fifth waits until one closes.

**Underneath, the dashboard now talks to the daemon the way other clients do,** through a shared RPC client, over a connection inside the process. The description of that protocol moves into its own small crate, from which a machine-readable document is generated and checked.

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- **New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope?** Yes. Non-admin dashboard accounts can chat through the daemon, under their own grants.
- **New external network calls?** No.
- **Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed?** Yes. The session's access token is presented to the in-process daemon connection.
- **PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs?** No. Test identities are synthetic.
- **Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed?** No.
- **Risk and mitigation:**
  - **The token** stays in memory only. Each chat keeps a copy until its conversation is closed, and the copies are wiped when dropped. No code in this PR logs or formats it, and `ConnectOptions` and `RpcClient` redact it in `Debug`. The handshake still copies it into `ConnectOptions` and the `initialize` frame as plain strings for the length of the handshake; wiping those is a follow-up (#12246).
  - **Bound to its provider.** The token is presented only on connections bound to the provider that issued it, checked by the daemon against the policy it would send the token under. A repointed provider never receives it.
  - **Remote, not local.** In-process connections get no authority from being in-process. They authenticate as socket clients do and are classed as remote for every local-only check: path attachments and chunked upload are refused.
  - **Grants at every step.** The gateway checks the chat's grants and agent before the socket opens and on every frame. The daemon re-checks grants at the current policy on every call.
  - **Size.** Chat input is bounded at the socket and again at the encoded frame, so a browser can't make the gateway buffer more than one frame or end the daemon connection with an oversized request.

The standard build keeps the working in-process dashboard. Sign-in stays off by default, preserving the existing pairing flow. Release gates are real-provider sign-in evidence; the five principal-isolation repairs (#11234, #11220, #11225, #11230, #11266, with #11198 tracked); schema V4 (#11218); and a build-time CLI-only option that omits gateway/web assets and directs dashboard users to the standard build.

Standalone zeroclaw-gw, full gateway IPC route/parity work, cross-process webhook handling and two-process desktop packaging move to v0.9.x. Channel listeners remain in core under existing documented exceptions. These deferrals do not complete the remaining gateway roadmap.

Source of truth: #7432 (https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/issues/7432), current release allocation. Existing implementation trackers keep their detailed work. Feature acceptance, current-head review/CI, recorded placement decisions and the v0.8.7-tag hold on breaking work remain in force.

prs.title: feat(gateway): scoped dashboard chat with review fixes
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`, refreshed through 2450c1775c97406b1d0293155c8ca3dad698a8f6.
- **What changed and why:**
  - Carry forward @JordanTheJet's scoped dashboard chat and shared RPC client/protocol work from #12244, preserving its complete commit ancestry and incorporated contributions.
  - Let a non-administrator dashboard account chat as its own principal, under its current grants, through a separate authenticated daemon connection for each socket. Administrators and paired browsers retain their existing chat path.
  - Finish the presentation follow-up: render `AGENT_NOT_DISPATCHABLE` through the dashboard catalogue in all 31 supported locales, retain the conversation after refusal, and add reproducible browser evidence for agent-list Retry and recovery.
  - Fix the adversarial-review blocker: check live session access and gateway shutdown before queued chat output, including the prompt-completion drain, so a busy stream cannot starve revocation checks.
- **Scope boundary:** The additional repairs cover dashboard error presentation and gateway chat revocation scheduling. Daemon/runtime implementation remains as carried from #12244. No cross-socket history restoration, scoped image upload/model switching, daemon-wide per-owner quotas, additional identity-provider support, or gateway process extraction.
- **Blast radius:** The RPC contract/client crates, runtime in-process transport and retirement wiring, scoped gateway chat/session routes, and dashboard chat. The added repairs change web error presentation and its browser regression, plus gateway output scheduling and authorization/backpressure regressions.
- **Linked issue(s):** Closes #11984. Supersedes #12244. Depends on #12297, which must be approved and merged first. Related #11963, #11964, #12232, #11965 and #7432. #11964 and #12232 are already merged and included.
- **Labels:** `risk:high`, `do-not-merge`, `release:v0.9.0`; path and size labels are maintained by automation.

## Issue and solution

Dashboard sign-in previously left scoped accounts without chat because the existing gateway chat used operator authority. The carried implementation gives each chat its own provider-bound daemon connection, pins the account's authenticated principal, and uses the daemon's existing session ownership and grants.

The execution bugs discussed on #12244 are already repaired in the retained head, 1525c9e97dd42e63b1bfd35c006cb9993b29a461: sign-out fences prompts and ordinary retries, and live agent eligibility is checked before connection, after authentication/reconnect, and before each prompt. This replacement does not claim those fixes as new work.

The presentation correction is [414257dda17f911c0188399fbc7fada6a757dee0](https://github.com/IftekharUddin/zeroclaw/commit/414257dda17f911c0188399fbc7fada6a757dee0). A refusal previously displayed the server's English string regardless of dashboard locale. It now displays catalogue text while allowing a later message on the same conversation. The preceding merge commit brings in `master` through #12286.

The revocation correction is [6eef55a74e](https://github.com/IftekharUddin/zeroclaw/commit/6eef55a74e108cf4b5a0af66bcc2dc92fe59cd95). A continuously queued response could win every biased-select poll, leaving the periodic permission check unpolled; the completion drain also bypassed that check. Both paths now poll the existing session watch and shutdown signal before each queued update. The check resolves current policy from the existing authority. The production recheck interval remains 60 seconds and an individual browser write remains bounded by the existing 10-second deadline. A write already in progress may finish before the next check; this does not promise instantaneous revocation.

The regressions use a real dashboard WebSocket, authenticated in-process daemon connection, and local synthetic OIDC/model servers. They revoke read, update, or agent access with queued output both during a running prompt and after core completion; require close code 4403 before the backlog drains; and verify that the conversation closes while history remains. An unchanged-access control receives all 32 chunks and the normal terminal result. The test clock is local to the fixture and does not add a production setting.

**Review and merge order:** #12297 records the principal pin separately from the feature, as requested in [the current review](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/pull/12244#pullrequestreview-5819564124). That amendment has independent Core approval (@Audacity88 on e6fa75597a) and must merge before this one; it is not merged yet. This replacement also needs two independent current-head Core approvals and reconciliation of the original review holds. The `do-not-merge` label preserves that hold; opening a replacement does not clear it. #12244 remains open for its history and discussion.

The combined size is inherited from the accepted placement boundary: the in-process adapter must land with its scoped-chat caller, not as unused runtime functionality. The two repairs can be reviewed separately through the commits above.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** Yes, for the scoped browser interaction and principal boundary.
- **Interface(s) exercised:** `web`, through the real dashboard's HTTP/WebSocket contracts.
- **Setup / preconditions:** For the full feature, configure dashboard OIDC sign-in and a non-administrator account granted an enabled agent plus session create/read/execute/update. For the reproducible UI smoke, use Node 24, install web dependencies, generate the API client, run the Vite server, and make Playwright available separately.
- **Steps to run:** Run `web/scripts/scoped-chat-smoke.cjs` against the Vite URL. It opens `/agents` and `/agent/support` with a failed agents response, clicks Retry after recovery, switches the persisted locale to Spanish, receives an unavailable-agent frame, and sends a later message on the same socket. For the revocation regression, run `cargo test --locked -p zeroclaw-gateway --lib queued_chat -- --nocapture`; its local servers need no external credentials. For full authorization review, use the retained gateway/runtime boundary tests and a configured provider.
- **Expected on this branch (after):** Both Retry controls recover, the Spanish refusal uses the catalogue, and a later message completes without a second conversation socket. The queued-output tests close revoked sockets with 4403 before the backlog drains, and authorized output completes normally.
- **Prior behavior on `master` (before):** Scoped dashboard chat is unavailable. Compared with #12244 at 1525c9e97d, the refusal used the English server text; the new regression fails on that presentation path. With the pre-fix relay from 414257dda1 restored, the new real-WebSocket regression fails because all 32 queued chunks are delivered before revocation. With only the drain ordering reverted, the helper regression times out because the permission watch is starved. This session did not rerun a complete live-provider A/B demonstration.

### How I tested

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** The revocation repair passed the full gateway library suite, strict gateway Clippy on all targets, formatting, and two failing negative controls. [CI Required Gate](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/actions/runs/42548377887/job/128941674961) passed on 6eef55a74e108cf4b5a0af66bcc2dc92fe59cd95, with all 46 applicable jobs successful. The [main test job](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/actions/runs/42548377887/job/128938241244) passed 20,350 tests (44 skipped), including all three new queued-output regressions and their six revocation cases. Hosted lint, runtime stress tests, platform, plugin, security and web checks passed. The prior web repair retains its local auth/session, build and browser evidence below.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** The browser smoke supplies deterministic HTTP/WebSocket fixtures; it does not re-prove real OIDC token validation, daemon authorization, multi-user isolation, or model/tool execution. The revocation regressions exercise the real gateway/session watch and daemon connection with synthetic local OIDC/model services and an accelerated fixture clock; they do not claim a live-provider timing demonstration. The previous live-provider evidence remains linked on #12244 with its original tested revisions.
- **Commands run and tail output:** New gateway repair at 6eef55a74e108cf4b5a0af66bcc2dc92fe59cd95:

```text
cargo fmt --all -- --check
passed

cargo clippy --locked -p zeroclaw-gateway --all-targets -- -D warnings
passed

cargo test --locked -p zeroclaw-gateway --lib
886 passed; 0 failed; 1 ignored

cargo test --locked -p zeroclaw-gateway --lib queued_chat -- --nocapture
3 passed; 0 failed (including six revocation cases)

Original-relay negative control
FAILED as expected: revocation waited for the backlog: 32 chunks

Update-first drain negative control
FAILED as expected: queued output cannot starve the actual permission watch
```

The existing ignored test is the slow sign-out-during-session-creation test, which is documented to run alone. The macOS linker emits an oversized `__eh_frame` warning for the gateway test binary; the unchanged 414257dda1 sources reproduce the same warning. Strict Clippy passed without warning suppression. Both negative-control source variants were restored before the full suite. Hosted Nextest marked two unchanged inherited-pipe subprocess tests as leaky; both passed. The three added gateway regressions have ordinary PASS results.

Prior web evidence at 414257dda17f911c0188399fbc7fada6a757dee0 (web files unchanged by the revocation repair):

```text
npm ci --ignore-scripts --no-audit --no-fund
added 226 packages

cargo run --locked --release -p xtask --bin web -- gen-api
Finished release profile
Generated api-generated.ts, api-descriptions.ts and api-enums.ts

npm run test:auth
210 tests passed across the invoked suites; 0 failed
Session lifecycle: 62 passed, 0 failed

npm run build

WEB_SMOKE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:43144 node scripts/scoped-chat-smoke.cjs
PASS: 12 dashboard states at 414257dda17f911c0188399fbc7fada6a757dee0
```

The commands ran on macOS arm64; web tests/build/browser checks used Node 24.21.0. The lifecycle regression failed before the presentation fix (61 passed, 1 failed) and passed after it. Existing `react-test-renderer` deprecation notices come from the unchanged test dependency. The Vite large-chunk warning also reproduces with the original #12244 production files restored; no warning was suppressed.

- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** Inspected the rendered Retry, localized-refusal and recovered-conversation states, source/author ancestry, and the separate placement wording. The browser asserts that no chat socket opens before sending, recovery uses one socket, no session-history listing occurs, and no page exception is raised.
- **Visual interface evidence:** Screenshots from the actual dashboard, with deterministic gateway-shaped fixtures.
- **Tested revision, interface, and evidence path:** 414257dda17f911c0188399fbc7fada6a757dee0, clean worktree; Chromium, 1280×800 and 390×844. Reproducer: `web/scripts/scoped-chat-smoke.cjs`.
- **Screenshot or exact-output evidence:** Attached below, with the run's states and viewport sizes.
- **Action or changed state and observed result:** Retry changes a failed agent-list load into the list/chat; an unavailable-agent frame renders in Spanish; a subsequent message completes on the existing conversation socket.
- **If any command was intentionally skipped, why:** Full workspace tests/Clippy were not duplicated locally; the changed gateway crate received full library tests and strict all-target Clippy. Hosted checks provide the broader workspace/platform coverage. The browser screenshots remain explicitly attributed to 414257dda1 because this gateway repair changes no web files.

<details>
<summary>Browser evidence on 414257dda1: Retry, recovery and localized refusal</summary>

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? **Yes, inherited:** scoped dashboard accounts gain chat under their own existing grants; the added repairs grant nothing and keep revocation checks ahead of queued output.
- New external network calls? **No new destinations or network mechanisms:** chat uses the configured authentication/provider/tool paths carried from #12244. Browser fixtures make no identity-provider or model call.
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? **Yes, inherited:** the session token authenticates its dedicated in-process daemon connection. Provider binding and canonical-principal pinning prevent presenting it to a repointed issuer or adopting another principal. Ordinary sign-out retries are fenced; cleanup can still close the owned conversation. Handshake-string zeroization remains #12246.
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? **No new private data:** browser accounts, agents and responses are synthetic. Original public contributor attribution is preserved.
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? **No change to handling:** scoped prompts use the existing agent/tool policy boundary; the added repairs change browser text and the scheduling of existing access checks.
- **Risk and mitigation:** in-process connections retain remote restrictions. Current grants and agent eligibility are checked at admission and prompts; periodic checks are polled even while output remains queued; account/session limits and encoded frame limits bound resource use. Each socket owns one conversation, which is closed rather than deleted when it ends.

**Retained limits:** conversations cannot be reopened from another socket. Gateway limits are four chats per sign-in and 32 per account, while the daemon's 64-session limit is shared (#12130). Failed cleanup relies on idle-orphan retirement; setting its timeout to zero disables retirement. Private-CA/extra-scope/resource-indicator/ES384 provider support remains outside this slice. Provider-outage, remaining token-copy and response/cache follow-ups remain #12096, #12245, #12246 and #12247. The inherited native-RPC/operator disabled-agent gap remains #12289; this change fences scoped dashboard chat.

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? **Yes:** sign-in stays off by default; administrator/paired-browser behavior and the RPC wire are retained.

- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? **No.**
- Upgrade steps: none beyond configuring the existing dashboard sign-in feature when desired.

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)

- **Fast rollback command/path:** Revert the landed squash commit. For the additional web repair alone, revert 414257dda17f911c0188399fbc7fada6a757dee0. Reverting 6eef55a74e108cf4b5a0af66bcc2dc92fe59cd95 alone undoes the scheduling repair and reintroduces the queued-output revocation defect; disable affected scoped chat while investigating instead.
- **Feature flags or config toggles:** Remove providers from `[gateway.dashboard_sign_in]` to disable sign-in and end its sessions/conversations. No new toggle is added.
- **Observable failure symptoms:** Scoped chat cannot open or reply, cleanup logs report that a dashboard conversation could not be closed, the daemon refuses sessions at its limit, the OpenRPC drift gate fails, or a revoked account continues receiving an entire queued response instead of an access-lost close.

## Supersede Attribution (required only when `Supersedes #` is used)

- **Superseded PRs + authors:** #12244 by @JordanTheJet. It carries the earlier #11165, #11186 and #11986 work by @JordanTheJet.
- **Scope materially carried forward:** The entire current #12244 implementation, RPC crates, gateway/runtime integration, tests and documentation. @IftekharUddin's incorporated connector/frame/composer/security fixes and @Aarlington's connector-retirement regressions remain under their original authorship.
- **`Co-authored-by` trailers added in commit messages for incorporated contributors?** **Yes.** Existing commit authors and trailers are preserved without rewriting. The presentation repair commit additionally credits @JordanTheJet and @Aarlington using public GitHub attribution addresses. The subsequent revocation repair preserves that history unchanged.
- **If `No`, why:** N/A.

prs.title: fix(oidc): hold the discovered authorization endpoint to the URL policy
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`. The commit is on 2450c1775c; the three master commits since then don't touch these files.
- **What changed and why:**
  - **The gap:** enrollment discovery holds `token_endpoint` and `device_authorization_endpoint` to `validate_discovered_endpoint`: https, or http on an exact loopback host, never with userinfo. It used `authorization_endpoint` as given. `pkce_start` only parsed it, yet that's the URL the gateway redirects the browser to (`/oidc/login/{alias}`, `/auth/sign-in/{alias}`) and the URL the CLI's browser enrollment hands to `open` or `xdg-open`.
  - **The fix:** `Enrollment::discovery` now checks `authorization_endpoint` with the same call, next to the device endpoint. As with the device endpoint, a document that advertises a bad one is refused for every flow before any request or authorize URL is built.
  - **A comment fix:** the `pkce_start` doc comment said RFC 8414 defaults an absent `code_challenge_methods_supported` to `plain`. Section 2 says omitted means the server doesn't support PKCE. The S256 check already refuses both cases; only the comment changes.
- **Scope boundary:**
  - **Unchanged:** the policy itself (`validate_discovered_endpoint`), the S256 check, the gateway, the CLI and the daemon's verification discovery (which already checks `jwks_uri` and `introspection_endpoint`).
  - **Nothing else is followed:** no other URL from a discovery document is read, so there's no `end_session_endpoint`, `userinfo_endpoint` or `revocation_endpoint` to cover.
  - **The device grant's `verification_uri`** comes from the device endpoint's answer, not from discovery. It's printed or returned to the caller and never opened, so it isn't changed here.
  - **Placement:** a fix inside the existing enrollment client in `zeroclaw-runtime`. It adds no functionality, so it needs no holding-crate exception row.
- **Blast radius:**
  - **Who calls it:** every `Enrollment` user: the CLI's browser, device and client-credentials enrollment, the gateway's enrollment relay (`/oidc/login/{alias}`, `/api/oidc/{alias}/device/*`), and the dashboard sign-in (`/auth/sign-in/{alias}`).
  - **What changes:** an issuer whose document advertises an `authorization_endpoint` outside the policy now fails discovery for those flows, with "discovery authorization_endpoint must use https (http is allowed only for an exact loopback host)" or "... must be an http(s) URL, got scheme '…'".
  - **Real issuers:** an https endpoint, or a test issuer on loopback, is unaffected. The hosted providers' discovery documents I checked (Google, Entra, Okta, Auth0, Cognito) all advertise https.
- **Linked issue(s):** Closes #12312

### What this does, simply

- **Background:** before you sign in with an identity provider, ZeroClaw reads a settings document the provider publishes, which lists its web addresses. ZeroClaw already required the addresses it sends secrets to to use HTTPS, or to stay on the same machine.
- **What was missing:** the address of the sign-in page itself, where your browser is sent to log in, wasn't checked that way.
- **What changes:** now it is. If the provider's document lists a plain-HTTP sign-in page on another machine, or something that isn't a web address at all, ZeroClaw refuses that provider's settings instead of sending you there. Real providers publish HTTPS addresses, so nothing changes for them.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** N/A. The change is one check in discovery, and the new tests drive `pkce_start`, `client_credentials` and `device_grant_start` against a mock issuer, which is the boundary the gateway and the CLI call.

### How I tested

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** `Test` runs the new enrollment tests, and `Lint` runs clippy at `ci-all`. I also ran the touched crate's gates myself (below).
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** none. The change is platform-independent Rust with unit tests.
- **Commands run and tail output** (Linux, Rust 1.98.0, this commit):

  ```text
  cargo fmt --all -- --check
  ```

v0.9.0 prioritizes opt-in OIDC dashboard sign-in, principal isolation, schema V4 and a CLI-only build option.

The standard build keeps the working in-process dashboard. Sign-in stays off by default, preserving the existing pairing flow. Release gates are real-provider sign-in evidence; the five principal-isolation repairs (#11234, #11220, #11225, #11230, #11266, with #11198 tracked); schema V4 (#11218); and a build-time CLI-only option that omits gateway/web assets and directs dashboard users to the standard build.

Scoped dashboard chat has a November 3 go/no-go, with sign-in alone as the fallback. November 10 is the earliest target, subject to the gates, not a committed date.

Standalone zeroclaw-gw, full gateway IPC route/parity work, cross-process webhook handling and two-process desktop packaging move to v0.9.x. Channel listeners remain in core under existing documented exceptions. These deferrals do not complete the remaining gateway roadmap.

Source of truth: #7432 (https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/issues/7432), current release allocation. Existing implementation trackers keep their detailed work. Feature acceptance, current-head review/CI, recorded placement decisions and the v0.8.7-tag hold on breaking work remain in force.
